title: Repair Notices: Tenant's 7-Day Remedies
bodyText:
Florida does not set a deadline for starting repairs.

Instead, a tenant's remedies start with a written notice. If Landlord materially fails to comply with the building, housing and health codes (or, where there are none, the structural and plumbing duties in Fla. Stat. §83.51(1)) or with material lease provisions, the tenant may deliver written notice specifying the problem and stating that the tenant intends to terminate. If Landlord has not complied within 7 days after delivery, the tenant may terminate the lease.

Promises Landlord makes in the lease beyond the statute, such as maintaining appliances, providing utilities or services, or broader repair duties, count as lease provisions for this purpose, so a material failure to keep them can also let the tenant end the lease, and the tenant may sue for damages for any lease breach.

Only for a failure to comply with the codes or the Fla. Stat. §83.51(1) duties (not for other lease promises), a tenant may instead give written notice specifying the problem and stating that the tenant intends to withhold rent; 7 days after delivery, the tenant may raise the material noncompliance as a complete defense to an eviction for nonpayment, and the court decides how much the rent is reduced for the lost value.

This notice may go to Landlord, the person designated to receive notices, a resident manager, or whoever collects the rent.

If the failure is due to causes beyond Landlord's control and Landlord keeps making every reasonable effort to fix it, the lease may be ended or altered: a tenant who vacates an untenantable unit owes no rent while it stays uninhabitable, and a tenant who stays in a unit that is not untenantable gets a proportional rent reduction.

Failures of the additional duties for apartment buildings and similar units (pest extermination, locks and keys, common areas, garbage removal, heat, running water and hot water, Fla. Stat. §83.51(2)) cannot be raised as a defense to an eviction for possession.

title: Self-Help Eviction and Other Prohibited Practices
bodyText: A Florida landlord may not cut off or interrupt any utility service to a tenant (including water, heat, light, electricity, gas, elevator, garbage collection or refrigeration), whether or not the landlord controls or pays for it. A landlord may not keep a tenant out by changing the locks or using a bootlock or similar device, and may not remove outside doors, locks, roof, walls or windows except for maintenance, repair or replacement. A landlord may not remove a tenant's belongings except after surrender, abandonment, the death of the last remaining tenant as the statute provides, or a lawful eviction. A landlord may not discriminate against a servicemember in renting or in lease terms, and may not stop a tenant from respectfully displaying one portable, removable cloth or plastic United States flag up to 4.5 by 6 feet, whatever the lease says. A violation makes the landlord liable for the tenant's actual and consequential damages or 3 months' rent, whichever is greater, plus costs and attorney's fees; repeated violations that are not part of the same incident are separate awards. The only lawful way to remove a tenant is a court action for possession, followed by a writ executed by the sheriff.

title: Retaliation
bodyText: A Florida landlord may not discriminatorily raise a tenant's rent, reduce services, or bring or threaten an eviction or other lawsuit primarily in retaliation against a tenant who acted in good faith. Protected conduct includes complaining to a code-enforcement agency, organizing or joining a tenant organization, giving the landlord a 7-day notice of noncompliance, a servicemember's lawful early termination, paying rent to a condominium, cooperative or homeowners' association on its demand, and exercising fair housing rights. The tenant must show different treatment as to rent, services or the action taken. Retaliation is a defense to eviction, but not if the landlord proves the eviction is for good cause, such as good-faith nonpayment actions or violations of the lease, reasonable rules or the statute.

title: Ending a Month-to-Month or Other Periodic Tenancy
bodyText:
Where a Florida lease has no fixed end date, either party may end it by written notice, delivered as the statute requires, given at least 7 days before the end of a weekly period, at least 30 days before the end of a monthly or quarterly period, or at least 60 days before the end of an annual period.

The length of the tenancy is set by how often rent is payable.

A tenant who stays after a fixed-term lease ends, with the landlord's permission, without giving the 30-day month-to-month notice owes the landlord one additional month's rent. A tenant who stays without permission can be sued for possession and for double rent for the time the tenant refuses to leave.

Florida has no rule requiring a landlord to have a reason to end a tenancy at the end of its term or period, and local just-cause or notice ordinances on these matters are preempted. Florida has no statute setting a notice period for a rent increase; for a periodic tenancy, a landlord who wants to raise the rent gives the termination notice above and offers new terms, and a fixed-term lease's rent cannot be raised mid-term unless the lease allows it. Local rent-increase notice ordinances are preempted.

title: Servicemember Rights
bodyText: A servicemember may end a Florida lease with written notice effective at least 30 days after the landlord receives it, if the servicemember receives permanent change of station orders to move 35 miles or more away; is prematurely or involuntarily discharged or released from active duty or state active duty; is released from active duty after leasing while on active duty and the unit is 35 miles or more from the home of record; receives orders to move into government quarters or becomes eligible for and opts into them; receives temporary duty, temporary change of station or state active duty orders to an area 35 miles or more away for more than 60 days; or receives a change of orders before moving in. The notice must include a copy of the orders or a commanding officer's written verification. If a servicemember dies on active duty, an adult immediate family member may terminate the same way, adding a death certificate. The tenant owes rent prorated to the termination date and no other rent or damages for the early termination; if the tenant terminates 14 or more days before moving in, no damages or penalties may be charged. These rights cannot be waived. A landlord who requires a rental application must process a servicemember's application within 7 days and notify the servicemember in writing of approval or denial and the reason for any denial; without a timely denial, the landlord must lease to the servicemember if all other terms are met. A landlord may not discriminate against a servicemember or retaliate against one who terminates under this law.

title: Landlord's Maintenance Duties
bodyText:
A Florida landlord must comply with applicable building, housing and health codes throughout the tenancy. Where there are no such codes, the landlord must keep the roof, windows, doors, floors, steps, porches, exterior walls, foundation and other structural components in good repair and able to resist normal forces and loads, keep the plumbing in reasonable working condition, install screens in reasonable condition at the start of the tenancy, and repair screen damage once a year when necessary.

For a single-family home or duplex, these duties can be changed in writing. Unless otherwise agreed in writing, the landlord of any other kind of unit must also make reasonable provision for extermination of rats, mice, roaches, ants, wood-destroying organisms and bedbugs; locks and keys; clean and safe common areas; garbage removal and outside receptacles; and functioning heat in winter, running water and hot water. If a tenant must leave for extermination, the landlord must give 7 days' written notice, abate the rent, and cannot require the tenant to stay out more than 4 days; the landlord is not liable for damages for the move-out. Unless otherwise agreed in writing, the landlord of a single-family home or duplex must install working smoke detection devices at the start of the tenancy.

The lease may make the tenant pay for garbage removal, water, fuel or utilities.

The landlord is not responsible for conditions the tenant, the tenant's family or the tenant's guests caused.

Air conditioning is not on the statute's list of duties; whether a landlord must provide cooling depends on the applicable local housing codes and on the lease, except that an apartment property licensed by the state (see "State Licence for Apartment Buildings") must be properly lighted, heated, cooled and ventilated (Fla. Stat. § 509.221(3)).

title: Lease Terms Florida Law Voids
bodyText: A Florida lease provision is void to the extent it waives or limits the tenant's or landlord's rights, remedies or requirements under the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, or limits either party's liability to the other that arises under law. If such a provision is included and the other party suffers actual damages because of it, that party can recover them. A court may refuse to enforce an unconscionable lease or provision, enforce the rest without it, or limit it. Every lease and every duty under the Act carries an obligation of good faith. In a lawsuit to enforce the lease or the Act, the winning party may recover reasonable attorney's fees and court costs, and a lease cannot waive that right. Separately, Florida's consumer collection law bars any person collecting a consumer debt from trying to enforce a debt the person knows is not legitimate, or claiming a legal right the person knows does not exist, with actual damages and up to $1,000 in additional statutory damages; whether unpaid rent is a consumer debt for this purpose is a question of case law, so do not try to collect under a lease term Florida law voids. Specific rights that cannot be waived include the notice requirements for terminating a tenancy, a servicemember's termination and application rights, and the tenant's right to use a flotation bed that meets code.

title: Landlord's Remedies When a Tenant Leaves Early
bodyText: When a Florida tenant breaches the lease and the landlord has a writ of possession, or the tenant surrenders or abandons the unit, the landlord may choose one of four remedies: (1) treat the lease as ended and retake possession for the landlord's own account, ending the tenant's further liability; (2) retake possession for the tenant's account, holding the tenant liable for the difference between the lease rent and what the landlord recovers by reletting, in which case the landlord must make good-faith efforts to relet, meaning at least the same efforts used for the initial rental or for similar units, though without preferring this unit over other vacancies; (3) stand by and do nothing, holding the tenant liable for rent as it comes due; or (4) charge liquidated damages or an early termination fee of up to 2 months' rent, but only if the tenant agreed to it in a separate signed addendum at the time the lease was made. A tenant is presumed to have abandoned the unit after being absent for half a rent period, unless the rent is current or the tenant gave written notice of the absence.

title: Tenants After Foreclosure
bodyText: Federal law (the Protecting Tenants at Foreclosure Act) protects tenants when a rental is foreclosed, and Florida has copied the same rules into a state statute that takes effect only if the federal act is ever repealed. Under these rules, a person who acquires a rental through foreclosure takes it subject to the rights of any bona fide tenant. The new owner must give a bona fide tenant at least 90 days' notice to vacate. A tenant with a bona fide lease made before the notice of foreclosure may stay until the lease ends, unless the new owner sells to a buyer who will live in the unit, and even then the tenant gets the 90-day notice. A tenant without a lease or with an at-will lease also gets the 90-day notice. A tenancy is bona fide only if the tenant is not the former owner or the former owner's child, spouse or parent, the lease was an arm's-length transaction, and the rent is not substantially below market (unless reduced by a subsidy).

title: When the Last Tenant Dies
bodyText: A Florida landlord may recover possession without a court order when the last remaining tenant has died, personal property remains in the unit, the rent is unpaid, at least 60 days have passed since the death, and the landlord has not been notified in writing of a probate estate or of the name and address of a personal representative. This does not apply to units in federally administered or regulated housing programs. After recovering possession this way, the landlord may remove the tenant's property; if the lease carries the statutory legend, the landlord is not liable for storing or disposing of it.

title: Background Screening of Apartment Employees
bodyText: A landlord of a Florida public lodging establishment licensed as a nontransient or transient apartment must require every employee to pass a background screening as a condition of employment. The screening must be done by a consumer reporting agency under the Fair Credit Reporting Act and must cover criminal history and the sexual predator and offender registries of all 50 states and the District of Columbia. The landlord may disqualify a person convicted of, or who pleaded guilty or no contest to, a felony or first-degree misdemeanor involving disregard for others' safety, or a violent offense such as murder, sexual battery, robbery, carjacking, home-invasion robbery or stalking.

title: Fraudulent Entry: Termination Without Cure
bodyText: Starting October 1, 2026, a Florida landlord may terminate a rental agreement on 7 days' written notice, without giving the tenant a chance to cure, for an act of fraudulent entry of a residential dwelling unit that violates Fla. Stat. §817.537(2), whether or not criminal proceedings have begun.

title: Eviction Notices and Process
bodyText: Florida uses three pre-suit notices, each in a form set by statute and delivered by mail, by hand delivery of a true copy, by e-mail under a signed e-mail addendum, or, if the tenant is absent, by leaving a copy at the residence. A lease cannot waive these notice requirements. For unpaid rent, the landlord delivers a written demand for payment or possession; the tenant has 3 days, not counting Saturdays, Sundays or court-observed holidays, to pay. For breaches the tenant can cure (such as unauthorized pets, guests or vehicles, improper parking, or failing to keep the unit clean), the landlord gives 7 days to cure; if the same or similar conduct recurs within 12 months, the landlord can file without a new notice. For breaches that allow no cure (intentional destruction, damage or misuse of property, fraudulent entry of a dwelling from October 1, 2026, or continued unreasonable disturbance, or a repeat within 12 months of a written warning), the landlord gives a 7-day notice terminating the lease. A landlord who accepts rent knowing of a breach waives that breach, but accepting partial rent does not, provided that after posting a nonpayment notice the landlord gives a receipt, deposits the partial payment into the court registry, or posts a new 3-day notice. For subsidized rent, waiver occurs if the landlord does not sue within 45 days of learning of the breach. The eviction is filed in county court using a summary procedure; where a court rule sets a different time period from the summary-procedure statute, the statute controls. If the lease is written, a copy must be attached to the complaint (Florida Supreme Court Form 1.947). A tenant who raises any defense other than payment must deposit the rent alleged into the court registry within 5 business days, or the landlord gets a default and a writ. After judgment, the sheriff posts 24 hours' notice (weekends and holidays do not stop it) and puts the landlord in possession; the landlord may then move the tenant's belongings to or near the property line and is not liable for them afterward.

title: Property Left Behind After a Tenancy
bodyText:
Florida gives landlords an optional procedure for belongings left after a tenancy ends, whether by eviction, surrender or abandonment.

The landlord sends written notice to the former tenant, and to anyone else the landlord reasonably believes owns the property, describing it, saying where to claim it and by what date (at least 10 days after hand delivery or 15 days after mailing), and warning that reasonable storage costs may be charged. The notice must say either that unclaimed property will be sold at a public sale after published notice, or that property believed to be worth less than $500 may be kept, sold or destroyed.

The landlord leaves the property in the unit or stores it with reasonable care. If it is unclaimed, the landlord sells it at a public sale advertised once a week for 2 weeks (or, if under $500, keeps or disposes of it) and pays any surplus after costs to the county within 30 days.

A landlord who follows the procedure is not liable to those notified; a landlord who skips it is judged under other law.

Two shortcuts exist: after a sheriff's writ, the landlord may move belongings to the property line with no liability; and if the lease carries the statutory legend, the landlord need not follow this procedure after surrender or abandonment and is not responsible for storing or disposing of the tenant's property.

title: State Preemption of Local Landlord-Tenant Rules
bodyText: Florida law preempts local regulation of residential tenancies. Since 2023, the state has preempted the landlord-tenant relationship and all matters covered by the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, and that preemption supersedes local rules on tenant screening, security deposits, rental applications and application fees, lease terms and conditions, landlord and tenant rights and responsibilities, disclosures, fees charged by landlords, and notice requirements. Separately, no county, city or other local government may adopt or keep any measure that has the effect of imposing controls on rents, although local governments may use land-use tools such as inclusionary housing ordinances to increase affordable housing. Counties and cities may, however, set maximum towing rates for vehicles towed from private property. The preemption reaches ordinances already on the books, not only new ones. Local building, housing and health codes still bind landlords, because Florida law requires landlords to comply with them. Whether local fair-housing ordinances that add protected classes (such as source of income, sexual orientation or gender identity) survive is unsettled: no court or Attorney General opinion has decided it, and some counties still list those classes. A landlord in such a county should treat those ordinances as enforceable until a court rules otherwise. Rental registration and inspection programs likely survive where they do not dictate lease terms, disclosures or notices.

title: Fair Housing
bodyText: Florida's Fair Housing Act protects the same classes as federal law: race, color, national origin, sex, disability, familial status and religion. Familial status covers anyone who is pregnant or in the process of getting legal custody of a child. It is unlawful to refuse to rent, set different terms, publish discriminatory advertising, misrepresent availability, or refuse reasonable modifications (at the tenant's expense) or reasonable accommodations for a person with a disability. The Act does not apply to a single-family house rented by an owner who owns no more than three and rents without a real estate licensee or discriminatory advertising, or to units in an owner-occupied building of four or fewer units; the advertising ban still binds the single-family exemption. Housing for older persons (62+, or 55+ meeting the 80 percent and policy tests) may exclude families with children. The Act does not require renting to someone whose tenancy would be a direct threat to others' health or safety or cause substantial physical damage to others' property, and allows action against a person convicted of illegally manufacturing or distributing a controlled substance. Separately, discriminating against a person with a disability in housing is a second-degree misdemeanor under Florida's service-animal statute.

title: Service Animal Penalties
bodyText: In Florida, a landlord who discriminates against a person with a disability in renting housing commits a second-degree misdemeanor. A person who knowingly and willfully misrepresents himself or herself, by conduct or by verbal or written notice, as using and being qualified to use a service animal, or as a service-animal trainer, also commits a second-degree misdemeanor and must perform 30 hours of community service. An emotional support animal registration, certificate, ID card or patch bought online does not by itself establish a disability or the need for the animal. Misrepresenting a disability-related need for an emotional support animal is a separate second-degree misdemeanor (Fla. Stat. § 817.265; see "False Service or Support Animal Claims").

title: Smoke and Carbon Monoxide Alarms
bodyText:
Unless otherwise agreed in writing, the landlord of a Florida single-family home or duplex must install working smoke detection devices at the start of the tenancy.

For other rentals, alarm duties come from the building, housing and fire codes the landlord must follow.

When a one- or two-family dwelling or townhome undergoes a repair or a level 1 alteration, newly installed or replacement battery-powered smoke alarms must use a 10-year sealed battery, unless they are part of a monitored, wireless or combination system. Every building or addition built on or after July 1, 2008 that has a fuel-burning heater or appliance, a fireplace, an attached garage, or another source of carbon monoxide must have an approved carbon monoxide alarm within 10 feet of each sleeping room; older buildings need not be retrofitted unless an addition is built.

title: Bounced Checks and Returned Payments
bodyText:
When a tenant's check, draft, debit card order or electronic funds transfer is refused for lack of funds, credit or an account (or payment is stopped with intent to defraud), a Florida payee may collect the bank fees actually incurred plus a service charge of $25 if the payment was $50 or less, $30 if it was over $50 up to $300, or $40 if it was over $300, or 5 percent of the face value if that is greater, without going to court.

If the maker does not pay the amount owed in cash within 30 days after a written demand in the statutory form (sent by certified or registered mail, or first-class mail with an affidavit of service), the payee can sue for three times the amount owed (at least $50), plus the amount of the instrument, court costs, reasonable attorney's fees and bank fees. A court may waive the statutory damages for economic hardship.

title: Homes for Veterans Landlord Incentive Pilot
bodyText: In Broward, Escambia, Hillsborough and Santa Rosa Counties, a landlord who rents to a veteran in the HUD-Veterans Affairs Supportive Housing (HUD-VASH) program may apply for two kinds of funding, while money is appropriated. First, vacancy relief: proportional rent for holding the unit for up to 45 days after it becomes available, or until the veteran moves in if sooner, applied for within 60 days after move-in. Second, if the veteran moves out during the first 12 months of a year-to-year lease or after any lease expires, up to $2,000 for property loss caused by the veteran beyond the deposit, applied for within 60 days after move-out. The second is available only to a landlord who applied for vacancy relief. After move-out the landlord must give the program administrator the move-out checklist with current photos and a copy of the landlord's written deposit-claim notice to the veteran.

title: No Mold Rule for Landlords
bodyText: Florida statutes do not require a residential landlord to disclose mold or to remediate it as a separate duty. The statutes on mold regulate mold assessors and remediators, who must be licensed; a residential property owner may assess mold on his or her own property without a license. Mold in a rental is handled through the landlord's general duty to comply with building, housing and health codes and to maintain the premises.

title: No Bed Bug Disclosure Rule
bodyText: Florida statutes do not require a residential landlord to disclose bed bug history or follow a bed bug treatment timeline. The only bed bug rule for landlords is the general extermination duty: unless otherwise agreed in writing, the landlord of a unit other than a single-family home or duplex must make reasonable provision for exterminating bedbugs and other pests, giving 7 days' written notice if the tenant must leave, abating rent, and limiting the move-out to 4 days.

title: No Eviction Record Sealing
bodyText: Florida statutes do not provide for sealing or expunging eviction court records. Florida's court rules have no eviction-specific sealing rule either; a party may ask the court to make specific information confidential under the general court-records rule. Eviction filings remain public records that tenant-screening companies may report, subject to federal credit-reporting law.

title: No Domestic Violence Lease Termination Right
bodyText: Florida statutes do not give a residential tenant who is a victim of domestic violence, dating violence, sexual violence or stalking a right to end a lease early or to have the locks changed. Unless the lease provides otherwise, such a tenant's early departure is handled like any other early termination. Some local ordinances have addressed this; state law now preempts local rules on rental agreement terms.

title: No Immigration-Status Rule for Landlords
bodyText: Florida statutes do not require or forbid a residential landlord to ask about or verify a tenant's immigration or citizenship status. Florida's immigration laws impose duties on employers, transporters and local governments, not on landlords. Federal fair housing law still bars discrimination based on national origin.

title: No Tenant EV Charging Right
bodyText: Florida statutes do not give a residential tenant a right to install an electric vehicle charger at a rental, and do not require a landlord to allow one. Florida's condominium law has its own electric vehicle charging rules for unit owners.

title: No Security Deposit Cap
bodyText: Florida law does not limit the amount of a residential security deposit a landlord may charge. Local limits are preempted. Separately, a condominium or cooperative association may require its own deposit from a unit owner's tenant, capped at one month's rent, and must handle it like a landlord's deposit.

title: No Late-Fee or Application-Fee Cap
bodyText: Florida law sets no maximum late fee and no maximum rental application fee for residential tenancies, and local caps are preempted. A late fee is still subject to the court's power to refuse to enforce an unconscionable lease term. Condominium and homeowners' association late fees, and self-storage late fees, have their own rules that do not apply to landlords.

title: Eviction Stay for State Active Duty
bodyText: In Florida, an eviction, distress action or requirement to deposit rent into the court registry may not proceed against a service member called into state active duty (or active duty), for as long as that duty lasts, if the service member has given the landlord written notice. This protection applies only where the agreed rent is $1,200 a month or less and the unit is occupied mainly as a home by the service member, the service member's spouse or a dependent. The court may on its own, and must on request, stay the case for up to 3 months unless it finds that the duty has not materially affected the tenant's ability to pay the rent.

title: Utilities: Former Occupant's Unpaid Bills
bodyText: A Florida city or county utility may not refuse or cut off water, sewer or utility service to a rental's owner, tenant or prospective tenant because a former occupant left unpaid charges, and those charges cannot become a lien on the rental property unless the current owner or tenant directly benefited from the service. The rule applies when the former occupant contracted for the service (or, for city utilities, when the city knew the occupant's name and service period), and a landlord's agreement with a city to guarantee tenants' bills cannot waive it. A city may still cut off a tenant who is 30 days or more in arrears. If a tenant does not pay a city for utility, water or sewer service, the landlord may start eviction proceedings.

title: Removing a Transient Occupant (Overstaying Guest)
bodyText:
A Florida property owner or other person entitled to possession can have a transient occupant removed without a Chapter 83 eviction. A transient occupant is someone staying briefly, not under a lease, with no ownership or leasehold interest; signs include no utility accounts, no government mail at the address in the past 12 months, little or no rent, no room of their own, few belongings and a home elsewhere.

After the occupant is told to leave and refuses, a law enforcement officer may, on the owner's sworn affidavit setting out those facts, direct the occupant to leave; refusing is trespass. The owner can also sue for unlawful detainer without prior notice.

The owner must let the former occupant retrieve belongings at reasonable times, generally within 10 days, and may impose conditions such as a police presence where there has been misconduct. A person wrongly removed can sue the person who asked for the removal.

This procedure is not for a tenant: if a court finds the person is a tenant, the owner must give the Chapter 83 notice and proceed by eviction. Squatters who entered unlawfully can be removed through a separate sheriff procedure.

title: Tenant Improvements and Construction Liens
bodyText:
In Florida, when a tenant makes improvements under an agreement with the landlord, a contractor's lien can reach the landlord's interest in the property.

A lease can prevent this, but only if the lease expressly says the landlord's interest is not subject to liens for the tenant's improvements and the landlord also records, in the county's official records before the contractor records a notice of commencement, either the lease (or a short form or memorandum containing that language) or a notice covering the parcel that states the lease language and that all or most leases on the parcel contain it. The tenant must tell its contractors about the provision.

If a contractor sends the landlord a written demand for a copy of the lease provision, the landlord must serve a verified copy within 30 days; failing to respond, or sending a false copy, exposes the property to the contractor's lien.

title: Condominium and HOA Rules for Renting
bodyText:
Florida condominium and homeowners' associations can affect a rental in three ways.
- First, approval: if the association's documents require it to approve leases, a condominium association may charge an approval fee only if its documents provide for one, capped at $150 per applicant (adjusted for inflation every 5 years) and not charged for a renewal with the same tenant; it may also require the tenant to put up a deposit of up to one month's rent to protect the common areas, handled like a landlord's deposit.
- Second, rental restrictions: a homeowners' association rule adopted after July 1, 2021 that prohibits or regulates rentals binds only owners who buy after it is adopted or who consent to it, except that any association may regulate leases shorter than 6 months and limit rentals to three times a year.
- Third, rent demands: if the owner of a condominium unit or of a home in a homeowners' association falls behind on association charges, the association can demand in writing, using a notice form set by statute, that the tenant pay the rent to the association until the owner's debt is paid. The tenant must then pay the association and is immune from the landlord's claim for the rent paid to it. The tenant also gets credit against the rent owed to the landlord, and the association can serve Chapter 83 notices and evict the tenant for not paying it.

A landlord may not retaliate against a tenant for paying rent to an association on its demand.

title: Removing Squatters (Unauthorized Occupants)
bodyText: A Florida property owner can ask the sheriff to remove squatters from a residential property without going to court if all of these are true: the owner or the owner's agent makes the request; the property includes a dwelling; the people entered unlawfully and are still there; the property was not open to the public when they entered; the owner told them to leave; they are not current or former tenants under a written or oral rental agreement the owner authorized; they are not the owner's immediate family; and there is no pending lawsuit about the property between the owner and them. The owner files a sworn complaint with the sheriff, who then serves a notice to vacate immediately and puts the owner back in possession; the sheriff may charge for standing by while locks are changed and belongings removed. A person wrongly removed can be restored to possession and recover actual damages, statutory damages of three times the fair market rent, costs and attorney's fees. This procedure cannot be used against a tenant or a former tenant, including one who stays after the lease ends; that requires an eviction.

title: Sales Tax on Short Rentals
bodyText: Florida charges a 6 percent state tax on rent for living quarters in a hotel, apartment house, rooming house, tourist or trailer camp, mobile home park, recreational vehicle park, condominium or timeshare resort. The tax does not apply to a tenant with a bona fide written lease longer than 6 months for continuous residence, to a tenant who has lived continuously in the same place for more than 6 months and has already paid the tax for the first 6 months, or to rentals in buildings intended primarily as people's permanent residence. Full-time postsecondary students and active-duty military are also exempt. A lease of 6 months or less, and a month-to-month tenancy during its first 6 months, can therefore carry sales tax, and county tourist taxes may apply as well. Whether the tax reaches a single-family house is not settled by this statute's list of facility types.

title: Uncashed Deposit Refunds
bodyText: If a tenant never cashes a Florida landlord's deposit refund, the money does not become the landlord's. Under Florida's unclaimed property law, intangible property a business holds or owes is presumed abandoned after a dormancy period, generally 5 years from when it became payable unless another period is specified by law, and must then be reported and delivered to the state. A landlord should keep records of the refund and the tenant's last known address.

title: Towing Tenants' and Guests' Vehicles
bodyText:
A Florida property owner, a tenant of the property, or someone either authorizes (including a condominium association's representative) may have a vehicle parked without permission towed by a regular towing business, without paying for the tow.

Except for property that is part of a single-family residence, or when the vehicle's owner is told in person that the space is reserved, the owner must first post permanent signs at each driveway entrance: within 10 feet of the road, with light-reflective letters at least 2 inches high stating that unauthorized vehicles will be towed at the owner's expense, the words "tow-away zone" in letters at least 4 inches high, the tower's name and phone number, mounted 3 to 6 feet above the ground, and in place at least 24 hours before any tow. The tower must store the vehicle nearby, notify the police within 30 minutes, release it within 1 hour of request, and stop and release it for half the posted rate if the owner arrives during the tow.

A person who improperly causes a tow is liable for the removal and storage costs, damages, attorney's fees and court costs.

Counties and cities may add rules and set maximum towing rates.

title: Florida Security Deposit Rules
bodyText:
Florida controls how a deposit and advance rent are held and returned (Fla. Stat. 83.49).

Don't commingle the funds with your own, or pledge or use them, until they're actually due to you. Where interest is owed, pay it or credit it against the current month's rent at least once a year; a tenant who wrongfully ends the tenancy early gets no interest.

If you won't claim against the deposit, return it with any interest within 15 days after the lease ends and the tenant vacates. If you will, give written notice of the claim and the reason within 30 days, by certified mail to the tenant's last known address (or by e-mail under an electronic-notice addendum), in the form 83.49(3)(a) prescribes; miss that and you lose the right to claim against the deposit (you may still sue for damages after returning it). The tenant has 15 days to object in writing; without an objection you may deduct the claim and must send the balance within 30 days of the notice, and the tenant can still sue.

The prevailing party in a deposit lawsuit recovers costs and a reasonable attorney's fee.

A renewal is a new rental agreement, and a deposit carried forward is a new deposit. On a sale or change of agent, transfer the deposit, advance rent and earned interest with an accounting.

title: Fire or Casualty: The Tenant's Options
bodyText: If the property is damaged or destroyed, other than by the tenant's wrongful or negligent act, so that the tenant's enjoyment of it is substantially impaired, the tenant may end the lease and move out immediately, or vacate the unusable part and pay rent reduced by that part's fair rental value (Fla. Stat. 83.63). If the lease ends, handle the deposit under 83.49, and give the tenant either the chance to collect belongings when it is safe, or notice of the date by which they can, within a reasonable time.

title: No Just-Cause Eviction Rule
bodyText: Florida has no just-cause or good-cause eviction rule. A fixed-term lease ends on its end date, and either party may end a month-to-month or other periodic tenancy without giving a reason, on the written notice the statute sets (at least 7 days before the end of a weekly period, 30 days before the end of a monthly or quarterly period, or 60 days before the end of a yearly period). Cities and counties cannot add a cause requirement: state law preempts local regulation of residential tenancies, including notice requirements and the terms of rental agreements. The limits are situational. A landlord may not raise rent, cut services or bring or threaten an eviction mainly to retaliate against a tenant who in good faith complained to a code agency, joined a tenant organization, gave a 7-day repair notice, ended a lease as a servicemember, paid rent to an association on its demand or used fair-housing rights, though an eviction for good cause such as nonpayment or a lease violation is not retaliation. Fair-housing law bars ending a tenancy for a discriminatory reason. After a foreclosure, federal law requires a buyer to honor a bona fide lease and give 90 days' notice. A developer converting a building to condominiums must let existing tenants extend their leases. An eviction against a servicemember on state active duty can be stayed.

title: When the Tenant Causes Damage
bodyText:
Florida law leaves the cost of damage a tenant causes with the tenant.

A tenant may end the lease or pay reduced rent after a fire or other casualty only if the damage was not caused by the tenant's own wrongful or negligent act. A landlord is not responsible under the maintenance statute for conditions caused by the negligent or wrongful act of the tenant, the tenant's family or another person on the property with the tenant's consent, so the tenant's 7-day repair notice, termination and rent-withholding remedies do not reach them.

The tenant must not damage the property or let anyone else do so. Intentional destruction or damage lets the landlord end the lease on a 7-day notice without a chance to cure; other damage is a breach the tenant must be given 7 days to cure.

The landlord may claim repair costs against the deposit, following the deposit claim-notice rules, and sue for the rest. If the tenant leaves or is evicted, the landlord chooses among the statutory remedies, including holding the tenant liable for rent through the end of the lease less what good-faith re-renting brings in.

The optional Damage Caused by Tenant clause states the rent consequences in the lease.

title: Florida Consumer Protection Law and Leases
bodyText: Florida's Deceptive and Unfair Trade Practices Act declares unfair or deceptive acts and unconscionable practices in trade or commerce unlawful, and trade or commerce expressly includes renting property. The Act carries no list of specific unfair lease practices (such as blank spaces filled in after signing or not giving the tenant a copy); it relies on general standards read in light of federal trade law. It also says it does not affect the remedies for residential tenancies under the landlord-tenant act. Florida has no plain-language statute for consumer contracts or leases. Separately, the consumer collection law bars anyone collecting a consumer debt from enforcing a debt they know is not legitimate. Fill in every blank before the tenant signs and give the tenant a signed copy.

title: No Algorithmic Rent-Setting Rule
bodyText: Florida statutes do not regulate using algorithmic or software pricing tools to set residential rents, or sharing rent data with other landlords. State and federal antitrust law may still apply. Local rent control is barred in Florida.

title: Fees and Rent
bodyText: In Florida, rent includes any other payment the written lease designates as rent, so a lease can turn a fee into rent. The library's lease does not call late fees or other charges rent, applies each payment to rent first, and labels only pet rent as rent. When you deliver a 3-day notice for unpaid rent, demand only the rent: a notice that also demands charges the lease does not designate as rent can be attacked as defective.

title: No Statute on Fixing a Tenant's Neglect
bodyText: Florida has no statute letting a landlord fix a tenant's failure to maintain the property and bill the cost as rent. A landlord may enter on at least 24 hours' notice, between 7:30 a.m. and 8 p.m., to make repairs, and is not responsible for conditions the tenant, the tenant's family or guests caused. The cost of damage the tenant caused can be claimed against the deposit or recovered as damages, but it is not rent unless the lease designates it as rent, and the library's lease does not.

title: No Rule on Blank Spaces in a Lease
bodyText: Florida has no statute barring a landlord from having a tenant sign a residential lease with blank spaces, or requiring the landlord to give the tenant a copy, and Florida's consumer protection act has no list of specific unfair lease practices. Fill in every blank before anyone signs and give each tenant a signed copy: a lease with blanks invites disputes over what was agreed, and a court may refuse to enforce an unconscionable term.

title: No Separate Quiet-Enjoyment Statute
bodyText: Florida's residential landlord-tenant act has no separate quiet-enjoyment covenant; any covenant comes from the common law and the lease. The act protects the tenant's possession directly instead: a landlord may not cut off utilities, lock the tenant out, remove doors, windows or the tenant's belongings except as the statute allows, or abuse the right of entry to harass the tenant. These violations cost the landlord actual and consequential damages or 3 months' rent, whichever is greater, plus costs and attorney's fees.

title: Statutory Forms
bodyText: Florida prescribes many forms a residential landlord uses, most of them 'in substantially the following form'. In or with the lease: the security deposit disclosure (landlords with five or more units), the fee-in-lieu-of-deposit disclosure, the e-mail notice addendum, the flood disclosure (separate document, leases of a year or more), the early termination fee addendum (separate, signed at signing), the abandoned-property legend, and the radon notice (exact words). During and after the tenancy: the deposit claim notice, the 3-day notice for rent, the 7-day cure and 7-day termination notices, the abandoned-property notices, and the bounced-check demand. Others concern associations and squatters: a condominium or homeowners' association's demand that the tenant pay rent to it, and an owner's sworn complaint to have the sheriff remove unauthorized occupants. Court forms for eviction (summons, complaint and answer) are set by the Florida Supreme Court.

title: No Tenant Security-Camera Rule
bodyText: Florida statutes do not address tenant-installed security cameras or video doorbells. The lease's alteration and installation terms govern. Laws on recording and surveillance (for example, video voyeurism and interception of communications) still apply to anyone who records.

title: Heat
bodyText: Florida's heat rule depends on the kind of unit. These rules cover ordinary residential rentals under Florida's Residential Landlord and Tenant Act; they do not cover a mobile home the tenant owns, or the occupancies the Act excludes, such as transient stays in a hotel or similar lodging. If you rent a unit other than a single-family home or duplex, such as an apartment, you must make reasonable provision at all times during the tenancy for functioning facilities for heat during winter, running water and hot water, unless you and the tenant agree otherwise in writing (Fla. Stat. § 83.51(2)(a)5.). The statute does not define winter or set a temperature. Licensed apartment buildings have a stricter rule. A building or complex with more than four rental units rented for 30 days or more is generally a public lodging establishment that must be licensed by the state Division of Hotels and Restaurants (a nontransient apartment, where 75 percent or more of the units are for nontransient tenants) (Fla. Stat. §§ 509.013(4), 509.242(1)(d)); it must be properly heated, cooled and ventilated (Fla. Stat. § 509.221(3)), and the Division's rule requires the heating system to be kept in good repair or installed to maintain at least 68 degrees Fahrenheit throughout the building (Fla. Admin. Code R. 61C-1.004(10)). A violation can bring fines of up to $1,000 per offense or license suspension (Fla. Stat. § 509.261(1)). For a single-family home or duplex there is no separate heat duty in the statute. For every unit, you must comply with applicable building, housing and health codes (Fla. Stat. § 83.51(1)(a)), and where a code requires heat, that code duty applies; where the code duty is the same as or greater than the apartment heat duty, the code duty governs (Fla. Stat. § 83.51(3)). The lease may make the tenant pay for fuel or utilities, so the tenant can be made to pay the gas or electric bill that runs the heat (Fla. Stat. § 83.51(2)(e)); that is not the same as making the tenant keep the heating system working. You are not responsible for heating problems caused by the tenant, the tenant's family or someone on the property with the tenant's consent (Fla. Stat. § 83.51(4)), and the tenant must use the heating in a reasonable manner (Fla. Stat. § 83.52(5)). What happens if the heat fails: a failure of the apartment heat duty is not a defense the tenant can raise against an eviction for possession (Fla. Stat. § 83.51(2)(c)), and the tenant's 7-day notice remedies (ending the lease, or withholding rent as a defense) are written for the code and structural duties in Fla. Stat. § 83.51(1), not for the apartment heat duty. The tenant can still sue for damages caused by the failure (Fla. Stat. § 83.55). A material failure to meet a code heating requirement is a failure under Fla. Stat. § 83.51(1)(a) that can carry the 7-day remedies if you do not comply within 7 days after the tenant's written notice, and so can a material failure to keep a heat promise the lease itself makes. You may not reduce services, including heat, to retaliate against a tenant (Fla. Stat. § 83.64(1)). The library offers no clause that shifts the apartment heat duty to the tenant; a landlord who wants that written agreement should take advice first.

title: No Required Habitability Statement in the Lease
bodyText: Florida law does not require your lease to state that the home is fit to live in or that you will deliver it in habitable condition. The duty itself applies whether or not the lease mentions it: for every rental covered by Florida's Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, you must comply with applicable building, housing and health codes throughout the tenancy, or, where there are none, keep the structure in good repair and the plumbing in reasonable working condition and install screens at the start of the tenancy (Fla. Stat. § 83.51(1)). A lease term that tries to waive that duty is void (Fla. Stat. § 83.47(1)(a)). The library's Maintenance & Repairs clause states your repair promise; no separate habitability statement is needed.

title: No Habitability Presumptions
bodyText: Florida law creates no presumption about habitability in a residential tenancy. No Florida statute, constitutional provision or civil procedure rule presumes that a unit with a code violation is uninhabitable, that a landlord who fails to repair within a set time acted in bad faith, or that a landlord action taken soon after a tenant's repair complaint is retaliatory. Under Florida's Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, the tenant who raises your failure to comply with the codes or the structural and plumbing duties as a defense to a nonpayment eviction must first have given you 7 days' written notice, and then the court decides how much, if anything, the rent is reduced for the lost value (Fla. Stat. § 83.60(1)(b)). A tenant who claims retaliation must have acted in good faith and must show different treatment, and the defense fails if you prove the eviction is for good cause (Fla. Stat. § 83.64). The presumptions Florida does have in this area are about abandonment, not condition. Cautious course: because nothing is presumed either way, keep dated records of repair requests, your responses and completed work.

title: When a Repair Problem Is "Material"
bodyText: Florida's tenant remedies for repair problems turn on how serious the problem is, but the statute does not define the line. Under Florida's Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, a tenant may end the lease only if you materially fail to comply with your code, structural and plumbing duties or with material lease provisions and do not fix the problem within 7 days after the tenant's written notice (Fla. Stat. § 83.56(1)). A tenant may withhold rent and use your failure as a defense to a nonpayment eviction only for a material noncompliance with those same duties, after the same 7-day notice (Fla. Stat. § 83.60(1)(b)). Where the failure is due to causes beyond your control and you keep making every reasonable effort to fix it, the statute separates two levels: if the unit is untenantable and the tenant moves out, the tenant owes no rent while it stays uninhabitable; if it is not untenantable and the tenant stays, the rent is reduced in proportion to the lost rental value (Fla. Stat. § 83.56(1)(a)-(b)). After a fire or other casualty not caused by the tenant, the test is whether the tenant's enjoyment of the property is substantially impaired (Fla. Stat. § 83.63). The Act defines none of material, untenantable or substantially impaired, so a court decides each case on its facts. Cautious course: treat any loss of water, hot water, sanitation, electricity, structural safety or code compliance as material, and respond to every written repair notice within the 7 days.

title: Shifting Maintenance Duties to the Tenant
bodyText:
Florida lets a written agreement move some of your maintenance duties to the tenant, and which ones depends on the kind of unit.
- Single-family home or duplex: your core duties (comply with building, housing and health codes or, where there are none, keep the structure in good repair, the plumbing working and the screens in place) may be altered or modified in writing (Fla. Stat. § 83.51(1)), and the duty to install working smoke detection devices at the start of the tenancy applies unless otherwise agreed in writing (Fla. Stat. § 83.51(2)(b)).
- Any other unit, such as an apartment: the core duties in Fla. Stat. § 83.51(1) cannot be shifted, and a lease term that tries is void (Fla. Stat. § 83.47(1)(a)); the added duties (extermination, locks and keys, clean and safe common areas, garbage removal and outside receptacles, and heat, running water and hot water) apply unless otherwise agreed in writing (Fla. Stat. § 83.51(2)(a)).

For any unit, the lease may make the tenant pay for garbage removal, water, fuel or utilities (Fla. Stat. § 83.51(2)(e)).

The statute asks only for a writing; it sets no consideration, rent reduction or separate-document requirement. Two limits remain: a court may refuse to enforce an unconscionable term (Fla. Stat. § 83.45), and any duty you keep stays yours even if the tenant agrees to help.

Conditions the tenant, the tenant's family or guests cause are the tenant's responsibility anyway (Fla. Stat. § 83.51(4)).

The library's optional "Tenant-Maintained Items (Single-Family Home or Duplex)" clause shifts routine items for a house or duplex and keeps code compliance, structure, plumbing and major systems with you. The library offers no clause shifting the added apartment duties. The narrow in-unit items a tenant controls are already the tenant's duties, since every tenant must keep the part of the premises the tenant occupies clean and sanitary and remove all garbage from the unit (Fla. Stat. § 83.52(2)-(3)); a broader shift of extermination, locks and keys, common areas, garbage removal and receptacles, heat or water is lawful in writing, but a landlord who wants it should take advice first.

Routine items the library's tenant-maintained items clause is built for: lawn and landscaping care; pest control for rats, mice, roaches, ants and bedbugs (not wood-destroying organisms such as termites); replacing heating and air-conditioning filters on the manufacturer's schedule; replacing smoke detector batteries after the start of the term; clearing drain and toilet clogs; pool or spa care; garbage removal and outside receptacles; replacing light bulbs; and repairing screen damage after the start of the term.

title: No Stove or Refrigerator Requirement
bodyText:
Florida state law does not require you to supply a stove, oven, range or refrigerator in a residential rental.

Two related rules do apply.
- First, you must comply with applicable building, housing and health codes (Fla. Stat. § 83.51(1)(a)), so a local housing code may require cooking or refrigeration equipment.
- Second, if refrigeration or other utility service is furnished to the tenant, you may not cause it to be cut off or interrupted, whoever controls or pays for it; a violation makes you liable for actual and consequential damages or 3 months' rent, whichever is greater, plus costs and attorney's fees (Fla. Stat. § 83.67(1), (6)).

If you do supply appliances, list them in the lease's "Appliances & Equipment Included" clause; once you promise to maintain them, the promise can be a material lease provision, and a material failure to keep it can let the tenant end the lease if you do not comply within 7 days after the tenant's written notice (Fla. Stat. § 83.56(1)).

title: No Carpet-Cleaning Rule
bodyText:
Florida law has no rule on carpet cleaning at move-out. No Florida statute lets or forbids you to require professional carpet cleaning, and none sets an age-and-condition test for carpet or paint deductions.

Florida's deposit statute does not define normal wear and tear; the phrase appears only in the fee-in-lieu-of-deposit statute.

So a move-out cleaning duty is a lease term, and any charge for it is a claim against the deposit like any other: within 30 days after the lease ends you must send the tenant written notice by certified mail (or by e-mail if the tenant signed the e-mail notice addendum) of your intention to impose a claim and the reason for it, in the statute's form; the tenant then has 15 days to object (Fla. Stat. § 83.49(3)(a)-(b)). If you miss the 30 days, you lose the right to claim against the deposit but may sue for damages after returning it.

The library's optional "Professional Carpet Cleaning at Move-Out" clause is used only where the carpets were professionally cleaned right before the tenancy, and limits the charge to the reasonable cost you actually pay; those limits are a drafting choice that keeps the charge a restoration of the move-in condition.

title: No Radiator Cover Rule
bodyText: Florida law has no rule on steam radiator covers and no lease rider about them. The boiler provisions apply to licensed public lodging establishments, which include licensed apartment buildings: any fuel-fired boiler room there must have a carbon monoxide detector (Fla. Stat. § 554.108(6)), and where the building has a low-pressure steam or vapor heating boiler, the insurance inspector's boiler report is required 'biannually for low pressure steam or vapor heating boilers and shall be posted in the boiler room' (Fla. Admin. Code R. 61C-1.004(10)); that word can mean every two years or twice a year, so confirm the schedule with the Division. If a unit has any hot surface a child could touch, your general duty to comply with building, housing and health codes applies (Fla. Stat. § 83.51(1)(a)), and an apartment landlord must also make reasonable provision for working heat in winter (see "Heat", "Heat"). Nothing needs to be added to the lease.

title: No Water Heater Temperature Rule
bodyText: Florida law does not require you to set a water heater to a maximum temperature before a new tenant moves in, and sets no maximum hot water temperature for rentals. What does apply: if you rent a unit other than a single-family home or duplex, you must make reasonable provision for running water and hot water unless agreed otherwise in writing (Fla. Stat. § 83.51(2)(a)5.), and every landlord must comply with applicable building, housing and health codes (Fla. Stat. § 83.51(1)(a)). An ordinary residential water heater is outside Florida's Boiler Safety Act as long as it stays within that Act's limits on heat input, water temperature (210 degrees Fahrenheit) and capacity (120 gallons) (Fla. Stat. § 554.109). Cautious course: check the setting at each turnover and keep it at a level that avoids scalding; the setting is a safety practice, not a statutory duty.

title: No Tenant Right to Install a Cooling Device
bodyText: Florida law gives tenants no right to install a portable or window air conditioner or other cooling device, and sets no rule on how a lease may restrict one. So the lease controls: you may allow, condition or forbid window and portable units, and the library's "No Alterations" clause applies to installations. The tenant must use any air-conditioning facilities and appliances in a reasonable manner (Fla. Stat. § 83.52(5)). Florida's general maintenance statute does not list cooling as a landlord duty, but two other rules can require it. If your building is licensed as a public lodging establishment (generally a building or complex with more than four units rented for 30 days or more, licensed as a nontransient apartment), it must be properly heated, cooled and ventilated (Fla. Stat. § 509.221(3)). And every landlord must comply with applicable building, housing and health codes (Fla. Stat. § 83.51(1)(a)). Florida has a statutory cooling-system protection for homeowners' association parcel owners, not tenants: an association may not require review of an owner's central air-conditioning system that is not visible from outside and is substantially similar to an approved one (Fla. Stat. § 720.3035(1)(b)2.).

title: Common-Area Lighting
bodyText: Florida's common-area lighting rules depend on the building. Any unit other than a single-family home or duplex: unless agreed otherwise in writing, you must make reasonable provision for the clean and safe condition of common areas (Fla. Stat. § 83.51(2)(a)3.); the statute does not mention lighting by name, but unlit stairways and halls bear on safety. Licensed apartment buildings (generally a building or complex with more than four units rented for 30 days or more, licensed as a nontransient apartment by the Division of Hotels and Restaurants): the building must be properly lighted, by daylight and by artificial light (Fla. Stat. § 509.221(3)), and halls, entrances and stairways must be clean, ventilated and well lighted day and night, with railings on all stairways and around porches and steps (Fla. Admin. Code R. 61C-1.004(9)). A licensed building that breaks these rules faces fines of up to $1,000 per offense or license action (Fla. Stat. § 509.261(1)). Lighting also matters for crime liability. The owner or principal operator of a multifamily residential property (at least five dwelling units on one parcel) that substantially implements a list of security measures has a presumption against liability for crimes on the property by third parties who are not its employees or agents; the list includes a parking lot lit from dusk to dawn at an average of at least 1.8 foot-candles at 18 inches above the surface, and dusk-to-dawn lighting in walkways, laundry rooms, common areas and porches, along with cameras, locks, peepholes, a crime prevention assessment and staff training (Fla. Stat. § 768.0706(2)). The owner must prove it substantially implemented the measures, and the section creates no private cause of action (Fla. Stat. § 768.0706(3), (5)). The measures are not required; they earn the presumption. Every landlord must also comply with applicable building, housing and health codes (Fla. Stat. § 83.51(1)(a)), which may set lighting levels. Paying for the electricity: the lease may make the tenant pay for utilities (Fla. Stat. § 83.51(2)(e)), but the statute does not single out common-area lights wired to a tenant's meter; if a tenant's meter serves common-area lights, say so in the lease's utilities clause so the charge is agreed in writing. The duty to keep common areas lit stays with you.

title: Locks and Security Devices
bodyText: Florida's lock rules depend on the building. Any unit other than a single-family home or duplex: unless agreed otherwise in writing, you must make reasonable provision for locks and keys at all times during the tenancy (Fla. Stat. § 83.51(2)(a)2.); a failure is not a defense to an eviction for possession (Fla. Stat. § 83.51(2)(c)) but can support a damages claim (Fla. Stat. § 83.55). Licensed apartment buildings (generally a building or complex with more than four units rented for 30 days or more, licensed as a nontransient apartment): each bedroom or apartment must have an approved locking device on each door opening to the outside, to an adjoining room or apartment, or to a hallway (Fla. Stat. § 509.211(1)); see also the key-control rules ("Key Control in Licensed Apartments", "Key Control in Licensed Apartments"). Multifamily properties with at least five units on one parcel: if the owner or principal operator substantially implements a list of security measures, it has a presumption against liability for crimes on the property by third parties who are not its employees or agents. The list includes at least a 1-inch deadbolt in each unit door; a locking device on each window, each exterior sliding door and other doors not used for community purposes; locked gates with key or fob access along pool fences; a peephole or door viewer on each unit door that has no window in or next to it; recorded security cameras at entry and exit points; required lighting; a crime prevention through environmental design assessment no more than 3 years old; and staff training (Fla. Stat. § 768.0706(2)). The owner must prove substantial implementation, and the section creates no private cause of action (Fla. Stat. § 768.0706(3), (5)). These measures earn the presumption; the statute does not order them. No Florida rule requires you to rekey or change locks between tenants, and none ties a peephole to a construction date. You may never change the locks or use a bootlock to keep a tenant out (Fla. Stat. § 83.67(2)). Codes may add requirements (Fla. Stat. § 83.51(1)(a)).

title: Key Control in Licensed Apartments
bodyText: If your property is licensed by the state Division of Hotels and Restaurants as a nontransient apartment or a transient apartment, Florida requires a key-control system. A nontransient apartment is a building or complex in which 75 percent or more of the units are available for rent to nontransient tenants; buildings with four rental units or fewer, and one- to four-family houses and condominium units where no more than four units in a complex are for rent, are generally not licensed (Fla. Stat. §§ 509.013(4), 509.242(1)(d)-(e)). A licensed apartment must: keep a log accounting for the issuance and return of all keys for each dwelling unit; establish policies and procedures for issuing and returning unit keys and for storing and controlling access to unissued keys; and require every employee to undergo a background screening as a condition of employment (see "Background Screening of Apartment Employees"). On request during the Division's annual inspection, you must show proof of compliance (Fla. Stat. § 509.211(5)). A violation can bring fines of up to $1,000 per offense or license suspension or revocation (Fla. Stat. § 509.261(1)). The rule does not depend on the number of units beyond the licensing test, and it applies whether or not the lease mentions keys. Smaller rentals that are not licensed have no statutory key-log duty, though apartment landlords outside the licensing rules must still make reasonable provision for locks and keys (Fla. Stat. § 83.51(2)(a)2.). Nothing needs to go in the lease; the library's "Keys" clause covers the tenant's side.

title: No Smart Lock Rule
bodyText: Florida law has no rule specific to smart locks, keypad or app-based entry, or other electronic access systems in residential rentals. No Florida statute lets a tenant ask whoever runs a connected device's user accounts to cut off another person's access. The general rules apply to an electronic system just as to a key. You may enter only as Florida's entry statute allows: at any time to protect or preserve the premises, on at least 24 hours' notice between 7:30 a.m. and 8:00 p.m. for repairs, and for inspections, agreed services or showings with the tenant's consent, in an emergency, when the tenant unreasonably withholds consent, or during an extended absence; you may not abuse access or use it to harass the tenant (Fla. Stat. § 83.53). An entry log from a smart lock does not widen those rights. You may not keep a tenant out by any means, including changing locks or disabling codes (Fla. Stat. § 83.67(2)); a violation makes you liable for actual and consequential damages or 3 months' rent, whichever is greater, plus costs and attorney's fees (Fla. Stat. § 83.67(6)). An apartment landlord's duty to make reasonable provision for locks and keys covers electronic locks too (Fla. Stat. § 83.51(2)(a)2.). Cautious course: give each tenant a unique code or credential, change or delete codes between tenants, and do not use access logs for anything but security and maintenance.

title: Pest Control Notices
bodyText:
Florida has one pest-control notice rule for landlords and several for pest control companies.

Your rule: if you rent a unit other than a single-family home or duplex, unless agreed otherwise in writing, you must make reasonable provision for extermination of rats, mice, roaches, ants, wood-destroying organisms and bedbugs; if the tenant must temporarily leave the unit for the extermination, you must give the tenant 7 days' written notice, in person, by mail, or by e-mail if the tenant signed the e-mail notice addendum; the tenant cannot be required to stay out more than 4 days; and you must abate the rent for that time, though you are not liable for damages (Fla. Stat. § 83.51(2)(a)1.).

The pest control company's rules: a licensed company must, on request, give its customer its name, the applicator's identification number, the pesticide's name and active ingredient, and label safety information (Fla. Stat. § 482.2265(1)); must post a notice when it applies pesticide to a lawn or exterior foliage (Fla. Stat. § 482.2265(2)); must notify, at least 24 hours ahead, any person on the state's medical registry whose home is within the registered distance before treating a lawn, plant bed or exterior foliage (Fla. Stat. § 482.2267(5)); and must post a notice of any termite or other wood-destroying organism treatment next to the attic or crawl-space access, which only the property owner may remove (Fla. Stat. § 482.226(5)).

If you hire the company, you are its customer, so ask for the pesticide information and pass it to the tenant before any indoor treatment.

No Florida statute requires a landlord to give tenants advance notice of routine pest treatment where the tenant need not leave. The entry rules still apply to any entry for treatment: 24 hours' notice between 7:30 a.m. and 8:00 p.m. where the treatment is a repair, and otherwise the tenant's consent or another ground the statute lists, such as an emergency (Fla. Stat. § 83.53(1)-(2)).

Licensed apartment buildings must also take effective measures against vermin and treat any infested room until the vermin are exterminated (Fla. Stat. § 509.221(7)).

title: Tenant Remedies When Repairs Aren't Made
bodyText: Under Florida's Residential Landlord and Tenant Act a tenant has four repair remedies, and repair-and-deduct is not one of them. (1) End the lease: if you materially fail to comply with your code, structural and plumbing duties or with material lease provisions for 7 days after the tenant's written notice saying the tenant intends to terminate, the tenant may end the lease (Fla. Stat. § 83.56(1)). (2) Withhold rent as a defense: 7 days after a written notice saying the tenant intends not to pay rent because of a material failure of those code, structural and plumbing duties, the tenant may raise it as a complete defense to an eviction for nonpayment, and the court reduces the rent by the lost value (Fla. Stat. § 83.60(1)(b)); the court's residential eviction answer form lists this defense (Form 1.947(b)). The notice may go to you, your designated agent, a resident manager or whoever collects rent. (3) Damages: either party may recover damages caused by the other's noncompliance with the lease or the Act (Fla. Stat. § 83.55). (4) Retaliation defense, if you respond to a complaint by raising rent, cutting services or suing (Fla. Stat. § 83.64). The rent goes into the court, not to the tenant: a tenant who raises any defense other than payment in an eviction must pay the accrued rent and the rent that comes due into the court registry, or lose the defenses (Fla. Stat. § 83.60(2)); if you are in actual danger of losing the property or face other hardship from the lost rent, you may ask the court to release all or part of the funds or to set a prompt final hearing (Fla. Stat. § 83.61). Failures of the added apartment duties (pests, locks, common areas, garbage, heat and water) are not a defense to possession (Fla. Stat. § 83.51(2)(c)). Florida's statutes, constitution and civil procedure rules give residential tenants no repair-and-deduct right. Florida's older withholding statute for a "wholly untenantable" property applies only to tenancies outside the residential act. See also "Repair Notices: Tenant's 7-Day Remedies".

title: Repair Requests and Written Notice
bodyText:
Under Florida's Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, a tenant's legal remedies for a repair problem start only with a written notice.
- To end the lease, the tenant must deliver written notice specifying the problem and stating the intention to terminate; you then have 7 days to comply (Fla. Stat. § 83.56(1)).
- To withhold rent as a defense to a nonpayment eviction, the tenant must deliver written notice specifying the problem and stating the intention not to pay rent, and 7 days must pass (Fla. Stat. § 83.60(1)(b)).

The withholding notice may go to you, your designated agent, a resident manager, or the person who collects the rent (Fla. Stat. § 83.60(1)(b)).

Notices may be delivered by mail, by hand, by e-mail only under a signed e-mail notice addendum in which the recipient agreed to receive notices by e-mail, or, if the tenant is absent from the premises, by leaving a copy at the residence, and these notice requirements cannot be waived in the lease (Fla. Stat. § 83.56(4)).

A phone call, text or verbal request does not by itself start the 7-day clock. A lease term that requires written repair requests is therefore consistent with the statute and does not take away a defense; but a lease term cannot remove or shorten the statutory notice rules.

If you actually knew of a problem, do not rely on the missing written notice: whether knowledge alone supports a damages claim is not settled by the statute. Respond to every repair request, written or not, and keep a record.

The library's "Maintenance & Repairs" clause asks the tenant to report repairs in writing.

title: Tenant Remedies When the Landlord Breaches
bodyText: Florida's Residential Landlord and Tenant Act gives a tenant these remedies when you break the lease or the Act. Any right or duty in the Act can be enforced by a civil lawsuit (Fla. Stat. § 83.54), and the tenant may recover the damages your noncompliance with the lease or the Act caused (Fla. Stat. § 83.55). If you materially fail to comply with your code, structural and plumbing duties or with material lease provisions, the tenant may end the lease if you do not fix the problem within 7 days after the tenant's written notice; if the failure is beyond your control and you keep trying, the lease may be ended or altered, with no rent owed for an untenantable unit the tenant leaves and a proportional rent cut for one the tenant stays in (Fla. Stat. § 83.56(1)). In a nonpayment eviction, the tenant may defend on your material failure of those duties after a 7-day written notice, or on any other legal or equitable defense, including retaliation (Fla. Stat. §§ 83.60(1), 83.64), but must pay rent into the court registry to keep any defense other than payment (Fla. Stat. § 83.60(2)). Prohibited practices (cutting off utilities, locking the tenant out, removing outside doors, locks, roof, walls or windows other than for maintenance, repair or replacement, removing the tenant's property outside the lawful routes) make you liable for actual and consequential damages or 3 months' rent, whichever is greater, plus costs and attorney's fees (Fla. Stat. § 83.67(6)). If you miss the 30-day deposit claim notice, you lose the right to claim against the deposit, though you may still sue for damages (Fla. Stat. § 83.49(3)(a)). In any lawsuit to enforce the lease or the Act, the winner may recover reasonable attorney fees and costs, and that right cannot be waived in the lease, but fees are not awarded under that rule on a personal-injury claim based on a breach of your maintenance duty (Fla. Stat. § 83.48). Paying rent while knowing of your noncompliance waives the tenant's right to terminate or sue for that noncompliance, but not for later or continuing noncompliance (Fla. Stat. § 83.56(5)(a)).

title: No Right to End a Lease Over Repair Costs
bodyText: Florida law gives a landlord no right to end a residential lease because repairs would cost more than a set amount or a share of the property's value, and sets no cost cap on any tenant repair remedy (Florida has no repair-and-deduct right). After a fire or other casualty not caused by the tenant that substantially impairs the tenant's enjoyment of the property, the statute gives the tenant, not you, the choice to end the lease or to vacate the unusable part and pay reduced rent (Fla. Stat. § 83.63); see "Fire or Casualty: The Tenant's Options". The only cost threshold in Florida's residential landlord-tenant act runs in the tenant's favor: if you were required to give the separate flood disclosure (a lease of 1 year or longer) and did not, and the tenant's personal property suffers flood loss costing 50 percent or more of its market value to repair or replace, the tenant may end the lease by written notice and surrender within 30 days after the loss, and you must refund rent paid in advance for the period after termination (Fla. Stat. § 83.512(2)-(3)). So unless the lease gives you a termination right, you cannot end a fixed-term lease early because repairs are expensive; you must make the repairs your duties require. A landlord who wants a right to end the lease after major damage needs an express lease term, and should take advice first.

title: No Rule on Written Repair Promises
bodyText: Florida law does not require a landlord's promise to clean, repair or improve a rental to be in writing, to carry a completion date, or to be made before the lease is signed. A promise you put in the lease is a lease provision, and under Florida's Residential Landlord and Tenant Act a material failure to keep it can let the tenant end the lease after a 7-day written notice (Fla. Stat. § 83.56(1)), and any failure can support a damages claim (Fla. Stat. § 83.55). Whether a spoken promise binds you is a question of general contract law (Florida's statute of frauds requires a signed writing for some agreements, including a lease longer than one year) and of the lease's "Entire Agreement" clause, not of a landlord-tenant statute. Cautious course: put every repair or improvement you agree to make in the lease or a signed addendum, with a target date, and do not make spoken promises you do not intend to keep.

title: Fire Sprinklers
bodyText: Florida's sprinkler rules turn on when and how a building was built, not on whether it is rented. Renting does not trigger a retrofit: a property owner may not be required to install fire sprinklers in any residential property because it is used as, or converted to, a rental property (Fla. Stat. § 633.208(10)). Buildings of three or more stories: except for single-family and two-family dwellings, any building of three or more stories whose construction contract was let after January 1, 1994 must have an automatic sprinkler system installed under the State Fire Marshal's rules and codes (Fla. Stat. § 553.895(2)). Houses and duplexes: the Life Safety Code part of the Florida Fire Prevention Code does not apply to one- and two-family dwellings, a local government that wants a sprinkler requirement for them must first prepare an economic cost and benefit report (Fla.
