Stat. § 633.208(8)(a)), and the International Residential Code's sprinkler mandate may not be adopted into the Florida Building Code or as a local amendment, except by a local government whose lawful fire sprinkler ordinance has been in effect since January 1, 2010 (Fla. Stat. § 553.73(17)). Transient lodging: hotels, motels and similar transient public lodging of three or more stories with interior corridors, or over 75 feet, built under contracts let after September 30, 1983, must be sprinklered, and the rule reaches only buildings where more than half the units are held out for transient occupancy (Fla. Stat. § 509.215). Condominium units: a residential condominium high-rise must retrofit a sprinkler or engineered life safety system unless the owners voted to forgo sprinkler retrofitting; if they did, the association must notify owners, and a unit owner must give a copy of that notice to a renter before the lease is signed (Fla. Stat. § 718.112(2)(n)). Where sprinklers exist, you must keep them in the condition the Florida Fire Prevention Code requires (Fla. Stat. §§ 83.51(1)(a), 633.208(6)).

title: Fire Code That Applies to Rentals
bodyText: Florida has one statewide fire code, the Florida Fire Prevention Code, adopted by the State Fire Marshal by rule and deemed adopted by every city, county and special district with firesafety responsibilities, which must enforce it as the minimum firesafety code (Fla. Stat. §§ 633.202(1), 633.208(1)-(2)). The current rule makes the code NFPA 1, the Fire Code, and NFPA 101, the Life Safety Code, both in their Florida 2021 editions, plus the other standards the rule lists (Fla. Admin. Code R. 69A-60.002(3)). The Marshal adopts a new edition every three years (Fla. Stat. § 633.202(1)), and a local government may adopt stricter amendments only under the statute's conditions (Fla. Stat. § 633.208(3)). For rentals: the Life Safety Code part does not apply to one- and two-family dwellings (Fla. Stat. § 633.208(8)(a)); the code's new-building provisions apply only to buildings permitted on or after the current edition's effective date, and for an existing building the local fire official first decides whether a threat to life safety or property exists, then applies the existing-building provisions to the extent practical or allows a reasonable alternative (Fla. Stat. § 633.208(4)-(5)); and a local government may require any structure to be maintained in accordance with the code (Fla. Stat. § 633.208(6)). Hotels, motels and some other uses listed in the statute follow separate uniform firesafety standards instead (Fla. Stat. § 633.206). Building construction follows the separate Florida Building Code, which the Florida Building Commission updates every three years by rule; where it conflicts with the fire code, the requirement offering the greatest degree of life safety wins (Fla. Stat. § 553.73(1)(d), (7)). Your maintenance duty includes complying with these codes (Fla. Stat. § 83.51(1)(a)).

title: Which Code Edition Applies
bodyText: Florida mostly adopts fixed editions of model codes, and the edition that applies to your building usually depends on its permit date. Building code: the Florida Building Commission adopts an updated Florida Building Code every three years by rule; a change a standards organization makes to a standard the code adopts by reference does not take effect in Florida until the Commission adopts it; and the edition in effect when a permit is applied for governs that permitted work for the life of the permit (Fla. Stat. § 553.73(6), (7)(a), (7)(d)). Fire code: the State Fire Marshal adopts a new edition of the Florida Fire Prevention Code every third year (Fla. Stat. § 633.202(1)); the current rule adopts NFPA 1 and NFPA 101 in their Florida 2021 editions and lists other NFPA standards by year (Fla. Admin. Code R. 69A-60.002(3), 69A-60.005(2)); new-building provisions apply only to buildings permitted on or after the current edition's effective date, while existing buildings follow the existing-building provisions as the local fire official applies them (Fla. Stat. § 633.208(4)-(5)). A few statutes name a frozen edition outright: the transient-lodging and timeshare sprinkler statute names NFPA No. 13 (1985) and NFPA 74 (1984) (Fla. Stat. § 553.895(1)). Others move with the agency's rule: the public lodging firesafety statute uses the NFPA publications most recently adopted by the State Fire Marshal's rule (Fla. Stat. § 509.215(7)). So for an older rental, ask the building and fire officials which edition and which existing-building provisions they apply.

title: Balcony and Structural Inspections
bodyText: Florida has two balcony and structural inspection regimes that can reach a rental, and neither applies to an ordinary house or small building. Licensed apartment buildings three or more stories tall: a public lodging establishment (which includes a licensed nontransient apartment building) that is three or more stories high must have safe and secure railings on all balconies, platforms and stairways, properly maintained and repaired (Fla. Stat. § 509.211(3)), and the Division of Hotels and Restaurants' rules must require it to file, every 3 years, a certificate that a competent person has inspected all balconies, platforms, stairways and railways and found them safe, secure and free of defects, with the Division and the local building and zoning authority; failure to file brings administrative sanctions (Fla. Stat. § 509.2112). Condominium and cooperative buildings three or more habitable stories tall: the owners must have a milestone structural inspection by an architect or engineer by December 31 of the year the building turns 30 (or 25, if the local agency requires it because of conditions such as nearness to salt water) and every 10 years after; the condominium or cooperative association arranges it, and an owner of a part of the building not under that form of ownership shares the duty (Fla. Stat. § 553.899(3)-(4)), and a condominium association must also obtain a structural integrity reserve study at least every 10 years (Fla. Stat. § 718.112(2)(g)). If you rent out a condominium unit, these are the association's duties, but the inspection summary the association sends you tells you about the building your tenant lives in. The milestone rule does not apply to one- to four-family dwellings with three or fewer habitable stories (Fla. Stat. § 553.899(4)). For everything else, the general duty applies: comply with building, housing and health codes, or keep porches, steps and other structural parts in good repair where there are none (Fla. Stat. § 83.51(1)).

title: Pool Safety
bodyText: Florida's pool rules depend on the kind of property. House, duplex or small townhouse: Florida's Residential Swimming Pool Safety Act covers a swimming pool, hot tub or nonportable spa over 24 inches deep on the premises of a detached one- or two-family dwelling or a one-family townhouse not more than three stories high (Fla. Stat. § 515.25(10)-(11)). To pass final inspection, a new residential pool must have at least one safety feature: a barrier meeting the statute's specifications (at least 4 feet high, no gaps a young child could get through, outward-opening self-closing and self-latching gates), an approved safety pool cover, exit alarms on doors and windows giving direct access to the pool, self-closing and self-latching devices on those doors with the release at least 54 inches above the floor, or a certified pool alarm (Fla. Stat. §§ 515.27(1), 515.29). Failing to equip a new residential pool with a feature is a second-degree misdemeanor, excused if a feature is added and a drowning prevention course is attended within 45 days (Fla. Stat. § 515.27(2)). The Act is written for new pools and does not itself require older pools to be retrofitted or require a pool notice to tenants; a city or county may have its own ordinance at least as strict (Fla. Apartment complexes and other properties of five or more units: a pool serving apartments, townhouses or other cooperative living projects of five or more units is a public swimming pool (Fla. Stat. § 514.011(2)) that needs an annual Department of Health operating permit, posted in a conspicuous place (Fla. Stat. § 514.031), and an anti-entrapment drain system (Fla. Stat. § 514.0315). Pools serving 32 or fewer condominium or cooperative units, or a homeowners' association of 32 or fewer units or parcels, that are not operated as public lodging are exempt except for water quality (and, for the association pools, the drain rule) (Fla. Stat. § 514.0115(2)-(3)). If you rent a unit in a condominium or community with a pool, the association, not you, holds these duties.

title: No Alarm-Tampering Fee Rule
bodyText:
Florida law sets no fee for a tenant who removes, disables or tampers with a smoke or carbon monoxide alarm, and has no statute specifically forbidding a tenant to do so.

The general rules cover it: the tenant must not destroy, damage, impair or remove any part of the property or your property in it, or let anyone else do so (Fla. Stat. § 83.52(6)); you are not responsible for conditions the tenant, the tenant's family or a person on the property with the tenant's consent caused (Fla. Stat. § 83.51(4)); and you may recover the damages a lease breach causes (Fla. Stat. § 83.55).

So charge the actual reasonable cost of repairing or replacing a disabled or damaged alarm, not a fixed fee; whether a fixed amount would be enforced as agreed damages or struck as a penalty is a case-law question. The library's optional "Smoke and Carbon Monoxide Detectors" clause states the tenant's duties and the actual-cost charge. Your own alarm duties are in "Smoke and Carbon Monoxide Alarms".

title: No Window Guard or Security Bar Rule
bodyText: Florida law has no window-guard rule for rentals: no duty to install child window guards, no window-guard lease notice, and no statute on security or burglar bars, their release mechanisms or a written disclosure of them. Florida's statutes have a release-mechanism rule for residential swimming pools (doors to the pool and pool gates) (Fla. Stat. §§ 515.27(1)(d), 515.29(3)); see "Pool Safety". Window safety for a rental otherwise comes from your duty to comply with building, housing and health codes or, where there are none, to keep windows in good repair (Fla. Stat. § 83.51(1)). Cautious course: if you install bars on a bedroom window, use bars with a quick-release mechanism that opens from inside without a key, and show the tenant how it works.

title: Asbestos
bodyText: Florida state law does not require a residential landlord to notify or disclose to tenants that a building contains asbestos. Florida's asbestos statutes regulate the work instead. Asbestos surveys, abatement plans and abatement work generally require a licensed asbestos consultant or contractor (Fla. Stat. § 469.003). The owner-builder exemption for moving, removing or disposing of asbestos-containing materials on a residential building applies only where the owner occupies the building and it is not for sale or lease, so it does not cover a rental (Fla. Stat. § 469.002(1)(d)); narrow exemptions exist for roofing contractors and for certain nonfriable floor coverings and outdoor pipe, each with conditions (Fla. Stat. § 469.002(2)-(4)). Residential dwellings are exempt from the state's asbestos removal inspection and notification fee (Fla. Stat. § 376.60). Your general duty to comply with building, housing and health codes still applies (Fla. Stat. § 83.51(1)(a)). Cautious course: before renovating an older building, have a licensed consultant survey materials that will be disturbed, and tell tenants about work that may affect them.

title: Well Water in Rentals
bodyText: If your rental gets its drinking water from your own well rather than a utility, Florida's Department of Health rules depend on how many homes the well serves. One or two residences (one of which may be a rental): a "private water system" under the Department's general supervision (Fla. Stat. § 381.0062(1)(k), (2)). Three or four residences, one of which may be a rental: a "multifamily water system," which needs Department approval to construct, modify or operate (Fla. Stat. § 381.0062(1)(h), (2)(b)). Five or more residences, or two or more rental residences: a "limited use community public water system," which needs Department approval and an annual operating permit, a microbiological sample from the distribution system every calendar quarter, and lead and nitrate testing at least every 36 months, all analyzed by a Department-certified laboratory (Fla. Stat. § 381.0062(1)(f), (2)(b), (2)(g); Fla. Admin. Code R. 64E-8.004(1), 64E-8.006(3)). When an acute health risk exists in a limited use community system, the supplier must deliver a printed notice to the people it serves within 4 hours, telling them not to drink the water and what is being done, and later a notice that the problem is fixed (Fla. Admin. Code R. 64E-8.008). As the well's owner you are the "supplier of water," and operating a regulated system without complying is a second-degree misdemeanor (Fla. Stat. § 381.0062(1)(n), (4)(a)). No Florida statute, constitutional provision or civil procedure rule requires a landlord to give routine well test results to tenants or to test a single-home well before each tenancy. Cautious course: test a private well before each new tenancy and give the tenant the results.

title: Code Enforcement Orders (No Receivership)
bodyText: Florida has no statute that lets a court or local government put a substandard rental under a receiver. Florida's receivership provisions concern condominium terminations, assisted living facilities and other businesses, not substandard housing. What Florida does have is local code enforcement under chapter 162. A county or city may set up a code enforcement board or special magistrate (Fla. Stat. § 162.03). When an inspector finds a violation, you get notice and a reasonable time to correct it, then a hearing if it continues; a repeat violation or one posing a serious threat to public health, safety and welfare can go straight to a hearing (Fla. Stat. § 162.06(2)-(4)). If you do not comply by the date set, the board may fine you up to $250 a day for a first violation and $500 a day for a repeat (larger counties and cities may adopt higher limits), and for a serious-threat violation the local government may make reasonable repairs itself and charge you their cost (Fla. Stat. § 162.09(1)-(2)). A recorded fine or repair order becomes a lien on the property and your other real and personal property, which the local government may foreclose after 3 months (except on a homestead) (Fla. Stat. § 162.09(3)). If you sell the property while a case is pending, you must disclose the proceeding in writing to the buyer (Fla. Stat. § 162.06(5)). Separately, the State Fire Marshal may order hazards corrected or a building vacated (Fla. Stat. § 633.228). None of these steps transfers rent collection to a receiver. Tenants keep their own remedies under the landlord-tenant act.

title: No Statutory Rent Bar After Condemnation
bodyText: Florida has no statute that expressly bars a landlord from collecting rent after a building is condemned or ordered vacated. Other rules reach the same practical result in most cases. The State Fire Marshal can order a building vacated or occupancy precluded (Fla. Stat. § 633.228), and local code enforcement can order corrections and repairs (Fla. Stat. §§ 162.06, 162.09). If the unit is damaged or destroyed, other than by the tenant's wrongful or negligent act, so that the tenant's enjoyment is substantially impaired, the tenant may end the lease and move out at once, or vacate the unusable part and pay rent reduced by that part's fair rental value (Fla. Stat. § 83.63). If a failure of your code, structural or plumbing duties makes the unit untenantable, the tenant may end the lease after a 7-day written notice, and where the failure is beyond your control and you keep trying to fix it, a tenant who leaves owes no rent while the unit stays uninhabitable (Fla. Stat. § 83.56(1)). A tenant sued for unpaid rent may defend on your material failure of those duties (Fla. Stat. § 83.60(1)). Cautious course: do not demand rent for any period the unit is under a vacate order, and refund rent paid in advance for that period.

title: No Alternate Housing Duty
bodyText: Florida law does not require a residential landlord to provide or pay for alternate housing while a rental is being repaired or is unfit to live in, whether or not the tenant asks. What the law does instead: rent stops or drops. If the tenant must leave an apartment or other non-house unit for extermination, you must give 7 days' written notice, the tenant need not stay out more than 4 days, and you must abate the rent (but owe no damages) (Fla. Stat. § 83.51(2)(a)1.). If a failure beyond your control makes the unit untenantable and the tenant moves out, the tenant owes no rent while it stays uninhabitable (Fla. Stat. § 83.56(1)(a)). After a casualty not caused by the tenant, the tenant may end the lease or vacate the unusable part and pay reduced rent (Fla. Stat. § 83.63). Florida's statutes have relocation rules for other situations: an optional tenant relocation payment of at least 1 month's rent that a developer may offer when an apartment building is converted to a condominium (Fla. Stat. § 718.606(4)), mobile home park closures and changes of use under chapter 723, and government takings and programs. Cautious course: if repairs you are responsible for force a tenant out for longer than a few days, abate the rent for that time and agree any temporary housing arrangement in writing.

title: No Repair Escrow or Exemption Notice
bodyText: Some states let a landlord with only a few units opt out of tenants' rent-escrow or repair remedies by giving a notice. Florida has nothing to opt out of: there is no statutory rent escrow for repair problems, no repair-and-deduct right, and no small-landlord exemption notice. Under Florida's Residential Landlord and Tenant Act the only place a tenant's rent is held pending a repair dispute is the court registry in your own eviction case: a tenant who raises any defense other than payment, including a withholding defense based on your failure to make repairs, must pay the accrued rent and the rent that comes due into the registry, or lose the defenses (Fla. Stat. § 83.60(2)); if you face actual danger of losing the property or other hardship, you may ask the court to release all or part of the money or to set a prompt final hearing (Fla. Stat. § 83.61). The tenant's other repair remedies (ending the lease after 7 days' written notice, damages) apply to every landlord regardless of size; see "Tenant Remedies When Repairs Aren't Made".

title: Subsidized Tenants and Repair Failures
bodyText: Florida state law has no rule on how a rent subsidy is reduced, prorated or stopped when a subsidized unit fails a habitability or housing-quality standard. For a housing choice voucher or other federal program, the federal program rules and your contract with the housing agency govern abatement of the agency's payments. Florida's Residential Landlord and Tenant Act touches subsidized rent in two places. In an eviction, a public housing tenant or a tenant receiving a rent subsidy who raises a defense other than payment must deposit into the court registry only the part of the rent the tenant owes under the program (Fla. Stat. § 83.60(2)); the court's eviction summons says the same (Form 1.923(a)). And accepting the government's subsidy payment does not waive your right to act on a tenant's noncompliance, though waiver occurs if you do not sue within 45 days after you actually know of it (Fla. Stat. § 83.56(5)(c)). Otherwise the ordinary remedies apply to a subsidized tenant's share as to any rent: the 7-day termination and withholding remedies and a court-ordered rent reduction for a material failure of your code, structural and plumbing duties (Fla. Stat. §§ 83.56(1), 83.60(1)(b)). Cautious course: when an agency abates its payment for a failed inspection, do not bill the tenant for the agency's share, and fix the deficiency within the agency's deadline.

title: No Code Variance Notice to Tenants
bodyText: Florida law does not require a landlord to give tenants, or attach to the lease, a copy of a variance, exception or waiver an agency has granted from a health, sanitary, housing or building code. Florida agencies do grant variances (for example, the Department of Health for septic systems, private and limited-use water systems, public pools and migrant housing, and the Division of Hotels and Restaurants for lodging construction standards), and a variance usually comes with conditions you must keep meeting. The closest rule is for residential migrant housing, where a structural variance must be in writing and state the alternative measures that protect occupants (Fla. Stat. § 381.0086(3)); it requires no notice to occupants and does not reach ordinary rentals. Cautious course: if your rental operates under a variance whose conditions affect the tenant (for example a water-system or septic variance), tell the tenant in writing what the conditions are.

title: Habitability Gaps in Florida Law
bodyText: Florida does have a statutory habitability duty: under its Residential Landlord and Tenant Act you must comply with applicable building, housing and health codes or, where there are none, keep the structure, plumbing and screens in repair, and an apartment landlord must also provide for pest extermination, locks and keys, common areas, garbage removal, heat, running water and hot water (Fla. Stat. § 83.51). This row lists what Florida law does not contain, so you know where the lease and the cautious course have to do the work. Florida's statutes, constitution and civil procedure rules contain no rule that: (1) requires the lease to state that the unit is habitable; (2) creates a presumption about habitability, bad-faith repair delay or retaliation; (3) lets a tenant repair and deduct, or puts rent into an escrow for repairs outside an eviction case (the only deposit is into the court registry in your eviction case); (4) lets a small landlord opt out of repair remedies by notice; (5) requires a stove or refrigerator; (6) sets a water heater temperature; (7) requires you to provide or pay for alternate housing during repairs; (8) expressly bars rent after a condemnation or vacate order; or (9) puts a substandard rental under a receiver. Florida's Residential Landlord and Tenant Act also sets no deadline for starting repairs: the tenant's remedies open 7 days after a written notice (Fla. Stat. §§ 83.56(1), 83.60(1)(b)). Florida's maintenance statute does not list cooling, although licensed apartment buildings must be properly heated and cooled (Fla. Stat. § 509.221(3)). Each gap has its own row with the details and the cautious course. Local housing codes may fill some of these gaps.

title: Eviction Grounds and Cure Notices
bodyText:
Florida's Residential Landlord and Tenant Act (Part II of chapter 83) covers the rental of a dwelling unit. It does not cover transient lodging, a condominium unit occupied by its owner, a cooperative proprietary lessee, certain buyers under a contract of sale, or residence that is incidental to care in a facility.

Under the Act you may end the rental agreement for tenant default on three tracks, each with its own written notice in substantially the form the statute prints.
- (1) Unpaid rent: a demand for payment of the rent or possession within 3 days, not counting Saturdays, Sundays and court-observed legal holidays.
- (2) A breach the tenant can cure: if the tenant materially fails to comply with a material lease term, reasonable rules, or the tenant's statutory maintenance duties (the statute's examples are unauthorized pets, guests or vehicles, unauthorized parking, and not keeping the unit clean and sanitary), you give 7 days to cure; if the tenant doesn't cure, the lease is terminated. If the same or similar conduct recurs within 12 months after the notice, you may file without a new notice.
- (3) A breach the tenant should not get a chance to cure: intentional destruction, damage or misuse of your or other tenants' property, fraudulent entry of a dwelling unit in violation of Fla. Stat. § 817.537(2) (from October 1, 2026, whether or not criminal charges are brought), or a subsequent or continued unreasonable disturbance, or a repeat of similar conduct within 12 months of your written warning. You give a 7-day notice that the lease is terminated, with no cure.

The statute's examples are not a closed list, so a court decides which track an unlisted breach belongs on.

Deliver every notice by mail, by handing over a true copy, by e-mail under a signed e-mail addendum, or, if the tenant is absent, by leaving a copy at the residence. The lease can't waive these notice requirements, so it can't shorten the 3-day or 7-day periods or change how notices are delivered, and Part II has no provision that lets a residential lease set its own cure period (the 15-day cure notice that applies only when the lease is silent is in Part I of chapter 83, which covers nonresidential tenancies and tenancies Part II doesn't govern).

The breach and the lease term must both be material. Part II doesn't let the lease decide which terms are material; that is for the court. Cautious course: where a breach could be seen as curable, use the 7-day cure notice.

If you accept rent knowing of a breach, you waive that breach (but not a later or continuing one).

A separate statute adds a ground: if a tenant doesn't pay a city for utility, water or sewer service, you may start eviction proceedings.

Apart from default, a tenancy also ends when a fixed term expires or on a periodic notice; Florida has no good-cause requirement.

title: Criminal Activity by Tenants
bodyText:
Florida's landlord-tenant act (Part II of chapter 83, which covers the rental of a dwelling unit) has no separate rule for criminal activity by a tenant. It gives no fast-track eviction for violent crime or drug dealing, doesn't require you to evict anyone for a crime, and says nothing about crime-free lease addenda.

Criminal conduct reaches eviction through the ordinary tracks. The tenant must not destroy, damage or remove your property and must not unreasonably disturb the neighbors or breach the peace, and must keep to material lease terms and reasonable rules. Intentional destruction, damage or misuse of property, fraudulent entry into a dwelling unit (from October 1, 2026) and a subsequent or continued unreasonable disturbance are examples of breaches the tenant need not be given a chance to cure: you give a 7-day notice that the lease is terminated. Other breaches get a 7-day notice to cure.

So a crime-free term in the lease is enforceable only as a material lease term on those tracks.

Florida's nuisance laws matter to you as an owner. A dwelling or other place visited for the unlawful use of controlled substances, or used to keep, sell or deliver them, is a public nuisance; willfully keeping or maintaining one in a building is a third-degree felony. The Attorney General, a state attorney, a city or county attorney, the sheriff or any citizen of the county may sue to enjoin a nuisance and the owner of the building. In such a case, if a tenant has been convicted of a drug offense or a prostitution offense, the court may order the tenant to vacate within 72 hours when the tenant and the owner are both parties and the order will end the nuisance.

Counties and cities may also run nuisance abatement boards.

title: Fast Action for Serious Tenant Misconduct
bodyText:
Florida has no separate, faster court track for evicting a residential tenant for criminal or dangerous conduct. Every eviction of a tenant under Part II of chapter 83 (the rental of a dwelling unit) is already filed in county court under a summary procedure that the court must advance on its calendar: the tenant has 5 days after service to answer, and a tenant who raises any defense other than payment must pay the rent into the court registry or face a default and a writ without a hearing.

What Florida does give you for serious conduct:
- (1) No cure period. For intentional destruction, damage or misuse of your or other tenants' property, fraudulent entry into a dwelling unit (from October 1, 2026) or a subsequent or continued unreasonable disturbance, you may give a 7-day notice that the lease is terminated, with no chance to cure, and then file.
- (2) An injunction. If you have given that 7-day notice for intentional destruction, damage or misuse of your property, you may ask the county or circuit court to order the tenant to stop; damage of more than twice the deposit you hold, or $300 if greater, counts as irreparable harm.
- (3) Nuisance abatement. In a suit under chapter 60 to abate a drug house or other statutory nuisance, which public officials or any citizen of the county may bring, the court may order a tenant convicted of a drug or prostitution offense to vacate within 72 hours if the tenant and the owner are both parties and the order will end the nuisance.

title: No Hardship Stay of Eviction
bodyText: Florida's statutes and civil procedure rules contain no rule letting a court postpone a residential tenant's removal because of hardship, such as illness, age, disability, children, weather or trouble finding housing. Once you win a possession judgment under Part II of chapter 83, the clerk issues a writ and the sheriff puts you in possession after posting 24 hours' notice on the property; Saturdays, Sundays and legal holidays don't stop that 24-hour period. What can delay a writ: (1) the court's general power, under the civil procedure rules, to stay execution of a final judgment for good cause on motion and notice to the other parties; (2) a person other than the tenant who is in possession and files an affidavit with the sheriff claiming a right to possession, which stops the sheriff until the court decides; (3) a servicemember called to state active duty who gave you written notice, where the rent is $1,200 a month or less and the unit is the family's home (see "Eviction Stay for State Active Duty"); and (4) an appeal, which must be filed within 30 days of the judgment. A tenant who appeals and wants the writ stayed must first move in the county court, which may grant, modify or deny a stay and may require a bond or other conditions; a stay the trial court enters lasts through the appeal unless modified.

title: Who Can Be Served With Eviction Papers
bodyText: Florida law gives a residential lease no way to name a person who will accept the eviction summons and complaint for the tenant, so don't rely on a lease clause for that. The summons must be served under the service-of-process statutes: by handing it to the tenant, or by leaving it at the tenant's usual home with a resident 15 or older and telling that person what it is. In an action for possession of residential premises, if the tenant can't be found in the county or no one 15 or older lives there after at least two attempts at least 6 hours apart, the summons may be attached to a conspicuous place on the property; you then give the clerk an extra copy of the complaint and a stamped envelope addressed to the tenant at the premises, the clerk mails it, and at least 5 days must pass after service before a final judgment for removal. Service by posting supports possession only: a money judgment for rent needs personal service or another method the law allows. Pre-suit notices (the 3-day and 7-day notices) are different: they may be mailed, handed over, e-mailed under a signed e-mail addendum, or left at the residence if the tenant is absent. One special case: an adult in Florida's Address Confidentiality Program for victims of domestic or dating violence designates the Attorney General as agent for service of process and for mail. If a tenant tells you they are a program participant, get legal advice on serving through the Attorney General as well as at the premises.

title: Who May Act for the Landlord in Court
bodyText: In a Florida eviction of a residential tenant, the complaint may be filed by you, your attorney or your agent, but an agent who is not an attorney may do nothing beyond the initial filing of the complaint. So a property manager or leasing agent can file the complaint for you, but can't sign later motions, ask for a default or a writ, or appear at a hearing unless that person is a Florida attorney. Anyone may conduct his or her own case in court, and practising law without a license is a third-degree felony. Florida's statutes don't say whether a corporation, LLC or partnership that owns the property is itself the landlord, so that its officer may act, or must act through an attorney. The Small Claims Rules, which cover county-court civil actions for money or property worth $8,000 or less, let a business entity be represented at any stage of the trial-court case by a principal (an officer, member, managing member or partner) with authority to bind it, or by an employee a principal authorizes in writing, but not on appeal. Whether that rule reaches a residential possession action, given the statute's limit on non-attorney agents, is unsettled. Cautious course: for a small money-only claim, an entity may appear through a principal or a written-authorized employee; for an eviction, have a Florida attorney handle everything after the complaint is filed.

title: No Right to Undo a Lease Forfeiture
bodyText: When a Florida tenant under Part II of chapter 83 (the rental of a dwelling unit) defaults, the statute gives one chance to keep the tenancy: paying the rent demanded within the 3-day notice period (not counting Saturdays, Sundays and court-observed holidays), or, for a breach the tenant can cure, curing it within the 7 days the notice gives. Florida statutes have no rule that lets a tenant undo the termination later, for example by paying the arrears and your costs after the notice runs out, before trial, after judgment or before the writ is carried out, and none that makes you accept a late payment. Your own conduct can revive the tenancy, though: if you accept rent knowing of the tenant's breach, you waive your right to terminate for that breach (not for a later or continuing one). Accepting partial rent doesn't waive it if, after posting the nonpayment notice, you give a receipt stating the date, amount, agreed date and balance due before you file, or deposit the partial payment in the court registry when you file, or post a new 3-day notice for the new amount due. In court the tenant may raise any legal or equitable defense, but must first pay the rent alleged into the court registry. Whether a court may still relieve a tenant from forfeiture as a matter of fairness is a case-law question.

title: Paying to Stop an Eviction
bodyText: Florida statutes give a residential tenant no right to stop an eviction by paying what is owed after the 3-day notice period has run, whether before trial, after judgment or before the sheriff executes the writ, and nothing in them says paying the money judgment stops the writ for possession. They prescribe no reservation wording for accepting a partial payment. Instead, if you accept partial rent after posting the nonpayment notice, you keep your right to evict only if you do one of three things: give the tenant a receipt stating the date and amount received and the agreed date and balance due before you file; put the partial payment into the court registry when you file; or post a new 3-day notice for the new amount due. Accepting rent knowing of a breach, other than partial rent handled that way, waives that breach. No Florida statute requires you to accept rent paid by a charity or government program on the tenant's behalf, or bars you from limiting how such payments are made; for the part of the rent paid by a government subsidy, waiver occurs only if you don't sue within 45 days after learning of the breach. Once the case is filed, a tenant who wants to contest it must deposit the rent alleged into the court registry; that deposit preserves defenses, it doesn't redeem the tenancy.

title: No Possession Bond
bodyText: Florida statutes provide no possession bond for residential tenancies: no end-of-term bond a tenant posts to secure surrender, no bond with a confessed judgment for possession, and no bond you must post to get possession before trial. In a residential eviction under Part II of chapter 83, the security mechanism is the court registry instead: a tenant who raises any defense other than payment must deposit the accrued rent alleged in the complaint, and the rent that falls due while the case is pending, or lose those defenses and face an immediate default and writ. Bonds do appear in Part I of chapter 83, which covers nonresidential tenancies and tenancies Part II doesn't govern: a tenant whose property is seized under a distress writ for rent may get it back by giving a bond with surety. Don't put a confession of judgment or warrant of attorney in a residential lease (see the library's row on lease terms Florida voids).

title: Tenant Property After the Writ
bodyText: After a Florida court enters a possession judgment for you under Part II of chapter 83, the sheriff executes the writ after 24 hours' posted notice. When the sheriff executes the writ, or at any time afterward, you or your agent may remove any personal property found in the unit to or near the property line. You may ask the sheriff to stand by to keep the peace while you change the locks and remove the property, at a reasonable hourly rate the sheriff sets, which the person asking pays. Neither you, your agent nor the sheriff is liable to the tenant or anyone else for loss, destruction or damage to the property after it has been removed. Florida's statutes set no duty to store, inventory or care for the property after a writ, and no rule for animals left behind. Instead of putting property at the property line, you may use the optional procedure in Florida's Disposition of Personal Property Landlord and Tenant Act, which applies to property left after a tenancy ends by eviction, surrender, abandonment or otherwise: written notice, storage with reasonable care and a sale or disposal (see "Property Left Behind After a Tenancy").

title: Rent Paid Into Court During an Eviction
bodyText: In a Florida action for possession of a dwelling unit, a tenant who raises any defense other than payment, including a claim that your 3-day notice was defective, must pay into the court registry the accrued rent alleged in your complaint (or the amount the court sets) and keep paying the rent as it falls due while the case is pending. The tenant must pay, or file a motion asking the court to decide the amount with documents showing your figure is wrong, within 5 days after service, not counting Saturdays, Sundays and legal holidays. The clerk's eviction summons tells the tenant this. If the tenant does neither, the tenant has absolutely waived every defense except payment and you are entitled to an immediate default judgment for removal and a writ without further notice or hearing; the court may not set mediation or trial until the deposit rule is met. A tenant in public housing or receiving a rent subsidy deposits only the tenant's own share. If you are in actual danger of losing the property, or face other personal hardship from the lost rent, you may ask the court to release all or part of the deposited money to you or to hold a prompt final hearing. The tenant may also defend a nonpayment case on your material failure to maintain the unit, after a 7-day written notice from the tenant, and the court then decides how much the rent is reduced. Under the civil rules, a claim the tenant has against you that arises out of the same transaction or occurrence as your claim must generally be raised as a counterclaim in the case. Part II doesn't say whether a counterclaim excuses the deposit; the nonresidential part of chapter 83 says it doesn't, and the cautious course is to treat the deposit as required either way. Florida has no rule requiring rent into court because a trial is postponed beyond the pending-rent rule.

title: No Self-Help Eviction
bodyText: For a dwelling unit covered by Florida's Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, self-help eviction is prohibited. You may recover possession only through a court action in which the right to possession is decided, or when the tenant has surrendered or abandoned the unit, or in the narrow case of a deceased last remaining tenant that the statute describes. You may not, directly or indirectly, cut off or interrupt any utility service to the tenant (water, heat, light, electricity, gas, elevator, garbage collection, refrigeration and others), even if the service is in your name or you pay for it. You may not keep the tenant out by changing the locks or using a bootlock or similar device. You may not remove outside doors, locks, the roof, walls or windows except for maintenance, repair or replacement, and you may not remove the tenant's belongings except after surrender, abandonment, recovery of possession after the last tenant's death, or a lawful eviction. If you violate any of these rules, you owe the tenant actual and consequential damages or 3 months' rent, whichever is greater, plus costs and attorney's fees, and each later violation that isn't part of the same incident is a separate award. A violation counts as irreparable harm, so the tenant can get an injunction, and the tenant keeps every other remedy. Each rule is a separate violation, so a utility shutoff alone triggers the remedy.

title: 3-Day Notice for Unpaid Rent
bodyText:
Before you can terminate a Florida residential rental agreement for unpaid rent, you must deliver a written demand for payment of the rent or possession of the premises, and the tenant must have 3 days to pay, not counting Saturdays, Sundays and legal holidays (court-observed holidays only).

The notice must contain a statement in substantially this form, filling in the amount, the property address including the county, the deadline date, and your name, address and phone number: 'You are hereby notified that you are indebted to me in the sum of ... dollars for the rent and use of the premises (address of leased premises, including county) ... Florida, now occupied by you and that I demand payment of the rent or possession of the premises within 3 days (excluding Saturday, Sunday, and legal holidays) from the date of delivery of this notice, to wit: on or before the ... day of ... (year) ... (landlord’s name, address and phone number)' (Fla. Stat. § 83.56(3)).

Demand only rent: late fees and other charges count as rent only if your written lease designates them as rent. Deliver the notice by mail, by handing over a true copy, by e-mail under a signed e-mail addendum, or, if the tenant is absent, by leaving a copy at the residence.

The lease can't waive this notice, shorten the 3 days or make itself the notice. The statute counts the 3 days from delivery and adds no extra days when you mail the notice. A court rule adds 5 days when a party must act within a set time after service by mail, but whether it reaches this pre-suit notice is unsettled, so if you mail the notice, set the deadline date at least 5 days later than the 3-day count, or deliver it by hand.

If the tenant pays in full within the 3 days, the default is cured. If you accept partial rent after posting the notice, follow the receipt, registry or new-notice rule to keep your right to evict.

title: No Good-Cause Notice Requirement
bodyText: Florida doesn't require a residential landlord to state or have a reason (good cause) in a notice ending a tenancy or declining to renew. A fixed-term lease ends on its end date, and either party may end a month-to-month or other periodic tenancy by written notice of the length the statute sets, without giving a reason (see "No Just-Cause Eviction Rule" and "Ending a Month-to-Month or Other Periodic Tenancy"). Good cause matters in one place: a tenant may defend an eviction as retaliation for protected activity, and that defense fails if you prove the eviction is for good cause, such as a good-faith action for nonpayment of rent or for violation of the rental agreement, reasonable rules or the statute. Mobile home park lot tenancies under chapter 723 are different: there a park owner may evict only on the grounds that chapter lists. Cities and counties can't add a good-cause rule because state law preempts local regulation of residential tenancies.

title: No Cold-Weather Eviction Rule
bodyText: Florida has no cold-weather rule: no statute or civil procedure rule requires a special notice before a residential tenant is made to vacate in winter or bars evictions or writs during cold weather. The ordinary notices and the 24-hour writ notice apply all year. Heat is a maintenance duty instead: for a dwelling unit other than a single-family home or duplex, unless otherwise agreed in writing, you must make reasonable provisions for functioning facilities for heat during winter.

title: Landlord's Remedies on Termination
bodyText: When a Florida rental agreement for a dwelling unit is terminated and the tenant doesn't leave, you recover possession by filing a complaint in the county court of the county where the unit is, using the summary procedure. In a possession case based on unpaid rent, if the court finds rent due, owing and unpaid, it must also enter a money judgment with costs for the unpaid amount, within its jurisdictional limit, but only if the tenant was served personally or by another method the law allows for money judgments (posting alone is not enough). Either party may recover the damages caused by the other's failure to comply with the rental agreement or the statute, so you can sue for unpaid rent with or without terminating, and a tenant sued for rent may raise the same defenses as in a possession case. If a tenant holds over without permission after the lease expires, you may also recover double the rent for the holdover period. Once you have a writ, or the tenant surrenders or abandons, you choose among the remedies in "Landlord's Remedies When a Tenant Leaves Early": end the tenant's liability, relet for the tenant's account, let rent accrue, or collect agreed liquidated damages or an early termination fee. The prevailing party in an action to enforce the rental agreement or the statute recovers reasonable attorney fees and court costs. County courts hear actions at law up to $50,000 (for cases filed on or after January 1, 2023), excluding interest, costs and attorney fees, and the simpler Small Claims Rules apply to county-court civil actions for money or property worth $8,000 or less.

title: Deadlines to Sue
bodyText: Florida's statute of limitations sets how long you have to sue a tenant (or a tenant to sue you), counted from when the claim accrues, which is when its last element occurs; for unpaid rent that is generally each due date. Claims on a written lease must be brought within 5 years. Claims on an oral rental agreement, or another contract not founded on a written instrument, must be brought within 4 years, and so must an action founded on a statutory liability. An action on a judgment of a Florida court of record may be brought within 20 years. A lease clause that gives less time than the statute is void. Partial payments: a payment of any part of the principal or interest of an obligation founded on a written instrument tolls (pauses) the running of the time; the statute gives no such rule for oral agreements. Once a debt is barred, an acknowledgment or promise to pay it counts only if it is in writing and signed by the tenant. The time is also tolled while the tenant is absent from Florida, uses a false name or hides so that process can't be served, unless service, including service by publication, can still be made.

title: Minors as Tenants
bodyText: In Florida the age of majority is 18: a person 18 or older has the rights and obligations of an adult and can sign a binding lease. A person under 18 generally lacks the capacity to contract, with these exceptions: a minor who is or has been married has the disability of nonage removed and may contract and sue and be sued; a circuit court may remove the disabilities of nonage of a minor 16 or older on petition, giving the minor the status of an adult; a 17-year-old in foster care or subsidized independent living may, with a court order, sign a residential lease that starts on the youth's 18th birthday; and a certified unaccompanied homeless youth 16 or older may petition to have the disabilities removed. Ask for the court order or proof of marriage before leasing to a minor. In an eviction, the defendant is the tenant, meaning a person entitled to occupy under the rental agreement; household members who are not parties to the agreement are not tenants. If a minor is a party, the court must appoint a guardian ad litem for a minor who isn't otherwise represented, or make another order to protect the minor. The statutes and rules read set no other bar on naming a minor in an eviction.

title: Late Benefit or Voucher Payments
bodyText: Florida statutes and civil procedure rules give a tenant no defense, continuance or reinstatement in an eviction because a Social Security check, another government benefit or a housing voucher payment arrived late. The ordinary rules apply: rent is due when the lease says (without demand, at the start of each period, unless otherwise agreed), and your 3-day notice gives the tenant 3 days, not counting weekends and court holidays, to pay. Two subsidy rules protect assisted tenants. In an eviction, a tenant in public housing or receiving a rent subsidy has to deposit into the court registry only the tenant's own share of the rent under the program. And the waiver-by-acceptance rule doesn't apply to the subsidy portion of the rent, but you waive a breach if you don't file within 45 days after learning of it. Under the federal rule for tenancies with a housing assistance payment (HAP) contract between you and a public housing agency, the family isn't responsible for the part of the rent the housing assistance payment covers, the housing agency's failure to pay is not a lease violation by the tenant, and during the lease term you may not terminate the tenancy for the agency's nonpayment; take up a missed payment with the agency.

title: When a Tenant Files Bankruptcy
bodyText: Florida's statutes and civil procedure rules say nothing about what happens to a residential eviction when the tenant files for bankruptcy, and Florida has no statute directing the sheriff to enforce a writ despite notice of a filing. Federal bankruptcy law controls. A bankruptcy petition generally operates as an automatic stay of starting or continuing a court case against the tenant, enforcing a judgment obtained before the filing, and any act to obtain possession of property of the bankruptcy estate. Two exceptions matter to landlords. (1) Judgment before filing: if you got a judgment for possession of the tenant's home before the petition was filed, the stay doesn't stop you continuing the eviction. But if the tenant files with the petition a sworn certification that state law would let the tenant cure the entire monetary default after the judgment, and deposits with the bankruptcy court clerk the rent due for the next 30 days, the exception applies only 30 days after the filing, and it is lost if within those 30 days the tenant certifies having cured the whole default under state law, unless the court orders otherwise. Florida's statutes give a tenant no right to cure after a possession judgment (see "Paying to Stop an Eviction"). If the petition shows a possession judgment and the tenant files no certification, the exception applies immediately and you need no relief from the stay to finish recovering possession. (2) Endangerment or drugs: an eviction based on the tenant endangering the property or illegally using controlled substances there is excepted if you file with the bankruptcy court, and serve on the tenant, a sworn certification that the eviction has been filed or that the tenant did so in the past 30 days; the exception applies 15 days later unless the tenant files an objection. In every other case, don't serve notices, file, ask for a writ or collect past-due rent after a filing without legal advice or a bankruptcy court order.

title: Barring Non-Tenants From the Property
bodyText: Florida's general trespass laws let an owner or lessee, or a person the owner authorizes, keep people off rental property. A person who enters or stays in a building without being authorized, licensed or invited, or who was invited but is warned by the owner, lessee or an authorized person to leave and refuses, commits trespass in a structure. Outdoor areas are covered if notice against entering or remaining has been given, either by telling the person directly or by posting signs, fencing or cultivation as the statute describes; enclosed land of 5 acres or less with a dwelling house on it needs no posting. An "authorized person" who may order someone to leave outdoor property includes the owner's agent, a community association authorized as the owner's agent, and a law enforcement officer whose department has the owner's written authorization to communicate an order to leave when public safety is threatened. Limits: these are criminal statutes about people who are not authorized, licensed or invited. Your tenant has the right to use the unit and the common areas held out for tenants generally, and a tenant's invited guest is not plainly "uninvited". Before you bar a tenant's guest, record the reason, give the person written notice naming the areas covered, and get legal advice; no Florida statute sets up a landlord "no-trespass list" procedure. Removing a tenant is never a trespass matter: it takes an eviction.

title: Double Letting
bodyText: Florida has no statute on double letting, that is, renting the same unit or room to two tenants for the same period, and none that sets a rent-abatement or other special remedy when you can't deliver possession. The general rules apply. If you fail to comply with a material provision of the rental agreement, the tenant may give you a 7-day written notice and then terminate, and either party may recover the damages caused by the other's noncompliance with the rental agreement. Money a tenant pays as a deposit or advance rent is deposit money you must hold and account for under the security deposit rules. The library's "Possession Delay" clause, which carries Florida, gives the tenant rent abatement and a right to cancel if you can't deliver possession by the start date. Practical course: keep one booking record per unit, don't take a second deposit or application for a unit already promised, and refund promptly if a letting falls through. Whether a double letting is also an unfair or deceptive practice is outside the sections read (see "Florida Consumer Protection Law and Leases").

title: Holdover Rent
bodyText:
Florida sets the holdover rate by statute for dwelling units under Part II of chapter 83.

If a tenant stays after the rental agreement expires without your permission, you may recover possession through an eviction and also recover double the rent due for the period the tenant refuses to surrender possession. If the tenant stays with your permission after the agreement ends and doesn't give the 30-day notice a month-to-month tenant must give, the tenant owes you one additional month's rent.

Florida sets no cap on a lease-stated holdover charge and no separate rule for subsidized units, so the statutory double rent is the measure the library uses; a lease charge above it could be challenged as an unenforceable penalty or as unconscionable. Accepting rent from a holdover tenant may create a month-to-month tenancy (see the shared "holdover" clause).

title: Tenancies Without a Fixed Term
bodyText: For a residential rental of a dwelling unit, Florida's Residential Landlord and Tenant Act (Part II of chapter 83) treats a rental with no fixed end date as a periodic tenancy. If the rental agreement says nothing about duration, the tenancy runs by the rent period: week to week if rent is payable weekly, month to month if monthly, and so on. An oral agreement is a rental agreement under Part II if it is for less than a year. Either party may end a periodic residential tenancy by written notice delivered as the statute requires: at least 7 days before the end of a weekly period, 30 days before the end of a monthly or quarterly period, or 60 days before the end of a yearly period. The older "tenancy at will" rules in Part I of chapter 83 (an unwritten lease is a tenancy at will; notice of 7 days weekly, 15 days monthly, 45 days quarterly or 3 months yearly; holding over after a written term is a tenancy at sufferance) apply to nonresidential tenancies and tenancies Part II doesn't govern, not to an ordinary residential rental. A residential tenant who stays after the agreement ends without your permission is a holdover you may evict and charge double rent; one who stays with permission becomes month to month and owes an extra month's rent if leaving without the 30-day notice.

title: Seasonal and Short-Term Rentals
bodyText: Florida has no special category of seasonal tenancy, such as one that ends automatically at the end of a season or skips the usual removal procedure. What matters is whether the stay is a tenancy or transient lodging. Florida's Residential Landlord and Tenant Act doesn't apply to transient occupancy in a hotel, condominium, motel, roominghouse or similar public lodging, and transient occupancy means the parties intend the stay to be temporary. Under the lodging law, a unit rented to guests more than three times a year for less than 30 days at a time, or held out as regularly rented that way, is a transient public lodging establishment, and a vacation rental is a condominium or cooperative unit or a house of up to four units used that way. Occupancy at a hotel, motel or vacation rental is transient unless a written rental agreement says the unit is the guest's sole residence. Lodging operators have their own licensing and guest-removal rules. If instead you rent a dwelling for a season as a home, the Act applies: state the exact end date in the agreement, because a fixed term ends on that date, and a tenant who stays without your permission must be removed by eviction and owes double rent for the holdover. Short rentals may also carry Florida's transient rentals tax (see "Sales Tax on Short Rentals").

title: When a Tenant May End a Lease Early
bodyText:
Florida statutes let a residential tenant end a lease early, without owing rent for the rest of the term, in these situations.
- (1) Your material noncompliance: if you materially fail to comply with your maintenance duties under the code-or-structure rule, or with material provisions of the rental agreement, within 7 days after the tenant's written notice specifying the problem and stating the intent to terminate, the tenant may terminate.
- (2) Casualty: if the premises are damaged or destroyed, other than by the tenant's wrongful or negligent acts, so that enjoyment is substantially impaired, the tenant may terminate and move out immediately; you must then give the tenant a chance to collect belongings when it is safe, or notice of a date within a reasonable time (see "Fire or Casualty: The Tenant's Options").
- (3) Military service: a servicemember may terminate on at least 30 days' written notice with a copy of the orders or a commanding officer's verification, for the listed reasons such as permanent change of station 35 miles or more away; the tenant owes rent prorated to the termination date and nothing more, and this right can't be waived or modified (see "Servicemember Rights").
- (4) Flood loss after a missing flood disclosure: for a rental agreement of 1 year or longer, if you didn't give the required flood disclosure and the tenant suffers substantial loss or damage to personal property from flooding (repair or replacement costing 50 percent or more of its market value), the tenant may terminate by written notice and surrendering possession within 30 days after the loss; you refund rent paid in advance for the period after termination (see "Flood Disclosure clause").

Florida has no statutory early termination for domestic violence (see "No Domestic Violence Lease Termination Right"), or for age, illness or moving to care (see "Early Termination for Illness or Care"), and the Part II sections read give none for the landlord's fraudulent misrepresentation.

Beyond these, a tenant may leave early only as the lease allows, for example under an early termination fee addendum the tenant signed (see "Early Termination clause").

title: Early Termination for Illness or Care
bodyText: Florida has no statute that lets an ordinary residential tenant end a lease early because of age, illness or disability, or because the tenant must move into a nursing home, assisted living or other care facility, and no rule that ends a periodic tenancy on a party's incapacity. Unless the lease gives that right, a tenant who leaves early for those reasons is treated like any other tenant who ends a fixed term early, and a month-to-month tenant can leave on the ordinary written notice. The one statutory rule is for assisted living facilities with 60 or more apartments that use leases: their lease must end automatically, without financial penalty, on the resident's death or relocation for psychiatric hospitalization or for medical reasons needing care beyond the facility's license. When the last remaining tenant dies, see "When the Last Tenant Dies". A request from a tenant with a disability to be released early may be a request for a reasonable accommodation under fair housing law (see "Fair Housing"); consider it rather than refusing automatically.

title: No Landlord Termination After a Disaster
bodyText: Florida gives a residential landlord no statutory right to end a lease because of a hurricane, flood, sinkhole, contamination or other environmental event. Florida's statutes give the tenant the termination rights instead. If the premises are damaged or destroyed, other than by the tenant's wrongful or negligent acts, so that the tenant's enjoyment is substantially impaired, the tenant may end the lease and leave at once, or move out of the unusable part and pay rent reduced by that part's fair rental value; you must give the tenant a chance to collect belongings when it is safe, or notice of a date within a reasonable time. Separately, a tenant on a lease of a year or more who suffers substantial flood damage to personal property may terminate if you didn't give the required flood disclosure. The library doesn't offer an optional landlord casualty-termination clause for Florida: a lease term that lets you end the lease after a casualty could cut off the tenant's statutory choice to stay in the usable part at reduced rent, and a provision that purports to waive or preclude rights under the Act is void. If the unit can't be lived in, work with the tenant to end the lease by agreement or rely on the tenant's statutory rights.

title: While a Notice to Vacate Is Pending
bodyText: Florida has no general statute limiting what you may do to the unit or the tenancy while a notice to vacate is running, such as a ban on alterations that make the unit unlivable. The tenancy and your duties simply continue until it ends: you must keep meeting your maintenance obligations, may not cut off utilities, change the locks or remove doors, windows or the tenant's property, and may not raise rent, cut services or bring an eviction mainly to retaliate against a tenant's protected activity. One special regime applies in a condominium conversion. After a developer gives the written notice of intended conversion, tenants who have lived there 180 days may extend an expiring lease on the same terms for up to 270 days after the notice (others up to 180 days), may cancel on 30 days' notice as the statute allows, and tenants who don't buy keep the same rights, privileges and services that tenants had before the notice and that purchasers receive, for the rest of the lease and any extension (see "Condominium Conversion: Tenant Rights").

title: Condominium Conversion: Tenant Rights
bodyText:
If you convert an existing residential building to condominium in Florida, the Condominium Act's conversion part (the Roth Act) protects your residential tenants.

Notice: before or at the same time as the first offering of any unit, you must deliver a dated, written notice of intended conversion to all tenants, all within a 72-hour period, containing the statement the statute prescribes (with its capitalized phrases in conspicuous type), after filing the notice with and getting it approved by the Division of Florida Condominiums, Timeshares, and Mobile Homes. Your notices to tenants count as given when mailed by certified or registered mail to the tenant's last known residence.

Extensions: a tenant who has lived there for the 180 days before the notice may extend an expiring lease on the same terms to end no later than 270 days after the notice; other tenants up to 180 days; the tenant must tell you in writing within 45 days. You may instead offer 180-day residents whose leases expire within 180 days a cash relocation payment of at least 1 month's rent for a shorter extension of up to 180 days. A county with a rental vacancy rate of 3 percent or less may add 90 days by ordinance.

Cancellation: after the notice, a tenant may end a lease, or an extension, with an unexpired term of 180 days or less on 30 days' written notice (older leases have limits).

Purchase: a 180-day resident has a right of first refusal; you must deliver purchase materials within 90 days of the notice (each late day extends the lease a day), the tenant has at least 45 days to decide, and if you later offer the unit at a lower price the tenant gets 10 more days. Tenants who don't buy keep the same rights, privileges and services as before the notice and as purchasers get.

A lease clause can't shorten the extension period or let you end a lease because of the conversion, except a lease signed after all tenants received the notice that conspicuously states the building will be converted, which may let you terminate on 60 days' written notice (see "Condominium Conversion Termination clause"). No Florida statute requires a conversion statement as the first clause of an ordinary lease.

Cooperative conversions and mobile home park changes of use have their own rules.

title: Tenant Absences
bodyText:
Florida law doesn't require a residential tenant to tell you about an extended absence, but the tenant's notice changes two of your rights, so a lease term asking for it is useful.

Abandonment: unless you actually know the tenant has abandoned the unit, it is presumed abandoned if the tenant is absent for half the rent period (for example, 15 days on a monthly lease), but not if the rent is current or the tenant has notified you in writing of an intended absence. Entry: you may enter when the tenant has been absent for half the rent period, but if the rent is current and the tenant has told you of the absence, you may enter only with consent or to protect or preserve the premises (you may always enter for that purpose).

Either party may recover damages caused by the other's failure to comply with the rental agreement, so a tenant who ignores a lease notice term is liable for the harm it causes.

The library offers an optional clause ("Notice of Extended Absence clause").

title: Rent Due Without Demand; Demand Before Eviction
bodyText: Unless the lease says otherwise, Florida rent is payable without any demand or notice from you, periodic rent is due at the start of each rent period, and rent is apportioned day by day. But before you can terminate the rental agreement for unpaid rent, you must deliver the written 3-day demand for payment of the rent or possession, in substantially the statute's form, and the tenant must fail to pay within 3 days not counting Saturdays, Sundays and court-observed holidays (see "3-Day Notice for Unpaid Rent"). The lease can't waive that demand. A lease may say rent is paid without deduction, but it can't take away the tenant's statutory defense: after giving you 7 days' written notice of your material failure to maintain the unit and of the intent to withhold rent, the tenant may defend a nonpayment case on that ground and the court reduces the rent for the period of noncompliance. A provision that purports to waive rights or remedies under the Act is void.

title: Interest on Unpaid Rent and Damages
bodyText:
Florida has a legal interest rate that applies when interest accrues without a contract rate: the rate the Chief Financial Officer sets each quarter for judgments (the federal discount rate averaged over 12 months plus 4 percentage points). A money judgment you win bears that rate, stated on its face and adjusted each January 1 to the rate then in effect, until paid.

For a residential tenancy, whether interest runs on unpaid rent or damages before judgment without a lease term is a case-law question (the older rule that every rent contract bears interest from the due date is in Part I of chapter 83, which covers nonresidential tenancies and tenancies Part II doesn't govern). If you want interest, put a rate in the lease (see "Interest on Unpaid Amounts clause").

Florida's usury law caps contract interest: a contract for interest on any loan, forbearance to collect a debt or "any obligation whatever" at more than the equivalent of 18 percent a year simple interest (for amounts of $500,000 or less) is usurious. Keep any lease rate at or below 18 percent simple, and don't stack interest on an amount that already carries a late fee, since charges in the nature of interest count toward the cap.

title: No Shutdown Rent Protection
bodyText: Florida has no statute that delays rent, bars eviction or requires a payment plan for federal or other government workers who go unpaid during a government shutdown. The ordinary rules apply: rent is due when the lease says, and your 3-day notice gives the tenant 3 days, not counting weekends and court holidays, to pay. The closest Florida rule protects service members called to state active duty: if the service member has given you written notice, the rent is $1,200 a month or less and the unit is the family's home, an eviction may not proceed during the duty and the court may stay it for up to 3 months (see "Eviction Stay for State Active Duty"). A payment plan with an affected tenant is a business choice.

title: No Energy Data Release Law
bodyText:
Florida has no law on releasing a tenant's energy or water usage data to you, and no building energy benchmarking requirement for residential rentals.

What does exist: an electric utility under the Public Service Commission's jurisdiction must, on the customer's request and not more than once a year, give the customer a statement of the customer's actual consumption for each billing period in the past 12 months. So if the tenant holds the account, the tenant can get the history and share it with you.

If you want usage data for a unit whose account is in the tenant's name, ask in the lease for the tenant's consent: the optional clause "Energy Usage Data Authorization" (tagged for Florida) has the tenant sign the utility's own release on request, and lets the tenant withdraw consent without breaching the lease.

title: Billing Tenants for Utilities: No Required Disclosure
bodyText: Florida prescribes no lease disclosure, notice or form for billing tenants for submetered, allocated or resold utilities. What Florida does regulate is how much you may charge. Electricity: where the electric utility does not meter each unit, you may allocate or submeter only your actual cost of the electricity billed to your account, with no late, returned-check or billing charges and no cost for your own wiring behind the master meter. Gas: if you distribute master-metered gas and charge for it on top of the rent, the gas resale rule applies, and submetering is allowed only in the narrow class of buildings the rule names. Water and sewer: you stay outside Public Service Commission regulation if you charge nothing extra, or if your fee is no more than the actual purchase price of the water and wastewater service plus your actual cost of meter reading and billing, which may not exceed 9 percent of the actual cost of service. The electric and gas rules govern service from utilities under the Commission's jurisdiction, not city utilities or electric cooperatives. Cautious course: before signing, tell the tenant in the lease which utilities you bill, how you measure or split them, that you pass on only your cost, and that you will show the utility bill on request; the optional clause "Shared or Submetered Utilities" does this. You may never cut off a utility to collect these charges.

title: Submetering Electricity
bodyText:
Florida's Public Service Commission rules require the electric utility itself to meter each separate unit of new residential buildings, condominiums, cooperatives, and mobile home and recreational vehicle parks. Exceptions include units built under a permit issued before January 1, 1981 that have been master-metered continuously since then, electricity for central heating, ventilating and air conditioning, specialized housing such as dormitories, and transient public lodging.

Where master metering is lawfully used, you as the customer of record or owner may split the bill among units, including by submeter, but only to recover your actual cost: the charges in the utility's tariff plus taxes and fees, with no late fees, returned-check fees, billing costs or charges for your own wiring. A utility customer takes electricity for its own use and not for use by others unless the Commission authorizes it, and this cost-allocation rule is that authorization, so charging tenants more than your cost falls outside it. Florida's statute and the Commission's rules do not settle whether doing so would make you a regulated public utility.

Each utility must file a submetering policy in its tariff, so check your utility's policy before you submeter. These rules govern utilities under the Commission's jurisdiction; if a city utility or an electric cooperative serves the building, ask that utility for its rules.

Florida requires no submetering disclosure to tenants (see "Billing Tenants for Utilities: No Required Disclosure").

title: What You May Charge for Utilities You Pay
bodyText:
If you pay a utility and charge tenants for it, Florida caps what you may collect.
- Electricity from a utility under the Public Service Commission's jurisdiction: what you collect from tenants, by submeter or any other split, may reimburse you for no more than your actual cost of the electricity billed to your account. Your cost means the utility's tariff charges plus taxes and fees; it does not include late fees, returned-check fees, your cost of billing the units, or your wiring behind the master meter.
- Gas: if you charge tenants for master-metered gas on top of the rent, the Commission's gas resale rule applies, and submetering is allowed only in the narrow class of buildings the rule names, again at cost. The safe course is to include gas in the rent.
- Water and sewer: you stay outside Commission regulation only if your charge is no more than the actual purchase price of the water and wastewater service plus your actual cost of meter reading and billing, and that add-on may not exceed 9 percent of the actual cost of service.

A fixed utility allowance with the tenant paying the overage is lawful if the total you collect stays within these caps. The rules name no penalty for a landlord who charges more; the Commission's penalty statutes reach entities subject to its jurisdiction, and whether an overcharging landlord is one is unsettled.

Cautious course: keep each month's utility bill and your calculation, and refund any overcharge.

title: No Cutoff of Submetered Utilities
bodyText: If you submeter a utility or bill tenants for service that runs through your own account, you may not shut off or interrupt that service to collect what a tenant owes. Florida's landlord-tenant act bars a landlord from causing, directly or indirectly, the termination or interruption of any utility service furnished to the tenant, including water, heat, light, electricity and gas, whether or not you control or pay for the service. This covers every dwelling unit under the act, so there is no notice or procedure that lets you disconnect submetered service. If you violate it, you owe the tenant actual and consequential damages or three months' rent, whichever is greater, plus costs and attorney fees, and a later separate violation brings a separate award. The 5-working-day disconnection notice in the Public Service Commission rules is a rule for the utility and its customer, not a route for you. To collect unpaid charges, sue for them, or, if a written lease designates the charges as rent, use the 3-day notice for nonpayment of rent. The optional clause "Shared or Submetered Utilities" sets the billing terms and repeats the no-cutoff rule.

title: Utilities in Your Name
bodyText:
When a utility account serving a tenant is in your name, for example a master meter or water you keep in your name at a house, Florida puts the risk on you.

The landlord-tenant act bars you from causing, directly or indirectly, the termination or interruption of any utility service furnished to the tenant, and it says so expressly for service you control or pay for. If your unpaid bill leads the utility to cut off a tenant's service, you face liability for actual and consequential damages or three months' rent, whichever is greater, plus costs and attorney fees. In a unit other than a single-family home or duplex you must also make reasonable provision for heat during winter, running water and hot water, unless you agreed otherwise in writing.

A utility's disconnection notice goes to its customer, which is you, not your tenants. Florida's statutes and the Public Service Commission's electric, gas and water rules have no rule requiring a utility to notify tenants before cutting off a landlord's account, no statute letting tenants pay your bill and deduct it from rent, and no rent receivership for unpaid landlord utilities.

If a material lease provision promises a utility and you materially fail to provide it, the tenant may give you written notice and end the lease if you have not complied within 7 days after the notice is delivered.

Cautious course: pay these accounts on time, and ask your electric and gas utilities to send copies of any delinquency notice to a designated third party such as your manager.

title: No Cutoff When a Tenant Does Not Transfer Utilities
bodyText: You may require a tenant to put utilities in the tenant's own name: Florida's landlord-tenant act lets the rental agreement make the tenant pay for water, fuel, garbage removal and other utilities, and the library's utilities-responsibility clause has the tenant arrange and pay for them directly. But if the tenant does not transfer a service that is still in your name, you may not cut it off or close the account to force the transfer.
