The act bars you from causing, directly or indirectly, the termination or interruption of any utility service furnished to the tenant, whether or not you control or pay for it; a violation costs actual and consequential damages or three months' rent, whichever is greater, plus costs and attorney fees. This applies to every dwelling unit the act covers, and a lease term allowing a cutoff would not change it. Instead: keep the account open, bill the tenant for the service under the lease, and if the tenant does not pay or transfer, treat it as a lease violation (a 7-day notice to cure is the likely route) or, if the written lease designates the charge as rent, use the 3-day notice for rent. Close your account only after the tenant's own account is active.

title: Utility Deposits
bodyText: A deposit paid to a utility is between the utility and its customer, whoever holds the account. For utilities the Public Service Commission regulates (investor-owned electric and gas utilities, and the water and sewer utilities under its jurisdiction): the utility pays at least 2 percent simple interest a year once the deposit has been held six months; refunds a residential customer's deposit after 23 months of continuous service with a good payment record; and when service ends may apply the deposit and interest to the final bill but must return any balance promptly, and no later than 15 days after service is discontinued. So if the account is in the tenant's name, the refund goes to the tenant; if it is in your name, it comes to you. A city may, by ordinance, apply a utility deposit it holds from an occupant or tenant to that person's unpaid charges. City utilities and electric cooperatives set their own deposit terms. If you collect your own money from a tenant to secure utilities you pay, it is deposit money under Florida's landlord-tenant act, and the security deposit rules apply (see "Florida Security Deposit Rules").

title: Utility Liens for a Tenant's Unpaid Bills
bodyText: Florida law can make unpaid water and sewer charges a lien on your rental property even when your tenant ran them up. Charges owed to a county water and sewer district are a lien on the property served, ranking ahead of the owner's, lessee's and tenant's interests, and the district may foreclose it like a mortgage once the charges are 30 days in default. A city that has issued revenue bonds for its water, sewer or gas system has a lien on the premises served for unpaid service charges, which it may foreclose once they are more than 30 days delinquent. Neither statute exempts an owner because a tenant contracted for the service. Florida's protection is for a former occupant's debt: a city or county utility may not refuse or cut off service because a former occupant left charges unpaid, and those charges may not be the basis for a lien on the rental property unless the current owner or tenant benefited directly; the rule applies where the former occupant contracted for the service (or, for a city, where the city knew the occupant's name and service period) (see "Utilities: Former Occupant's Unpaid Bills"). No Florida statute provides a procedure by which a lease, or an affidavit filed with the utility, keeps a current tenant's unpaid bill from becoming a lien. Cautious course: have the tenant pay the city or district directly, ask for proof of payment, and act early on arrears; if a tenant does not pay a city for utility, water or sewer service, you may begin eviction proceedings.

title: No Meter Conservation Charge Rule
bodyText: Florida has no meter conservation charge and no rule requiring you to tell tenants about a utility-bill charge that repays energy-efficiency work, or to reduce rent for one. The word "conservation" appears in the utility rules only as one of the tariff charges you may pass through at cost when you allocate a master-metered bill. Florida's program for financing qualifying improvements, including energy-efficiency and renewable energy work, is open to property owners, and the law says that term does not include people renting or occupying the property. If you submeter water, Florida sets a fee cap but does not require a monthly statement showing meter readings. Cautious course: if any charge for improvements will reach a tenant, state it in the lease before signing, and give tenants their meter readings with each submetered water bill.

title: No Utility Disclosure Attachment
bodyText: Florida does not require a utility disclosure attached to a residential lease, such as a statement of average utility costs, a billing history, or a separate page on how shared utilities are split. Florida has a disclosure rule for mobile home parks with 10 or more lots: a park owner may pass utility charges on to a mobile home owner during the term only if, among other routes, the pass-on was disclosed before the tenancy. That rule does not reach an ordinary apartment or house rental. Who pays which utility is a lease term: the library's utilities-responsibility and utilities-paid-by-landlord clauses carry it, and if you bill tenants for a shared or submetered utility, use the optional "Shared or Submetered Utilities" clause, which states the method and the cost limit.

title: Electric Vehicle Charging Rules
bodyText:
Florida gives a residential tenant no right to install an electric vehicle charger, so whether a tenant may install one is your decision (see "No Tenant EV Charging Right" and the optional consent clause "Tenant EV Charger Installation").

If you provide charging, Florida's rules are light.
- Charging provided to the public by someone who is not a utility is not a retail sale of electricity, and its rates, terms and conditions are not regulated by the Public Service Commission.
- A charger at a charging station that will be used by the public must be registered with the Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services before it goes into service (the Department's guidance says owners or operators of public chargers must register every year, under its rule, Florida Administrative Code chapter 5J-28), and the Department sets standards for placement, installation and operation.
- Regulation of charging stations is reserved to the state, so local governments may not adopt their own ordinances on them, and they must issue permits based only on the Department's standards and other state law.

The charging statute does not itself affect anyone's ability to install or use a charger for their own vehicles; it gives a tenant no right to install one at your property. Whether a charger reserved for your tenants is "for use by the public" is not settled by the statute; if you charge tenants for use, register the charger to be safe and bill only your actual electricity cost.

title: Shared Electric Vehicle Charging
bodyText: Florida gives tenants no right to install a charger in a shared parking area, and sets no rule for how a landlord shares charging among tenants. If you install chargers in a shared lot, you set the terms: charging provided by someone who is not a utility is not a retail sale of electricity, and its rates and terms are not regulated by the Public Service Commission. A charger used by the public must be registered with the Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services before it goes into service; local governments may not regulate charging stations. State law makes it unlawful to stop, stand or park a vehicle that cannot use the charger in a space designated for charging an electric vehicle; it is a noncriminal traffic infraction a law enforcement officer may charge. Mark charging spaces clearly and put your charging-space rules in your parking rules. In a condominium, the association may install chargers on the common elements and set the charges for owners, residents and guests.

title: No Rule on Chargers at Move-Out
bodyText: Florida has no rule on what happens to a tenant-installed electric vehicle charger when a residential tenancy ends. Because Florida gives tenants no right to install a charger, the terms are yours to set when you consent: say whether the tenant must remove the charger and repair any damage, or leave it in place as yours. The optional clause "Tenant EV Charger Installation" does this. Condominium law has a rule for unit owners, not tenants: a unit owner who decides the charger is no longer needed pays to remove it. Labor or materials a tenant orders for the installation can support a construction lien, so use the library's "No Liens for Tenant Improvements" clause as well.

title: Solar Devices at a Rental
bodyText: Florida gives a tenant no right to install a plug-in, balcony or other portable solar device at a rental. Florida's solar rights law is aimed at owners: a deed restriction, covenant, declaration or similar binding agreement may not prohibit solar collectors or other renewable energy devices on buildings, and a body with power to approve alterations may not deny a property owner permission to install them. The law also says it does not apply to patio railings in condominiums, cooperatives or apartments, so a device hung on a balcony railing falls outside it. Whether a residential lease counts as a "similar binding agreement" that cannot ban a tenant's solar device elsewhere on the building is not settled by the text, and the winner of a lawsuit under that law recovers costs and attorney fees. Cautious course: treat a tenant's solar device as an alteration that needs your written consent (the library's no-alterations clause), decide each request on safety, wiring, insurance and building code grounds, and do not rely on a lease term that bans every solar device outright.

title: Cable and Satellite Access
bodyText: If your rental is in a condominium, a resident of the unit, whether tenant or owner, may not be denied access to any available franchised or licensed cable television service, and may not be made to pay anything for it beyond the normal charges single-family homes in the area pay, plus agreed installation charges. In a homeowners' association community, a resident, whether tenant or parcel owner, may not be denied access to available franchised, licensed or certificated cable or video providers if the resident pays the provider directly, on the same no-extra-charge terms. For an ordinary apartment building or house outside those communities, no Florida statute, constitutional provision or civil procedure rule gives tenants access to cable, satellite or internet providers, or bars a rent difference for subscribers. Federal law also limits what any lease can restrict. An FCC rule prohibits a lease provision that impairs the installation, maintenance or use of a satellite dish or fixed-wireless antenna one meter or less across, a TV broadcast antenna, or a mast supporting one, on property within the tenant's exclusive use or control, such as a private balcony or patio. A restriction impairs if it unreasonably delays or prevents installation or use, unreasonably increases its cost, or prevents an acceptable signal. A restriction is allowed only if it is needed for a clearly defined safety objective or to preserve a historic property, and is no more burdensome than necessary. The rule does not reach areas outside the tenant's exclusive use or control, such as common areas. So do not ban dishes or antennas in the tenant's own space; set only rules that do not unreasonably delay, add cost or block the signal, and handle installation through your alterations and rules clauses.

title: No State Recycling Notice Rule
bodyText: Florida has no state rule requiring you to tell tenants where and how to recycle. Two state rules touch rental property. First, where a county or city has a residential or commercial recycling program that provides receptacles and regular pickup, a multifamily residential property that received its certificate of occupancy on or after July 1, 2012 must, in accordance with local ordinances, provide adequate space and an adequate receptacle for recycling by its tenants and owners. Second, local governments may adopt ordinances requiring multifamily dwellings and apartment complexes to set up programs separating designated recyclable materials, and may prohibit knowingly disposing of those materials. So the details, including any notice to tenants, come from your county or city. Florida's landlord-tenant preemption covers matters in the landlord-tenant act, and the statute does not say whether it reaches a local recycling ordinance. Cautious course: check your local solid waste ordinance, and tell tenants in your rules where the recycling receptacles are.

title: No Ordnance, Demolition or Shared-Meter Disclosure
bodyText: Florida does not require you to tell a prospective tenant that the rental is near a former military ordnance location, that you have applied for or obtained a demolition permit, or that a utility meter is shared with other units. Florida's lease disclosures are others, among them radon and flood (see "Radon Gas Notification" clause and "Flood Disclosure" clause). If a meter serves more than one unit and you bill tenants for it, the cost limits in "What You May Charge for Utilities You Pay" apply, and the optional clause "Shared or Submetered Utilities" tells the tenant how the bill is split. Cautious course: if you know of a planned demolition or a shared meter, say so in writing before the tenant signs, because Florida's consumer protection law may reach a misleading silence (see "Florida Consumer Protection Law and Leases").

title: No Property Tax Rent Statement
bodyText: Florida does not require you to tell tenants what part of the rent goes to property taxes, either yearly or when the rent changes. If your lease passes a share of property-tax increases to the tenant, the tagged optional clause "Tax and Insurance Increases" has you send the tax bill and your calculation with each charge (see "No Property Tax Pass-Through Rule"). Mobile home park owners have their own pass-on rules under the mobile home park law; they do not apply to ordinary rentals.

title: No Property Tax Pass-Through Rule
bodyText:
Florida has no statute on passing increases in property taxes or insurance to a residential tenant.

So the tenant pays a share of a tax increase only if the written lease says so in advance with an objective formula; you cannot add a tax pass-through in the middle of a fixed-term lease on your own. The optional clause "Tax and Insurance Increases" (tagged for Florida) states the tenant's percentage, requires the tax bill and your calculation, and credits back a share of any reduction.

A separate rule lets mobile home park owners pass on property taxes if disclosed before the tenancy, but it applies only to mobile home lots in parks of 10 or more lots.

A court may refuse to enforce an unconscionable lease term, so keep the share clear and tied to the bill.

title: Utility Shutoff Rules
bodyText:
Florida's utility shutoff rules come from the Public Service Commission and bind the utilities it regulates (investor-owned electric and gas utilities, and the water and sewer utilities under its jurisdiction), not city utilities or electric cooperatives.

Before cutting off service for nonpayment, the utility must give its customer at least 5 working days' written notice, separate from the bill; an electric or gas customer may ask that a copy go to a third party. Electric and gas utilities may not disconnect a non-commercial customer, and water utilities any customer, from noon Friday to 8 a.m. Monday or from noon on the day before a holiday (for electric and gas, one the rules list; for water, a public holiday) to 8 a.m. the next working day, unless the customer requests or agrees to it, there is a hazard, or, for electric and water, there is tampering or fraud; the gas rule's only exceptions are a customer request and safety. A previous occupant's unpaid bill is not a reason to refuse or cut off a new customer, unless that customer lived there when the debt arose and the old customer still lives there. An electric customer certified as needing medically essential service gets a call or visit before a scheduled disconnection. A city utility may cut off a tenant who is 30 days or more behind.

Florida's statutes, constitution and civil procedure rules set no winter, heat or hurricane bar or extension on shutoffs for nonpayment.

These rules are between the utility and its customer. You may never cause a tenant's service to be cut off yourself.

title: Association Documents and Notices for Renters
bodyText: Florida has no general rule that a lease of a condominium, cooperative or homeowners' association home must disclose the association's rules, assessments or other obligations to the tenant, or come with copies of the association's documents. Florida's statutes set two specific duties instead, both on the unit owner who rents out a unit. (1) Fire sprinklers: if the owners of a residential condominium or cooperative voted to forgo retrofitting a fire sprinkler system, you must give the renter a copy of the association's notice of the vote before the lease is signed. (2) Handrails and guardrails: if the owners of a condominium or cooperative that qualifies as housing for older persons voted to forgo retrofitting handrails or guardrails, you must give the renter a copy of the association's notice of that vote before the lease is signed. Neither statute states a penalty for skipping the copy. Separately, a condominium renter has a right to inspect and copy the declaration of condominium, the association's bylaws and rules, and the building's milestone and turnover inspection reports; a cooperative renter may inspect and copy the bylaws and rules and the inspection reports. No comparable renter right appears in the homeowners' association statute. A developer that leases a condominium unit for an unexpired term of more than 5 years must deliver the full set of condominium documents, as on a sale; an ordinary landlord's lease is not covered. What to do: ask the association whether either opt-out vote was taken, give the tenant a copy of any notice before signing, keep a signed receipt, and give the tenant a copy of the association rules, since the library's association-compliance clause asks the tenant to follow them (see "Homeowner / Condominium Association Compliance" clause and "Condominium and HOA Rules for Renting").

title: Fire Sprinkler Disclosure
bodyText: Florida does not require a landlord to tell a tenant, in the lease or otherwise, whether the building has fire sprinklers or when they were last inspected. Florida's statutes set one narrow duty. If you own and rent out a unit in a residential condominium or cooperative whose owners voted to forgo retrofitting a fire sprinkler system, you must give the renter a copy of the association's notice of the vote results before the lease is signed. Ask the association whether such a vote was taken; if it was, hand over the copy before signing and keep a signed receipt. The statutes state no penalty for missing it. Whether a building must have sprinklers at all is a building and fire code question (see "Fire Sprinklers"). Don't describe a unit as sprinklered, or a system as working, unless that is true. See "Association Documents and Notices for Renters" for the related handrail notice.

title: What a Landlord Need Not Disclose
bodyText: Florida law says two kinds of facts are not material facts that must be disclosed in a real estate transaction: that an occupant of the property has or had HIV or was diagnosed with AIDS, and that the property was, or was suspected to have been, the site of a homicide, suicide or death. No lawsuit may be brought against an owner, the owner's agent, the transferee's agent or a person licensed under Florida's real estate licensing law for not telling the transferee those facts. The statute does not define "real estate transaction" or "transferee"; it plainly covers sales, and a lease of real property is probably covered too, but no Florida statute says so expressly. Unlike some states, Florida's statute does not add a duty to answer truthfully when asked, but it only excuses silence: it does not protect a false statement. Separately, you may not discriminate in housing against a person because the person has, or is regarded as having, HIV; such a person has every protection given to people with disabilities, and a violation carries liquidated damages of $1,000, or $5,000 if intentional or reckless, or actual damages if greater, plus attorney's fees. What to do: you need not volunteer a death, suicide or homicide at the property; if a prospective tenant asks, don't answer falsely (decline to discuss or answer accurately), never ask about or comment on anyone's HIV status, and disclose physical defects that remain.

title: No Sex Offender Disclosure Rule
bodyText: Florida law does not require a landlord to tell a tenant or applicant that a registered sexual predator or sexual offender lives in the building or nearby, or to check the registry before renting. Notifying the public is law enforcement's job: when a sexual predator establishes a residence, the county sheriff or the city police chief must notify the community and the public, and the Florida Department of Law Enforcement must post every designated sexual predator on the Internet. One registry check does bind some landlords, but it concerns employees, not tenants: the landlord of a licensed nontransient or transient apartment property must have each employee background-screened, including against the sexual predator and sexual offender registries of all 50 states and the District of Columbia (see "Background Screening of Apartment Employees"). What to do: you need not volunteer registry information; if a prospective tenant asks, point them to the public registry rather than characterizing anyone yourself, and don't make statements about neighbors you can't verify. Screening applicants for criminal history raises fair-housing questions not covered here (see "Fair Housing").

title: Sex Offender Residency Restrictions
bodyText: Florida's residency restriction binds the offender, not the landlord. A person convicted of certain sex offenses against a victim under 16 (the statute lists them by section) may not reside within 1,000 feet of a school, child care facility, park or playground; for offenses on or after July 1, 2026, and for an existing restricted person who changes permanent residence on or after that date, the list adds public swimming pools, which expressly include pools serving apartments, condominiums, mobile home parks or townhouses. A person already living lawfully in a home is not forced to move when one of those places opens nearby later. Violation is a crime of the offender. No Florida statute makes it a crime or violation for a landlord to rent to a registered offender, forbids two registered offenders living together, or requires a landlord to check whether a unit is within 1,000 feet of a restricted place. One crime can reach anyone, including a landlord: helping a sexual predator or offender whom you have reason to believe is out of compliance with registration evade law enforcement, by harboring or concealing the person, withholding information about the noncompliance, or giving false information, with intent to help the person elude law enforcement, is a third-degree felony. Renting in the ordinary course is not harboring without that intent. What to do: if a registered applicant asks whether your property complies with the 1,000-foot rule, tell them it is their responsibility to confirm; answer law enforcement's questions about a tenant truthfully. Cities and counties may have their own residency ordinances.

title: Florida Lease Disclosure Checklist
bodyText:
Florida has no single list of lease disclosures, no state form that must be the first page of a lease, and no notice telling tenants whether a rent or eviction law covers the unit (Florida has neither kind of law; see "No Just-Cause Eviction Rule").

The disclosures that apply, with their triggers:
- (1) Landlord's name and address: in writing, at or before the tenancy starts, for every tenancy.
- (2) Radon: the statutory radon paragraph, word for word, on at least one document signed at or before the lease, except a transient stay of 45 days or less ("Radon Gas Notification" clause).
- (3) Flood: the statutory flood disclosure, as a separate document, at or before signing a lease of 1 year or longer; if you skip it and the tenant's belongings suffer substantial flood loss, the tenant may end the lease ("Flood Disclosure" clause).
- (4) Deposits: if you rent five or more units, the deposit and advance-rent notice, in the lease or within 30 days after you receive the money ("Security Deposit and Advance Rent Notice" clause).
- (5) Fee in lieu of a deposit: if you offer one, the signed agreement with its capitalized disclosure ("Fee in Lieu of Security Deposit" clause).
- (6) Condominium or cooperative units: a copy of any association notice that owners voted to forgo sprinkler or handrail retrofitting, before signing ("Association Documents and Notices for Renters").
- (7) Lead paint: the federal disclosure for older housing.

Optional addenda, such as e-mail notice and an early termination fee, have their own forms ("Statutory Forms").

Lease with an option to buy: no Florida statute requires a general property-condition disclosure by a seller, but Florida's sale disclosures (flood, property tax, radon, and coastal construction line for beach property) are due at or before the sale contract is signed. Whether a lease-option is a sale contract when signed is unsettled, so give them at lease signing and again when the tenant exercises the option.

title: No Shoreline Disclosure for Leases
bodyText: Florida does not require a landlord to tell a tenant about shoreline access, beach erosion or coastal regulation affecting a rental. Florida's statutes have one coastal disclosure, and it runs to buyers, not tenants: a seller of an interest in real property lying partly or wholly seaward of the coastal construction control line must give the purchaser a written statement, in the form the statute sets out, that the property may be subject to coastal erosion and to coastal regulation, at or before the sale contract is signed, and a survey or affidavit showing the line at closing unless the buyer waives it in writing. Missing the statement does not undo the sale. If your lease gives the tenant an option to buy beachfront property, see "Florida Lease Disclosure Checklist" on when to give sale disclosures. For an ordinary lease, no coastal statement is required; if the unit is beachfront, it is still sensible to tell the tenant in writing about any rules on beach access, dune walkovers or sea-turtle lighting the property is subject to.

title: No Military or Airport Zone Disclosure
bodyText: Florida does not require a landlord to tell a tenant that a rental lies near a military installation or airfield, or in an aircraft noise or accident potential zone, and gives tenants no right to end a lease on learning it. No Florida statute requires such a disclosure for leases or for sales. Florida deals with these areas through land-use planning instead: local governments near the military installations named in the statute must send the base commander proposed plan and zoning changes that would affect land near the installation, including requests to vary height, lighting or noise-attenuation rules, and must consider the commander's comments; and local governments must adopt airport land-use compatibility zoning that, among other things, limits incompatible uses in airport noise areas. Those rules bind governments and new development, not landlords. Ownership near military installations is restricted for certain foreign principals (see "Foreign Ownership Restrictions and Leasing"). What to do: no lease statement is required; if a rental is under a flight path or beside a range, telling applicants in writing avoids complaints and misrepresentation claims.

title: Foreign Ownership Restrictions and Leasing
bodyText: Florida restricts real property interests of "foreign principals": the governments of the listed foreign countries of concern (China, Russia, Iran, North Korea, Cuba, the Maduro regime of Venezuela and Syria), their officials and political parties, entities organized or based there, people domiciled there who are not U.S. citizens or lawful permanent residents, and anyone listed who controls an entity formed to own Florida real property. Such a foreign principal may not own, control or acquire by purchase, grant, devise or descent any interest (beyond a tiny indirect stake through public shares) in agricultural land, or in real property on or within 10 miles of a military installation or listed critical infrastructure facility. China, its ruling party, their officials, Chinese entities and people domiciled in China who are not U.S. citizens or permanent residents may not acquire any interest in Florida real property at all. A narrow exception lets a person holding a non-tourist visa or asylum papers buy one home of up to 2 acres not within 5 miles of a military installation. Holdings acquired before July 1, 2023 may be kept but must be registered. Buyers sign an affidavit at purchase; violations can mean forfeiture and criminal penalties, and knowingly selling in violation is a crime. The law does not mention leases, has no carve-out for short leases, and puts no duty on a landlord to ask whether a tenant is a foreign principal. Whether renting a home to a foreign principal counts as an "interest" acquired by "purchase" or "grant" is unsettled. Cautious course: an ordinary residential lease is not a sale, but take legal advice before a long lease, a lease with an option to buy, or a lease to a foreign government or entity, especially near a military base or critical infrastructure. Never screen applicants by national origin or citizenship as a shortcut (see "Fair Housing").

title: No Rent-Cap, Just-Cause or Purchase-Right Notice
bodyText: Florida has no statewide rent cap and no just-cause eviction law, so there is no notice telling a tenant whether the unit is covered by one, and cities and counties may not adopt or keep any measure that would have the effect of imposing controls on rents (they may still use land-use tools such as inclusionary housing to add affordable units). See "No Just-Cause Eviction Rule" and "State Preemption of Local Landlord-Tenant Rules". Florida's statutes also give residential tenants no general right to buy, or to get a first offer, when an owner sells a building, and owe tenants no sale notice. Two narrow purchase rights exist. (1) Condominium or cooperative conversion: a tenant who has lived in the building for the 180 days before the notice of intended conversion has a right of first refusal to buy the unit, with purchase materials due within 90 days of the notice, at least 45 days to decide, and 10 more days if the developer later offers the unit for less (see "Condominium Conversion: Tenant Rights"). (2) Mobile home parks: when a park owner offers a park for sale, the homeowners, acting through their homeowners' association, have a right to buy on the same price and terms; this is a mobile home park rule and does not apply to ordinary rentals. What to do: on an ordinary sale of a rented home or building, no tenant notice or offer is required; the lease continues, and the deposits must move to the buyer (see "Florida Security Deposit Rules").

title: No Exemption Notice Needed
bodyText: Some states make an owner whose property is exempt from a rent cap, a just-cause eviction law or a tenant purchase law give tenants a written exemption notice. Florida has no such notice because it has none of those laws for ordinary rentals: no statewide rent cap or just-cause rule, a ban on local rent controls, and no general tenant right to buy on a sale (see "No Rent-Cap, Just-Cause or Purchase-Right Notice"). Florida's statutes require no exemption notice, filing or statement of any kind. The only tenant purchase right, in a condominium or cooperative conversion, has its limits built in: it belongs only to a tenant who lived in the building for the 180 days before the notice of intended conversion, and it ends when the rental agreement and its extensions end, when the tenant waives it in writing after the notice, or when the decision periods run out. Nothing needs to be sent to show that a tenant falls outside it. What to do: nothing to file or send on an ordinary sale or lease; on a conversion, follow the conversion steps exactly (see "Condominium Conversion: Tenant Rights").

title: No Sunset on Florida Tenant Laws
bodyText: No Florida tenant protection is on a dated repeal clock. No section of the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act or of the other chapters that govern residential tenancies (abandoned property, condominium and cooperative conversions, mobile home parks) expires or stands repealed on a set date. The dated repeals that do exist concern other subjects, such as funding programs and court pilot programs. One landlord-tenant section works the other way, as a standby rule rather than a sunset: the state copy of the federal Protecting Tenants at Foreclosure Act is printed in the statutes but takes effect only if the federal act is repealed, so it is not in force today and the federal act governs (see "Tenants After Foreclosure"). Florida tenant law changes by amendment, often every year (for example the 2025 changes to deposit and notice rules and the new flood disclosure), so check for new acts each July and October rather than for expiry dates.

title: No State Lead Notice Beyond the Federal Rule
bodyText:
Florida has no state lead notice, pamphlet or certificate that a landlord must give a tenant on top of the federal lead-paint disclosure for older housing.

Florida's Lead Poisoning Prevention Screening and Education Act does define rental units built before 1960, or built from 1960 to 1978 where the owner knows of lead-based paint, as "affected property", and defines "owner" to include a property manager or leasing agent, but the act imposes no duty on owners. It sets up a state education program aimed at tenants, owners and others, has health care providers and child care operators hand out state information to parents, and sets blood-lead screening priorities for young children, including those living in buildings that have faced lead enforcement.

What to do: give the federal disclosure and pamphlet where they apply, keep paint in good repair, use lead-safe work practices on older buildings, and see "Landlord's Maintenance Duties" for your general code-compliance duty.

title: No Lead-Safe Certificate Requirement
bodyText: Florida does not require a lead-safe or lead-free certificate for a rental, an inspection or registration of older units for lead, or a certificate attached to the lease. Florida's lead law is an education and child blood-screening program: it labels pre-1960 rental units, and 1960-1978 units where the owner knows of lead-based paint, as "affected property", but puts no inspection, certification or notice duty on the owner (see "No State Lead Notice Beyond the Federal Rule"). For the separate federal lead-paint disclosure on older housing, use the library's clause "Lead-Based Paint Disclosure". What to do: no state certificate is needed; if you renovate older housing, use workers trained in lead-safe practices.

title: Contamination Notices to Tenants
bodyText: Florida has no general rule that a landlord must tell a prospective tenant about known soil or groundwater contamination, or must write recorded cleanup restrictions into a lease. Florida's statutes provide one tenant notice, tied to state-supervised cleanups. If a site is being cleaned up under the state's risk-based programs (petroleum, drycleaning solvent, brownfield or other contaminated sites) and the person responsible for the cleanup learns from lab results that contamination has spread beyond the property's boundaries, that person must notify the Department of Environmental Protection on its form within 10 days, by certified mail, and at the same time mail a copy to the district office, the county health department and all known lessees and tenants of the property where the cleanup began. If you are the person responsible for a cleanup on your rental property, your tenants must get that copy. Separately, cleanups may rely on recorded restrictions on use, such as deed restrictions or restrictive covenants; those run with the land and no statute requires repeating them in the lease, but your tenant should be told about any restriction that limits how the tenant may use the property (for example, a ban on using groundwater). A landowner may also record a notice that land is a former phosphate mine; that is a title notice, not a tenant disclosure. Radon has its own lease notice (see "Radon Gas Notification" clause).

title: No Meth Lab Disclosure Rule
bodyText: Florida has no rule requiring a landlord to disclose that a rental was used as a methamphetamine or other drug lab, no duty on an owner to report a suspected lab, no state cleanup standard for drug-lab contamination, and no ban on re-renting before cleanup. What Florida does have are crimes and remedies aimed at owners who knowingly allow drug activity. It is a third-degree felony to own, lease or rent any place knowing it will be used for drug trafficking, sale, or manufacture for sale. An owner, lessor or sublessor may not let a tenant use utility service the owner knows, or reasonably should believe, was illegally connected, and finding drug-manufacturing materials in a visibly modified grow house, with the owner's knowledge, is prima facie evidence of intent; a willful violation is a first-degree misdemeanor. A place used repeatedly for drug sale or manufacture can be declared a public nuisance by a local board, which can order the owner to abate it or close the premises (see "Criminal Activity by Tenants"). What to do: if you learn a unit was used to make drugs, have it professionally assessed and cleaned before re-renting, keep the records, and don't tell a new tenant it is clean unless you have confirmed it.

title: No Defective Drywall Disclosure Rule
bodyText: Florida has no statute requiring a landlord, or a seller, to disclose defective or corrosive (sometimes called "Chinese") drywall. Florida's statutes mention drywall only where condominium, cooperative and homeowners' associations may remove and dispose of wet drywall after a disaster to stop mold, and in a coastal-construction definition. Drywall that corrodes wiring or plumbing or gives off odors is still a condition you must deal with: you must comply with applicable building, housing and health codes or, where none apply, keep the structural components in good repair and the plumbing in reasonable working condition, unless for a single-family home or duplex the lease alters that duty in writing (see "Landlord's Maintenance Duties"). What to do: if you know a unit has problem drywall, remediate before renting, and don't describe the unit as free of it unless you have confirmed that.

title: No Chemical Exposure Warning Rule
bodyText: Florida has no counterpart to California's Proposition 65: no list of chemicals known to cause cancer or reproductive harm and no requirement that a landlord post or give tenants a chemical exposure warning. Separate, specific notices still apply where their own conditions are met: radon ("Radon Gas Notification" clause), the federal lead-paint disclosure ("Lead-Based Paint Disclosure" clause), and the 7-day notice when a tenant must leave the unit for extermination ("Pest Control Notices"). What to do: no general chemical warning is required in a Florida lease.

title: No Certificate of Occupancy Disclosure
bodyText: Florida does not require a landlord to give a tenant a copy of the building's certificate of occupancy, to state in the lease that one exists, or to post it in the unit. Florida's statutes and state rules use certificates of occupancy for other purposes: as a building-permit and construction milestone, in condominium and cooperative developer and turnover rules, in construction lien, prompt-payment and deposit timing, and in tax and impact-fee provisions. None makes the certificate a lease disclosure. A unit without lawful occupancy approval (an unpermitted garage conversion or added unit, for example) can still put you in breach of your duty to comply with applicable building, housing and health codes (see "Landlord's Maintenance Duties") and can draw local code enforcement (see "Code Enforcement Orders (No Receivership)"). What to do: confirm before renting that the unit was permitted and approved for residential occupancy, and keep the record.

title: No Duty to Disclose Code Orders to Tenants
bodyText: Florida does not require a landlord to tell a prospective tenant about an outstanding code-enforcement case, inspection order, unsafe-building order or condemnation. Florida's statutes require code-enforcement disclosure only on a transfer of ownership: if you sell or otherwise transfer the property while a code case is pending before a local enforcement board, special magistrate or court (or, for county citations, before county court), you must disclose the proceeding in writing to the buyer, hand over the case papers, say in writing that the new owner will be responsible for compliance, and notify the code official within 5 days after the transfer; skipping the disclosures creates a rebuttable presumption of fraud. A lease is not a transfer of ownership, so the rule does not reach tenants. The case itself still matters to a tenancy: an uncorrected violation can breach your duty to comply with building, housing and health codes and can lead to fines, liens or closure (see "Code Enforcement Orders (No Receivership)"). What to do: clear open code cases before renting; if one is pending, tell the prospective tenant in writing what it is and when it will be fixed, and never rent a unit under an order not to occupy it.

title: No Health-Department Rental Rules Duty
bodyText: Florida does not require a landlord to keep or hand out copies of health-department rental rules, or to refer tenants to the health department. Florida's statutes have no separate health-district housing code for ordinary rentals. Health enforcement reaches rentals in other ways. The Department of Health and local health authorities may investigate any condition that threatens health, such as sewage, garbage, improperly built or maintained septic tanks or toilets, or conditions that breed mosquitoes or flies; they serve notice to remove a sanitary nuisance within 24 hours or another reasonable time, may abate it themselves at the responsible person's cost, and may bring criminal or other proceedings. Licensed apartment properties are also inspected by the state lodging division. Your lease duties already include complying with applicable health codes (see "Landlord's Maintenance Duties"), and the radon notice tells tenants they can get radon information from the county health department ("Radon Gas Notification" clause).

title: No Foreclosure Disclosure Before Leasing
bodyText: Florida does not require an owner whose property is in foreclosure, or who has been served with a foreclosure complaint, to tell a prospective tenant before signing a lease. What happens to a tenant after a foreclosure sale is governed by the federal Protecting Tenants at Foreclosure Act; Florida's statutes print a state copy of it, but that copy takes effect only if the federal act is repealed, so it is not in force (see "Tenants After Foreclosure"). If you are buying a home in foreclosure from its owner and renting it back to them, Florida's foreclosure-rescue law sets separate contract and cancellation requirements. What to do: no foreclosure statement is required, but renting a unit you know is about to be lost exposes the tenant to a move and you to claims; if a foreclosure is pending, telling an applicant in writing is the cautious course.

title: Selling the Property or Changing Managers
bodyText: When a Florida rental is sold or management changes, three rules apply. (1) Deposits and advance rent: on a sale or transfer of title, or a change in the designated rental agent, all security deposits and advance rent held for tenants must go to the new owner or agent with any earned interest and an accurate accounting of each tenant's credit. Once the money and records are transferred and a written receipt is given, the former owner or agent is freed from the duty to hold the money. A new owner or agent is presumed to have received each deposit, but only up to 1 month's rent, and the transfer does not excuse earlier violations (see "Florida Security Deposit Rules"). (2) Who the tenant deals with: you must give the tenant in writing the name and address of the landlord or of the person authorized to receive notices; that person keeps the authority until the tenant is notified otherwise, so when the owner or manager changes, deliver written notice of the new name and address to the tenant's home (or another address the tenant named in writing, or by e-mail under a signed e-mail addendum) (see "Landlord's Name and Address" clause). (3) Showings: the tenant may not unreasonably withhold consent to entry to show the unit to prospective buyers or lenders; without consent you may enter for that purpose only in an emergency, when consent is unreasonably withheld, or when the tenant has been absent for half the rent period (but not if the rent is current and the tenant told you of the absence), and you may not abuse access or use it to harass (see "Landlord's Access to the Property" clause). No Florida statute requires a separate notice of the sale itself or states what happens to the lease on a sale. Plan for the lease to continue with the buyer. For foreclosure, see "Tenants After Foreclosure".

title: Out-of-State Landlords: Agents, Service and Foreign LLCs
bodyText: Florida does not require an out-of-state individual owner to appoint a Florida agent before renting, to name one in the lease, or to file anything before suing a tenant, unless the owner rents under a fictitious name, which must be registered before doing business under it and in any case before any suit (see "Squatters, Cash Receipts and Registration"). An out-of-state limited liability company is different: owning income-producing real property in Florida counts as transacting business here, so it must obtain a certificate of authority, which names a Florida registered agent, and until it has one it may not maintain an eviction or other suit in a Florida court. An out-of-state corporation that transacts business here faces the same bar on suing; whether renting out property is more than merely owning it is a case-law question, so get advice before filing. The state has no income-tax withholding on rent paid to nonresident owners (no Florida statute provides for it; the constitution's bar on a state personal income tax protects residents and citizens of Florida). No Florida statute requires a nonresident landlord to appoint or name an agent. One general rule can still reach you: a nonresident individual or out-of-state entity that carries on a business or business venture in Florida, and a former Florida resident who has moved away, is deemed to have appointed the Florida Secretary of State as agent for service of process in suits arising from that business, so a tenant may be able to sue you by serving the Secretary of State. Whether renting out property counts as a "business venture" for this rule is a case-law question; assume it may, and keep your notice address current. What every landlord must do, wherever they live, is disclose in writing at or before the tenancy starts the name and address of the landlord or of a person authorized to receive notices and demands, and notify the tenant of any change (see "Landlord's Name and Address" clause). If you hire someone in Florida to rent or manage the property for pay, that person generally needs a Florida real estate licence: anyone who, for another and for compensation, rents or negotiates rentals of real property, or procures tenants, is a "broker", and operating as a broker without an active licence is a third-degree felony. Owners leasing their own property, salaried on-site leasing staff of an apartment community, and salaried condominium or cooperative managers arranging rentals of up to 1 year are exempt.

title: No Special District Statement for Leases
bodyText: Florida does not require a landlord to tell a tenant, in the lease or otherwise, that the property lies in a community development district or other special taxing or assessment district. Florida's statutes require the district statement for buyers only: after a community development district is established, each contract for the initial sale of a parcel or residential unit in it must carry, just above the purchaser's signature line and in bold type larger than the rest of the contract, a statement that the district may impose and levy taxes or assessments for its public facilities and services, in addition to county and other local taxes; the district must also record a notice of its establishment with that statement. A homeowners' association's disclosure summary to purchasers also warns of special assessments by a municipality, county or special district. District taxes and assessments fall on the owner; a tenant pays them only if the lease validly makes the tenant pay them. What to do: no district statement is needed in a lease; if you want the tenant to reimburse any district charge, say so expressly in the lease as rent or an agreed charge (see "Fees and Rent").

title: No Communal Land Lease Approval
bodyText: Florida has no communal, family or native land system that requires a government officer to approve a private residential lease before it is valid; a private owner leasing privately owned land needs no government approval. Florida's statutes address only the state-held Seminole reservation lands: title to Seminole Indian lands held by the state is vested in the Board of Trustees of the Internal Improvement Trust Fund, and the trustee may lease parts of the reservation those statutes describe under an improvement lease, limited to 15 years (25 years with a renewal option of up to 25 more for a Florida Indian, and 50 years for a Florida Indian's housing lease), with the lessee's improvements becoming part of the reservation when the lease ends. Reservation lands held in trust by the United States are governed by federal law. What to do: for an ordinary rental no approval is needed; if a property is on or near tribal or reservation land, check the recorded title and get legal advice before leasing.

title: Hunting on Rented Land
bodyText: Florida has no statute deciding whether a tenant of farmland or other rural land gets the hunting or fishing rights, or whether the landlord keeps them unless granted in writing. The lease decides. Three related rules matter. (1) Trespass: for the rule that unauthorized entry on enclosed and posted land is prima facie evidence of trespass, the "owner" whose permission counts includes a lessee or occupant entitled to possession, so a tenant in possession can usually authorize entry. (2) Written authorization: if the land is enrolled in the state's Voluntary Authorized Hunter Identification Program, every hunter must carry written authorization from the owner or the owner's authorized representative, and failing to produce it within 7 days after demand is prima facie evidence of armed trespass. (3) Liability: an owner or lessee who, without charge, makes an area available primarily for hunting, fishing or wildlife viewing is protected from liability to users only if written notice of that protection is given before or at entry or is posted conspicuously. What to do: if you rent out land with hunting value, say in the lease who may hunt or fish, whether the tenant may let others do so, and who may sign written hunting authorizations.

title: Property Taken by Eminent Domain
bodyText:
Florida has no statute saying what happens to a residential lease, or to the rent, when the government takes the property by eminent domain. The lease decides; the library offers an optional condemnation clause that ends the lease on a total or disabling taking, apportions rent, reduces rent on a partial taking, and gives the award to you except the tenant's own relocation or personal-property payments.

Florida's constitution requires full compensation paid to each owner, and the condemning authority must name lessees, as well as owners and lenders, in its petition. Where owners and tenants make conflicting claims to the award, the court decides each party's share and how it is apportioned, so a lease clause allocating the award binds you and the tenant but does not stop the court from hearing the dispute.

On federally funded projects the state may make relocation payments to displaced persons, including tenants.

title: No Plain-Language Rule for Leases
bodyText: Florida has no plain-language law for residential leases: no readability test, no rule that a lease be divided into captioned sections, no type-size floor for the lease as a whole, and no dollar threshold. Florida's statutes set readability rules for other contracts, such as insurance policies (a minimum Flesch reading-ease score of 45 and captioned section titles) and rent-to-own agreements for goods (clear and coherent wording, divided and captioned by sections), which do not apply to a lease of a home. This agrees with the library's Florida consumer-protection row ("Florida Consumer Protection Law and Leases"), which notes that Florida's Deceptive and Unfair Trade Practices Act covers renting property and relies on general unfairness and deception standards. Specific lease notices have their own wording and type rules (see "Statutory Forms"). What to do: write the lease in plain English with a heading for each section, put rent, deposit and fee terms near the start, and fill every blank before signing.

title: No Consumer Restriction Statement
bodyText: Florida does not require a residential lease to carry a statement listing the waivers or restrictions it places on the tenant, to pass a readability test, or to be preapproved by the Attorney General, and so has no dollar exclusion either. See "No Plain-Language Rule for Leases". The protection Florida gives instead works on the terms themselves: a lease provision is void and unenforceable to the extent it purports to waive the tenant's rights, remedies or requirements under the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, or to limit either party's liability arising under law, and either party who suffers actual damages from such a provision may recover them (see "Lease Terms Florida Law Voids"). What to do: no restriction statement is needed, but don't include terms the Act voids, and make any lawful term that limits the tenant easy to find.

title: No Lease Translation Duty
bodyText: Florida does not require a landlord to translate a lease, or to give a translation when the lease is negotiated in Spanish or another language. Florida's statutes set translation duties only for other contracts: for example, a health maintenance organization that negotiates a contract in a language other than English must supply a written translation that becomes part of the contract, and similar rules apply to prepaid health clinic and prepaid limited health service contracts. None applies to residential leases, and Florida's foreclosure-rescue law, which covers sale-and-lease-back deals with homeowners, has no translation rule either. What to do: no translation is required, but if you advertise or negotiate in another language, giving the tenant a translation (marked as a courtesy copy, with the English lease controlling, if you wish) reduces disputes over what the tenant agreed to.

title: No Truth-in-Renting Law
bodyText: Florida has no truth-in-renting law: no state-published statement of landlord and tenant rights you must hand out, and no separate rule penalizing lease terms that violate clearly established legal rights. Florida covers similar ground in three ways. (1) A lease provision is void and unenforceable to the extent it purports to waive the tenant's rights, remedies or requirements under the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, or to limit either party's liability arising under law, and a party who suffers actual damages because such a provision was included may recover them (see "Lease Terms Florida Law Voids"). (2) Florida's Deceptive and Unfair Trade Practices Act declares unfair or deceptive acts in trade or commerce unlawful, and trade or commerce includes renting property (see "Florida Consumer Protection Law and Leases"). (3) Cities and counties may not impose their own disclosures about the rights and responsibilities of landlords and tenants, because state law preempts them (see "State Preemption of Local Landlord-Tenant Rules"). The deposit disclosure itself ends by telling the tenant to refer to the statute for their legal rights and obligations (see "Security Deposit and Advance Rent Notice" clause). What to do: keep void terms out of the lease and describe the unit, rent and fees accurately in ads and the lease.

title: Accessory Dwelling Units
bodyText: Florida lets, but does not require, a county or city to adopt an ordinance allowing accessory dwelling units (a secondary living unit with its own kitchen, bathroom and sleeping area, in the main house or on the same lot) in any area zoned for single-family use. The state statute's purpose is affordable rentals, and it says an application for a building permit to build an accessory dwelling unit must include the applicant's affidavit that the unit will be rented at an affordable rate to an extremely-low-, very-low-, low- or moderate-income person; "affordable" means monthly rent and utilities of no more than 30 percent of the relevant income figure. The statute states no penalty and no period for the affidavit, and it does not say whether it reaches permits issued under local rules adopted on some other basis. No Florida statute requires the owner to live on the lot, sets a minimum rental term for an accessory unit, or bars its rental. What to do: if you obtained a permit on an affordability affidavit, rent the unit within the affordable-rent limit and keep proof of the tenant's eligibility; check your local ordinance for owner-occupancy, parking or rental-term conditions. Short-term stays have their own tax rules (see "Sales Tax on Short Rentals").

title: No State Limit on Renting in Single-Family Zones
bodyText: Florida has no state statute limiting the rental of homes in single-family zones, requiring the owner to live on the lot, or setting a minimum rental term there. Two state rules work in the other direction. (1) Vacation rentals: a local law may not prohibit vacation rentals or regulate how long or how often they are rented, unless the local law was adopted on or before June 1, 2011. (2) Homeowners' associations: a rental restriction an association adopts after July 1, 2021 binds only owners who acquire title afterward or who consent, except that any association may regulate leases shorter than 6 months and limit rentals to three times a year (see "Condominium and HOA Rules for Renting"). How far the state's landlord-tenant preemption reaches zoning is not settled by the statutes (see "State Preemption of Local Landlord-Tenant Rules").

title: No Single-Family Rental Disclosure
bodyText: Florida requires no special disclosure when a single-family home is rented: no statement of the home's permitted occupancy, and no rule on type size or first-page placement for single-family leases. Single-family homes and duplexes are treated differently in one area, maintenance: your duty to comply with building, housing and health codes (or, where none apply, to keep the structure and plumbing in repair) may be altered or modified in writing for a single-family home or duplex, and the extra duties for other units (extermination, locks and keys, common areas, garbage removal, heat during winter, running water and hot water) do not apply to a single-family home or duplex, which instead must have working smoke detection devices installed at the start of the tenancy unless otherwise agreed in writing (see "Tenant-Maintained Items (Single-Family Home or Duplex)" clause and "Landlord's Maintenance Duties"). The disclosures every Florida lease needs are listed in "Florida Lease Disclosure Checklist".

title: Automatic Renewal Clauses
bodyText:
Florida has no statute written for the automatic renewal of a residential lease.

These rules cover the rental of a dwelling unit under Florida's Residential Landlord and Tenant Act (Part II of chapter 83), outside its exclusions such as transient lodging.

Two statutes still reach a clause that renews the lease unless someone gives notice.

First, a lease with a specific duration may require the tenant to give notice before moving out at the end of the term only if it also requires you to notify the tenant, within the same notice period, if the lease will not be renewed. Your notice must be delivered by mail, hand delivery, agreed e-mail, or by leaving a copy at the home if the tenant is absent. Neither notice may be shorter than 30 days or longer than 60 days (Fla. Stat. § 83.575(1)). A renewal-by-silence clause asks the tenant for exactly this kind of notice, so keep it inside these limits.

Second, Florida's consumer automatic-renewal law (Fla. Stat. § 501.165) covers a seller's written "service contract". No statute says whether a residential lease is one. If it does apply, a renewal for more than 1 month that keeps the contract in force more than 6 months must be disclosed clearly and conspicuously in the contract, the tenant must be able to cancel the same way they accepted, and a violation makes the renewal provision void and unenforceable.

This library does not offer an automatic renewal clause for Florida. It offers the end-of-term notice clause instead. A landlord who wants renewal by silence may add their own clause, set it out conspicuously, keep the notice within 30 to 60 days, and should take legal advice first.

Without a renewal clause, a tenant who stays after the term with your permission and leaves without the 30-day month-to-month notice owes you an extra month's rent (Fla. Stat. § 83.575(3)). A tenant who stays without your permission is a holdover (Fla. Stat. § 83.58).

title: Leases Longer Than One Year Must Be in Writing
bodyText: Florida's statute of frauds draws its line at one year. No one can be sued on a lease of land for a period longer than 1 year unless the lease, or a note or memorandum of it, is in writing and signed by the person being held to it or by someone that person lawfully authorized (Fla. Stat. § 725.01). The same section covers any agreement that is not to be performed within 1 year of when it is made. A separate conveyancing rule says a term of more than 1 year in land can be created, assigned or surrendered only by a signed written instrument, though no witnesses are needed for a lease or an instrument about a lease (Fla. Stat. § 689.01(1)). So sign every lease longer than a year yourself (or through an authorized agent), and have every tenant sign it. Shorter leases may be oral. Florida's Residential Landlord and Tenant Act (Part II of chapter 83), which governs the rental of a dwelling unit, treats as a rental agreement any written agreement and any oral agreement for less than 1 year. An oral residential agreement for less than 1 year is therefore fully covered by the Act, and a written one is covered whatever its length; there is no exclusion for long leases. An oral agreement for 1 year or more falls outside that definition, and which rules govern it is a question for case law. For tenancies outside Part II, such as nonresidential ones, a lease is a tenancy at will unless it is in writing signed by the lessor (Fla. Stat. § 83.01).

title: Lease Length and Signing Formalities
bodyText: Florida sets no maximum or minimum length for a private residential lease. Florida's statutes set term caps for leases by or of public bodies and other special property. What Florida does regulate is how a longer lease is made. A lease for a term of more than 1 year must be created by a signed written instrument, but no witnesses are required for a lease of real property, and no seal is needed (Fla. Stat. § 689.01(1)). The lease may be signed by you or by your lawfully authorized agent (Fla. Stat. §§ 689.01(1), 725.01). See the statute-of-frauds row for the writing rule. If you are married and the rental is your homestead, the constitution says the owner of homestead real estate, joined by the spouse if married, may alienate the homestead by mortgage, sale or gift (Fla. Const. art. X, § 4(c)). It does not mention leases, and no Florida statute says whether a lease needs the spouse's joinder. The cautious course for a long lease of a married owner's homestead is to have both spouses sign. A court-appointed guardian may lease a ward's property, including homestead property, for a term within or beyond the guardianship, but only after court approval (Fla. Stat. § 744.441(5), (12)). A condominium or homeowners' association's documents may also limit lease terms; see the association leasing row.

title: Recording a Lease
bodyText: Florida does not require you to record or register a residential lease, and no right under Florida's Residential Landlord and Tenant Act depends on recording. Recording is optional, but it matters for longer leases. A lease for a term of 1 year or longer is not good against creditors or later purchasers who pay value without notice unless it is recorded (Fla. Stat. § 695.01(1)). That rule protects the tenant's lease against a later buyer or lender of your property; it does not affect the lease between you and the tenant. Whether a tenant's possession alone gives a buyer notice is a question for case law. The county clerk records leases presented with the required charges (Fla. Stat. § 28.222(3)(a)). To be recorded, the lease must be acknowledged before a notary or other officer, or proved by a subscribing witness (Fla. Stat. § 695.03), and it must carry printed names and addresses and the clerk's blank space (Fla. Stat. § 695.26). One recording rule can help you directly. If the lease says your interest is not subject to liens for improvements the tenant makes, recording the lease or a memorandum containing that language before a notice of commencement is recorded keeps your interest free of the tenant's contractors' liens (Fla. Stat. § 713.10(2)(b)). See the construction liens rows.

title: What a Florida Lease Must Contain
bodyText: Florida's Residential Landlord and Tenant Act (Part II of chapter 83), which governs the rental of a dwelling unit, has no list of terms every lease must contain and no rule about what goes on the first page. A rental agreement may even be oral if it runs for less than 1 year (Fla. Stat. § 83.43(13)). No Florida statute, constitutional provision or civil rule requires the start and end dates, or anything else, on a lease's first page; Florida's statutory first-page rules are for mobile home park prospectuses and condominium sale contracts, plus one recording rule: a lease you want recorded must leave a 3-inch by 3-inch space at the top right of the first page for the clerk (Fla. Stat. § 695.26(1)(e); see "Recording a Lease"). What Florida does require are specific disclosures, each with its own trigger: your name and address in writing at or before the tenancy starts, the radon paragraph, the flood disclosure for leases of 1 year or longer, and the deposit notice if you rent five or more units (see the required disclosures row). Some terms work only if the lease contains them in the statute's shape. A tenant notice before vacating at the end of a fixed term is valid only if the lease also requires your matching nonrenewal notice, within 30 to 60 days (Fla. Stat. § 83.575(1)). An early termination fee of up to 2 months' rent needs a separate addendum in the statutory form, signed when the lease is signed (Fla. Stat. § 83.595(4)). Fees count as rent only if a written lease designates them as rent (Fla. Stat. § 83.43(12)). A fee in lieu of a security deposit needs a written agreement with the statutory disclosure (Fla. Stat. § 83.491). In practice, state the parties, the dwelling, the term with its start and end dates, the rent and when and where it is due, the deposit, and who pays utilities and maintains what. Local ordinances are preempted on lease terms (see the preemption row).

title: No Duty to Give the Tenant a Lease Copy
bodyText:
Florida law does not require you to give a residential tenant a copy of the lease, and failing to do so is not a defense to enforcing it.

Give every tenant a fully signed copy anyway: the lease is your proof of its terms, and a tenant who has a copy is harder to surprise with a rule you later enforce.

Two related rules.
- A licensed real estate broker must keep at least one legible copy of brokerage records, including any rental or lease agreement that engages the broker's services, for at least 5 years (Fla. Stat. § 475.5015). That is a record-keeping duty to the regulator, not a duty to hand the tenant a copy.
- In a mobile home park of 26 or more lots, the park's prospectus must include a copy of the lot rental agreement (Fla. Stat. §§ 723.011(1)(a), 723.012); that is a mobile home park rule, not one for ordinary rentals.

The library's optional receipt clause records that the tenant received the lease and any written rules before signing.

title: No Rule Requiring Tenant Initials
bodyText: Florida law does not require a residential tenant to initial any lease clause or notice for it to be valid. Where Florida wants the tenant's separate assent, it uses a signed addendum with check boxes instead. The e-mail notice addendum has the tenant tick whether they agree to receive notices by e-mail (Fla. Stat. § 83.505(1)). An early termination fee or liquidated damages term works only if the tenant signs a separate addendum, at the time the lease is made, ticking the agreement box (Fla. Stat. § 83.595(4)). Use those forms as the statutes set them out; initials in the margin do not replace them. Florida has an initialing rule for rentals of personal property or equipment, such as a rented appliance or car: the theft statute's warning must be in the rental agreement and initialed by the renter before failure to return can be prosecuted (Fla. Stat. § 812.155(6)). It does not apply to a dwelling. Having tenants initial important clauses is still a sensible practice for proving they saw them.

title: No Type-Size Rule for Leases
bodyText: Florida sets no minimum type size, typeface or legibility rule for a residential lease, and no rule makes a small-print lease harder to enforce or prove; the only legibility rule found is that a lease presented for recording must show each signer's name and address legibly printed, typed or stamped (Fla. Stat. § 695.26(1)(a)). The type-size and "conspicuous type" rules found are for other documents: condominium and cooperative sale contracts and disclosures, a condominium conversion notice to tenants, mobile home park prospectuses, motor vehicle leases, retail installment contracts, rental car insurance and construction-loan warnings. Within the Act itself, two terms have presentation rules: the e-mail notice addendum must conspicuously advise both parties that the election is voluntary and can be revoked (Fla. Stat. § 83.505(1)), and a lease term releasing you from storing a departed tenant's property must carry its legend printed or clearly stamped on the lease (Fla. Stat. § 83.67(5)). Two practical points. Where Florida prescribes a form for a lease or addendum (the fee-in-lieu-of-deposit disclosure, the early termination fee addendum, the e-mail notice addendum, the radon paragraph), copy the statute's words and layout as printed, including any capital letters, since each must follow the statute's form substantially or, for radon, its exact language. And a court may refuse to enforce an unconscionable term, so a key term buried in tiny print invites that argument. Use a readable size throughout.

title: No Rule on Month-to-Month vs. Fixed-Term Pricing
bodyText: Florida has no rule that a month-to-month tenant's terms may not be more burdensome than a fixed-term tenant's, or the reverse, and no cap on how much more rent you may charge for one kind of tenancy than the other. You may price a month-to-month rental differently from a 12-month lease, and local governments cannot add such a rule, since rental agreement terms are preempted to the state (Fla. Stat. § 83.425). Two limits still apply to how you treat individual tenants. You may not discriminatorily raise a tenant's rent or cut services primarily to retaliate for protected conduct, such as a good-faith code complaint, joining a tenant organization or exercising fair housing rights; "discrimination" here means treating the tenant differently as to rent, services or action taken (Fla. Stat. § 83.64(1), (4)). And fair housing law bars different terms based on a protected characteristic (see the fair housing row). Apply any month-to-month premium the same way to every tenant who chooses that option.

title: No Rent Concession Rule
bodyText:
Florida has no statute on rent concessions such as free months, move-in specials or rent credits in a residential lease: no disclosure rule, no limit on taking a concession back, and no rule on how a concession counts toward the rent.

A concession is an ordinary lease term, so write it into the lease: what is given, its amount, and the rental periods it covers. The library's rent concession clause does that.

Be careful with any condition that makes the tenant repay a concession if they leave early or default. That works like a charge for early termination, and Florida limits liquidated damages and early termination fees for a tenant's early exit to 2 months' rent, available only if the tenant accepts them in the separate statutory addendum at signing (Fla. Stat. § 83.595(4)). A repayment term outside that addendum may not be enforceable.

title: Paying Rent in Installments
bodyText:
For a rental of a dwelling unit under Florida's Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, the default rule is that rent is payable without demand or notice at the beginning of each rent payment period and is uniformly apportionable from day to day, unless otherwise agreed (Fla. Stat. § 83.46(1)).

So you and the tenant may agree in the lease to split each month's rent into installments with their own due dates. The library's installment clause sets the schedule.

Each installment is then rent due on its own date. If an installment is unpaid, the 3-day notice works as for any rent: the tenant has 3 days, excluding Saturday, Sunday and legal holidays, after delivery of your written demand (Fla. Stat. § 83.56(3)).

Accepting a partial payment of rent for the period does not waive your right to terminate, but if you accept partial rent after posting the 3-day notice, you must either give the tenant a receipt stating the date and amount received and the agreed date and balance due before filing, put the partial rent in the court registry when you file, or post a new 3-day notice for the new amount (Fla. Stat. § 83.56(5)(a)).

Stating in the lease that scheduled installments are not partial payments helps keep the two apart.

title: Rent Increases Built Into the Lease
bodyText:
During a fixed-term lease of a dwelling unit, the rent is what the lease says. You may raise it mid-term only if the lease itself provides for the increase (see the rent increase notice row).

Florida has no statute that regulates a scheduled increase, an index-based adjustment or a mid-term increase clause in a residential lease, sets a notice period for one, or caps the amount. Local rent control is barred (see the preemption row).

So if you want the right to change rent during the term, put it in the lease: a schedule of amounts and dates, a published-index adjustment, or an increase on written notice. The library offers optional clauses for each.

Three limits.
- First, you may not discriminatorily raise a tenant's rent primarily to retaliate for protected conduct such as a good-faith code complaint or fair housing complaint (Fla. Stat. § 83.64(1)); a written escalation clause applied to every tenant on its terms is the safest course.
- Second, a consumer-price-index escalation clause is void in a lease of recreational facilities, land or other commonly used facilities serving residential condominiums or communities (Fla. Stat. §§ 718.4015(1), 720.31(5)); that rule reaches association facility leases, not your lease of a unit.
- Third, mobile home park lot rent increases follow chapter 723's own reasonableness rules.

A court may also refuse to enforce an unconscionable term.

title: No Rent Reporting Rule
bodyText: Florida state law does not require you to offer tenants positive rent reporting to credit bureaus, does not bar you from requiring a tenant to enroll in a reporting program, and does not require a written notice before you report late rent. One related rule: if you offer a fee in lieu of a security deposit, the written fee agreement must say that a default on the fee will not adversely affect the tenant's credit rating if the security deposit is timely paid, and that paying the deposit means a fee default or termination may not adversely affect the tenant's credit report (Fla. Stat. § 83.491(4)(a)3., 5.). If you report rent payments, federal credit-reporting law governs accuracy and disputes; take advice before you start reporting.

title: Guarantors and Lease Renewals
bodyText:
Florida has no statute on residential lease guaranties: nothing says whether a guarantor stays liable after the lease is renewed, extended or continues month to month, nothing requires a stated maximum or end date, and nothing limits a deposit taken from a guarantor.

The one rule that applies is the statute of frauds: no one can be sued on a special promise to answer for the debt, default or miscarriage of another person unless the promise, or a note or memorandum of it, is in writing and signed by the guarantor or someone the guarantor lawfully authorized (Fla. Stat. § 725.01).

So write the guaranty down, have the guarantor sign it, and say plainly whether it covers renewals, extensions and any month-to-month continuation, and whether it covers rent increases. Whether a guarantor is released by a renewal or change the guaranty does not mention is a question for case law. The library's guaranty clause states a maximum and makes the renewal choice explicit.

title: Which Notices Must Be in Writing
Agreeing on How Notices Are Delivered
bodyText:
For a rental of a dwelling unit, Florida fixes how the key notices are delivered, and the lease can add only one method.

The 7-day and 3-day notices under Fla. Stat. § 83.56(1)-(3), and periodic-tenancy termination notices, must be mailed, hand-delivered, e-mailed under the statute's e-mail rules, or left at the home if the tenant is absent; those requirements may not be waived in the lease (Fla. Stat. §§ 83.56(4), 83.57).

The one method the parties may add is e-mail.
