Either party may e-mail any notice required under the Act only if both have signed an addendum, in substantially the statute's form, agreeing to e-mail delivery and giving an e-mail address; the election is voluntary and can be revoked or the address updated by written notice. An e-mailed notice is delivered when sent unless it bounces, and the sender must keep a copy and proof of transmission (Fla. Stat. § 83.505).

Florida has no rule letting the parties agree to text messages, app messages or portal posts for these notices. Use those channels only as an extra courtesy copy.

For notices the Act does not tie to a method, such as notice before entry for repairs, the lease may say how you will give it.

title: Proceedings Against the Property
bodyText: Florida law does not require you to tell a residential tenant about a foreclosure, lawsuit, lien, condemnation or code-enforcement case against the property, and it does not require the tenant to tell you about one the tenant learns of. The library's optional clause asks the tenant to pass on any notice of a proceeding to recover the property. Three related rules. If someone sues your tenant in ejectment, claiming a superior right to possession, and you are not a party, you must be made a party before the case goes further unless the court orders otherwise (Fla. Stat. § 66.021(4)). In a mortgage foreclosure, a bona fide residential tenant's rights come from the federal Protecting Tenants at Foreclosure Act; Florida's own standby version (Fla. Stat. § 83.5615) is not in force (see the foreclosure row). And if you own a condominium or homeowners' association unit and fall behind on assessments, the association may demand that your tenant pay the rent to it (see the association leasing row). Telling tenants early about a foreclosure or a code case that could force them out is good practice, even though no statute requires it.

title: No Emergency Contact Rule
bodyText: Florida law does not require you to give a residential tenant an emergency or after-hours telephone number, a management website or any hotline notice, in the lease or elsewhere. What Florida does require is your name and address, or the name and address of a person authorized to receive notices and demands for you, disclosed in writing at or before the start of the tenancy (Fla. Stat. § 83.50). Your 3-day notice for unpaid rent must also show your name, address and phone number, since the statutory form includes them (Fla. Stat. § 83.56(3)). Giving tenants a number to call for emergencies such as leaks, fire or a lockout is still sensible: the Act lets you enter at any time to protect or preserve the premises, and a tenant who can reach you quickly limits the damage. Local codes are preempted on matters the Act covers (see the preemption row).

title: Rules That Depend on How Many Units You Rent
bodyText: Florida's Residential Landlord and Tenant Act applies to every residential landlord, however small. There is no small-landlord exemption from the Act itself. A few rules turn on size or building type: (1) Deposit notice: the written notice of where you hold the deposit and whether it earns interest, with its statutory disclosure, does not apply if you rent fewer than five individual dwelling units (Fla. Stat. § 83.49(2)). The holding rules and the 30-day claim notice apply to everyone. (2) Surety bond: instead of a separate account, you may post a surety bond for the deposits you hold; if you rent in five or more counties you may post one bond with the Secretary of State instead of one in each county (Fla. Stat. § 83.49(1)(c)). (3) Building type: in a single-family home or duplex your code-compliance and structural repair duties may be altered in writing, and you must install working smoke detection devices at the start of the tenancy unless otherwise agreed in writing; the extra duties for other dwellings (extermination, locks and keys, common areas, garbage, heat and water) apply unless otherwise agreed in writing (Fla. Stat. § 83.51(1)-(2)). (4) Licensing as public lodging: a place renting four rental units or less is not a public lodging establishment unless advertised as regularly rented to transients. Houses of one to four families and condominium units rented for at least 30 days or a month are also excluded, but only if both conditions hold (not advertised for stays under a month) and no more than four rental units in a single complex are available (Fla. Stat. § 509.013(4)(b)3.-4.). Larger apartment buildings are licensed as nontransient or transient apartments, and their landlords must background-screen employees (Fla. Stat. §§ 509.242(1)(d)-(e), 83.515(1)). (5) Mobile home parks: chapter 723 applies to parks offering 10 or more lots (Fla. Stat. § 723.002(1)).

title: Florida's Statutory Limits and Figures
bodyText: Florida caps few landlord charges. It sets no maximum security deposit, late fee or application fee for a residential rental, and local caps are preempted (see the no-deposit-cap and no-fee-caps rows). The figures Florida does set for a rental of a dwelling unit: (1) Early exit: liquidated damages or an early termination fee may not exceed 2 months' rent, the fee may require no more than 60 days' notice, and the tenant must accept it in the separate statutory addendum (Fla. Stat. § 83.595(4)). (2) End-of-term notice: a lease may not require less than 30 or more than 60 days' notice from either party (Fla. Stat. § 83.575(1)). (3) Returned payments: in place of other service charges, bank fees actually incurred plus $25 (face value up to $50), $30 (over $50 up to $300), $40 (over $300), or 5 percent of the face value, whichever is greater (Fla. Stat. § 68.065(2)). (4) Deposit interest and bonds: an interest-bearing deposit account must pay the tenant at least 75 percent of the account's annualized average rate or 5 percent simple interest, as you elect; a surety bond is the deposits held or $50,000, whichever is less (or $250,000 for one statewide bond if you rent in five or more counties), plus 5 percent interest to the tenant (Fla. Stat. § 83.49(1)(b)-(c)). (5) Fee in lieu of deposit: the fee may not be increased during the term (Fla. Stat. § 83.491(4)(a)1.). (6) Entry for repairs: at least 24 hours' notice, between 7:30 a.m. and 8:00 p.m. (Fla. Stat. § 83.53(2)). (7) Penalties you can face or claim: double rent against a tenant holding over without permission (Fla. Stat. § 83.58), and, if you violate the prohibited-practices section, actual and consequential damages or 3 months' rent, whichever is greater (Fla. Stat. § 83.67(6)). Any charge Florida does not cap is still subject to the court's power to refuse an unconscionable term.

title: Renter's Insurance
bodyText:
Florida has no statute on requiring renter's insurance in a residential lease: nothing stops you from requiring it, nothing lets the tenant insist on choosing the carrier or limits charging for coverage you place, and nothing requires a general advisory that your insurance does not cover the tenant's belongings.

A requirement to carry renter's insurance is an ordinary lease term; the library's renter's insurance clause sets it.

Three Florida rules touch insurance.
- First, for a lease of 1 year or longer, the flood disclosure you must give in a separate document at or before signing tells the tenant that renters' insurance policies do not cover flood damage and encourages separate flood coverage (Fla. Stat. § 83.512(1)).
- Second, if a tenant uses a waterbed or other flotation bedding, which you may not prohibit if it meets building codes, the tenant must carry flotation insurance in the tenant's name in a reasonable amount, with a loss payable clause to the building owner (Fla. Stat. § 83.535).
- Third, if you offer a fee in lieu of a security deposit and use any of it to buy insurance, you must tell the tenant in writing that the tenant is not insured and is not a beneficiary of that coverage (Fla. Stat. § 83.491(3)(i)).

Do not use the lease to disclaim your own liability for the tenant's property: a term that limits a liability arising under law is void (see the waiver row).

title: No Landlord Insurance Requirement
bodyText: Florida state law does not require a residential landlord to carry liability or property insurance on a rental, or to register proof of insurance with any government. Local registration or insurance rules on matters the Act covers are preempted (see the preemption row). Insurance is still prudent. Your liability to a tenant arising under law cannot be limited by the lease (see the waiver row), and your mortgage lender, a condominium or homeowners' association's documents, or a government housing program may require coverage by contract. If you rent a condominium unit, the association insures what its declaration and the condominium statutes assign to it, not your own liability as a landlord.

title: Insurance Claims Between You and the Tenant
bodyText: Florida has no statute on whether you may require a tenant to claim on the tenant's renter's insurance for damage or repairs, or on how claims on either party's policy are handled between you. Your repair duties under the Act stay yours whatever insurance the tenant has, and a lease term that waives them or limits your liability arising under law is void (see the waiver row). Florida does regulate one kind of claim. If the tenant pays a fee in lieu of a security deposit (an option you may offer under a rental agreement that requires a deposit), you must notify the tenant within 30 days after the tenancy ends of any unpaid rent, fees, repair costs or other amounts due. You may not submit a claim to an insurer for those losses until at least 15 days after that notice, and the claim must include an itemized list with due dates, documentation of damages and repair costs, and a copy of any written objection or report of an objection by the tenant. If the insurer pays and has subrogation rights, it may seek reimbursement from the tenant within 1 year after the tenancy ends, must give the tenant all your supporting documents and the settlement statement, and the tenant keeps every defense the tenant would have had against you. You may not accept payment from both the tenant and an insurer for the same amounts (Fla. Stat. § 83.491(2)).

title: Landlord's Lien on a Tenant's Belongings
bodyText: In a residential tenancy, Florida gives you a lien on all of the tenant's personal property located on the premises for accrued rent due under the rental agreement. The lien attaches when the sheriff gives you possession of the premises; the tenant's property need not be removed for you to get possession. A written rental agreement may modify or waive the lien in whole or in part. If the tenant is the head of a family, $1,000 of personal property the tenant owns is exempt, no more than the constitution allows. The old remedy of distress for rent is abolished for residential tenancies (Fla. Stat. § 713.691). You enforce the lien in court, not by taking things. A landlord may claim the lien in a summary court action describing the property; if you win, the judgment includes a 15 percent attorney's fee and costs and is a prior lien on the property described (Fla. Stat. § 85.011(5)). Until then, you may not remove the tenant's personal property from the dwelling unless after surrender, abandonment, a lawful eviction, or the death of the last remaining tenant under the statute's conditions, and doing so otherwise makes you liable for actual and consequential damages or 3 months' rent, whichever is greater (Fla. Stat. § 83.67(5)-(6)). Property left after surrender or abandonment follows the abandoned-property rules (see those rows). The broader landlord's lien and distress procedure in Part I of chapter 83 (Fla. Stat. §§ 83.08-83.19) apply to nonresidential tenancies and tenancies Part II does not govern. Hotels and transient lodging have their own liens. This library offers no lien clause: the statute already supplies the lien, and a clause widening it would add risk under the self-help ban.

title: Homestead and Exemption Waivers
bodyText: Start with what a tenant has to waive. Florida's constitution exempts from forced sale a homestead owned by a natural person and $1,000 of personal property (Fla. Const. art. X, § 4(a)). A renter usually owns no homestead land, but a person who owns and occupies a house, mobile home or modular home on land they possess by lease may claim it as a homestead exempt from levy and sale (Fla. Stat. § 222.05). Statutes add other exemptions, including a debtor's interest of up to $5,000 in one motor vehicle and, if the debtor claims no homestead exemption, up to $4,000 in personal property (Fla. Stat. § 222.25(1), (4)). For your landlord's lien, a head of family's personal property worth $1,000 is exempt (Fla. Stat. § 713.691(2)). No Florida statute, constitutional provision or civil rule lets a lease waive the homestead or these property exemptions. Do not put such a waiver in a lease; a court is likely to refuse it. One waiver does exist by statute: a head of family whose disposable earnings exceed $750 a week may agree in writing to allow those earnings to be garnished, up to the federal limit the statutory form recites, but only in a separate document attached to the contract, in the contract's language, in substantially the statutory form and in at least 14-point type (Fla. Stat. § 222.11(2)(b)). Earnings at or below $750 a week stay exempt. This library does not offer that waiver: it is a separate consumer-credit document, and a landlord who wants one should take legal advice.

title: Arbitration Clauses in Florida Leases
bodyText: Florida has no statute written for arbitration in residential leases. None authorizes, bars or shapes an arbitration clause in a rental of a dwelling unit. The general law is the Revised Florida Arbitration Code. An agreement contained in a record to submit any existing or later controversy to arbitration is valid, enforceable and irrevocable except on a ground that exists at law or in equity for revoking a contract (Fla. Stat. § 682.02(1)). Before a dispute arises, a party may not waive the right to be represented by an attorney at any arbitration hearing (Fla. Stat. §§ 682.07, 682.014(2)(d)). Parties to a civil dispute may also agree in writing to voluntary binding arbitration in place of litigation, provided no constitutional issue is involved (Fla. Stat. § 44.104(1)). The Residential Landlord and Tenant Act points the other way for possession. Your eviction is filed in county court, where you are entitled to the summary procedure (Fla. Stat. § 83.59(2)), and a lease term is void to the extent it purports to waive or preclude the rights, remedies or requirements the Act sets out (Fla. Stat. § 83.47(1)(a); see the waiver row). Whether a lease arbitration clause precludes the tenant's statutory remedies, such as the rent-into-court defense or the court's determination of rent reduction, is a question for case law. This library does not offer an arbitration clause for Florida, because an arbitration clause may slow your own eviction remedy and may be void in part. It offers the narrow jury waiver and the informal dispute resolution clause instead. A landlord who wants arbitration of money claims should have a lawyer draft it, keep possession actions in court, and preserve each party's right to counsel.

title: Trying to Settle Disputes Before Court
bodyText:
Florida has no statute requiring, permitting or limiting a lease term that makes the parties try to resolve a dispute informally before going to court.

A lease may ask for it, as long as it does not delay or limit a notice, deadline or remedy the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act gives, since a term that waives or precludes those is void (see the waiver row). Keep possession actions out of any such clause. The library's optional clause does this.

Florida's own deposit notice, which landlords renting five or more units must give, already tells tenants: 'YOU SHOULD ATTEMPT TO INFORMALLY RESOLVE ANY DISPUTE BEFORE FILING A LAWSUIT' (Fla. Stat. § 83.49(2)(d)).

Mediation in court works differently for landlord-tenant cases. A court must refer a civil action for money damages to mediation on one party's request, but that rule does not apply to a landlord and tenant dispute that does not include a personal injury claim (Fla. Stat. § 44.102(2)(a)). In an eviction where the tenant raises defenses other than payment, the court may not set mediation or trial until the tenant has paid the rent into the court registry as the statute requires (Fla. Stat. § 83.56(5)(b)).

title: House Rules in Florida
bodyText:
Florida's Residential Landlord and Tenant Act lets you enforce reasonable rules.

If a tenant materially fails to comply with the tenant's statutory duties, material provisions of the rental agreement, or reasonable rules or regulations, you may give the 7-day notice to cure or, for conduct that should not be given a chance to cure, the 7-day notice of termination (Fla. Stat. § 83.56(2)).

Good-faith action for violation of reasonable rules is also good cause that defeats a retaliation defense (Fla. Stat. § 83.64(3)).

The Act says nothing else about rules. It sets no test for when a rule is reasonable, no procedure or notice for adopting or changing rules during a tenancy, and no limit on mid-term changes that substantially modify the bargain. Outside mobile home parks, which follow chapter 723's own posting and change procedures, Florida's statutes, constitution and civil rules have none.

So the lease should do the work: attach the rules in effect at signing, and say whether and how you may adopt or change rules during the term. The library's Florida rules clause does this.

Whether a rule is reasonable is for the court, every lease carries an obligation of good faith, and an unconscionable term may be refused enforcement. On a month-to-month tenancy, the cautious way to impose a new term is the statutory termination notice with an offer of new terms (see the term change notice row).

Association rules bind your tenant separately (see the association rows).

title: Illegal Use of the Rental
bodyText:
No Florida statute makes a residential lease void or annulled because the premises are used for an illegal purpose.

Your remedy against a tenant who misuses the home is the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act: the tenant must not damage your property or unreasonably disturb the neighbors (Fla. Stat. § 83.52(6)-(7)), and a material breach of the lease, including its residential-use and criminal-activity terms, supports the 7-day notices (Fla. Stat. § 83.56(2)).

See the residential use and criminal activity rows.

Criminal and nuisance law also reaches you as the owner. It is a crime to let or rent any place knowing it will be used for lewdness, assignation or prostitution (Fla. Stat. § 796.06(1)).

A place of prostitution, illegal gambling or any violation of state law, and a dwelling used to keep, sell, deliver or use controlled substances unlawfully, is a nuisance that can be enjoined, and the owner can be sued along with those maintaining it (Fla. Stat. §§ 823.05(1), 823.10(1), 60.05(1)). In such a case, if a tenant has been convicted of a drug offense under chapter 893 or of prostitution under Fla. Stat. § 796.07, the court may order the tenant to vacate within 72 hours if you and the tenant are parties and the order will abate the nuisance (Fla. Stat. § 60.05(5)).

Local nuisance boards may, where a local ordinance provides for it, fine owners of repeat drug, prostitution and similar sites, but a rental property may not be abated or forfeited for a nuisance someone else committed if you begin rehabilitation within 30 days and finish within a reasonable time (Fla. Stat. § 893.138(12)).

Act quickly when you learn of illegal use.

title: Parking Rules and Towing Notices
bodyText:
Florida has no rule that your parking or towing rules must be given to the tenant before the lease is signed, carry a set heading, stay unchanged during the term, or limit the vehicle information you may ask for.

Put your parking rules in the lease or its rules (see the parking and rules clauses).

Parking in an unauthorized manner, or permitting it, is the Act's own example of noncompliance you must, for a first violation, give the tenant 7 days to cure before terminating (Fla. Stat. § 83.56(2)(b)); a repeat within 12 months is treated more strictly (Fla. Stat. § 83.56(2)(a)-(b)).

Florida's notice rules for parking are posted signs. To tow an unauthorized vehicle without paying for the tow, you must post the statutory tow-away signs at each driveway entrance at least 24 hours before towing, unless the property is part of a single-family residence or the vehicle's owner was told in person the space is reserved (Fla. Stat. § 715.07(2); see the towing row).

If you instead charge parking fees or violation charges on private property used for parking, you may set rules and rates, but you must post legible signs stating the property is not operated by government, the violation charges, a working phone number and e-mail address, and the grace period and appeal process. Invoices must carry the statutory uppercase statement and an appeal route to a neutral adjudicator, late fees must wait, you must allow at least a 15-minute grace period on entry, and you may not sell personal information obtained from people who park (Fla. Stat. § 715.075).

Whether that section reaches an apartment lot used only by tenants and guests is not settled by statute, so follow it if you levy parking charges.

title: No Unbundled Parking Rule
bodyText: Florida state law does not require you to price parking separately from rent, to offer tenants the option of renting without a parking space, or to include parking in the rent. You may include parking in the rent or charge for it separately; say which in the lease (see the parking and assigned parking space clauses). If you charge a separate parking fee and want it to be treated as rent for nonpayment purposes, the written lease must designate it as rent (see the fees as rent row). Zoning rules on how much parking a new building must provide are a matter for local governments and the planning statutes, not for your lease.

title: Leasing When You Do Not Own Outright
bodyText: Florida has no civil-law "usufruct", and no Florida statute says what happens to a lease granted by someone who holds the property only for life when that person dies. Whether such a lease ends with the life estate is a question for case law. If you hold a life estate, or rent from someone who does, the cautious course is to have the remainder owners join in signing the lease, or to limit the term so it cannot outlast your interest, and tell the tenant in writing. Fiduciaries have express powers. A personal representative of an estate may, without court order unless the will or a court provides otherwise, enter into a lease as lessor for a term within or extending beyond the period of administration (Fla. Stat. § 733.612(7)). A trustee may enter into a lease for a period within or extending beyond the duration of the trust (Fla. Stat. § 736.0816(10)). A guardian of property may do so only after court approval (Fla. Stat. § 744.441(5)). If a fiduciary signs your lease as landlord, ask for proof of authority and keep it with the lease. When the last remaining tenant dies, a separate procedure applies (see the deceased tenant row).

title: Elevators and Other Building Facilities
bodyText: Beyond the core repair duties, few Florida statutes address particular building facilities. For a dwelling unit other than a single-family home or duplex, unless otherwise agreed in writing, you must make reasonable provision for the clean and safe condition of common areas and for garbage removal and outside receptacles (Fla. Stat. § 83.51(2)(a)3.-4.). You may not cause any utility service furnished to the tenant to be cut off or interrupted, and the statute names elevator service and garbage collection among those services (Fla. Stat. § 83.67(1)); a violation makes you liable for actual and consequential damages or 3 months' rent, whichever is greater (Fla. Stat. § 83.67(6)). The tenant in turn must use and operate the facilities and appliances, including elevators, in a reasonable manner (Fla. Stat. § 83.52(5)). Elevators, platform lifts, stairway chairlifts, escalators and dumbwaiters are covered by Florida's elevator safety chapter, except hand-operated dumbwaiters and elevators, chairlifts and wheelchair lifts located in private residences (Fla. Stat. § 399.02(2), (3)(q), (3)(u)). As the elevator owner you are responsible for its safe operation, proper maintenance, inspection and correction of code deficiencies once a certificate of operation is issued, though a lease may assign those responsibilities (Fla. Stat. § 399.02(5)(b)). Each must be inspected annually by a certified elevator inspector, unless it is a non-escalator, non-dumbwaiter unit serving only two adjacent floors under a service maintenance contract, and service contracts must be reported to the state each year (Fla. Stat. § 399.061(1)). No Florida statute imposes a landlord duty for garage door openers, laundry rooms, mailboxes or similar facilities. If you provide them, list them in the lease and say who maintains them. Locks, lighting, pools and fire safety have their own rows.

title: Optional Terms Florida Lets the Lease Add
bodyText: Several Florida rules apply only if the lease invokes them, or let the lease change the default. For a rental of a dwelling unit, the main ones are: (1) End-of-term notice: in a fixed-term lease, require the tenant's notice before moving out, paired with your nonrenewal notice, 30 to 60 days, with liquidated damages only after your reminder notice (Fla. Stat. § 83.575; end-of-term notice clause). (2) Early termination fee or liquidated damages of up to 2 months' rent, accepted in a separate statutory addendum at signing (Fla. Stat. § 83.595(4); early termination addendum). (3) E-mail delivery of notices by signed addendum (Fla. Stat. § 83.505; electronic notice addendum). (4) A fee in lieu of a security deposit, by written agreement with the statutory disclosure (Fla. Stat. § 83.491; fee-in-lieu clause). (5) Fees designated as rent in the written lease (Fla. Stat. § 83.43(12)). (6) Tenant payment of garbage, water, fuel or utility charges (Fla. Stat. § 83.51(2)(e)). (7) Shifting maintenance in writing: for a single-family home or duplex, your code and structural duties may be altered in writing; for other dwellings, the extra duties apply unless otherwise agreed in writing (Fla. Stat. § 83.51(1)-(2); tenant-maintained items clause). (8) Release from storing property after surrender or abandonment, in the lease with the statutory legend printed or stamped on it, or in a separate written agreement (Fla. Stat. § 83.67(5); abandoned property release clause). (9) A different vacating notice from the default 7 days by certified mail or personal delivery (Fla. Stat. § 83.49(5)). (10) Rent timing other than the default due date at the start of each period (Fla. Stat. § 83.46(1); rent and installment clauses). (11) For housing furnished with employment to an employee or resident manager of an apartment house or complex, a written agreement displaces the wage-period default (Fla. Stat. § 83.46(3)). (12) Rules and changes to rules (rules clause), a narrow jury waiver, rent escalation and concessions (see those rows). Options the library declines, each with its own row: an automatic renewal clause, an arbitration clause, a clause modifying your statutory landlord's lien (Fla. Stat. § 713.691(1)) and a wage-garnishment waiver. A lease with an option to purchase: once the buyer has paid at least 12 months' rent, or 1 month's rent plus a deposit of at least 5 percent of the price, under a contract of sale, the Act no longer applies (Fla. Stat. § 83.42(2)); see the required disclosures row for sale disclosures.

title: Children in the Household
bodyText: Florida's Fair Housing Act makes it unlawful to refuse to rent, to otherwise make a dwelling unavailable, or to set different terms, conditions or services because of familial status, and to advertise or state a preference against families with children. Familial status means a child under 18 living with a parent, a legal custodian, or someone the parent or custodian has designated in writing; the protection also covers anyone who is pregnant or in the process of getting legal custody of a child. The Act covers any dwelling except a single-family house rented by an owner who owns no more than three and rents without a real estate licensee and without a discriminatory advertisement, and rooms or units in a building of four or fewer units where you live in one of them. Housing for older persons (62 and over, or 55 and over meeting the 80 percent occupancy, published-policy and verification tests) may exclude families with children. Florida has no separate landlord-tenant rule, of the kind some states have, on ending or refusing to renew a tenancy because a child joined the household during it, and nothing in Florida law requires your lease to say anything about children. But the Act's ban on making a dwelling unavailable because of familial status is not limited to applicants, so do not end, refuse to renew or change the terms of a tenancy because a tenant has a baby, takes custody of a child or becomes pregnant. You may apply a reasonable local maximum-occupancy restriction, which the Act leaves in place; apply the same number to every household and base it on the size of the unit and its bedrooms, never on whether the occupants are children. The library's occupant clause ("Permitted Occupants" clause) names who lives in the home; don't add a children limit to it. See "Fair Housing" for the Act as a whole.

title: Disability Accommodations and Modifications
bodyText:
Florida's Fair Housing Act bars discrimination in renting because of the disability of the applicant or tenant, of anyone who lives or will live in the home, or of anyone associated with them.

Two duties follow.
- First, you must make reasonable accommodations in your rules, policies, practices and services when they may be necessary to give a person with a disability an equal opportunity to use and enjoy the home: a reserved parking space near the door, a waiver of a no-pets rule for an assistance animal, or extra time or a different way to pay or give notice are common examples.
- Second, you may not refuse to let a tenant with a disability make reasonable modifications to the home, at the tenant's expense, when they may be necessary for the tenant's full enjoyment of it: grab bars, a ramp or wider doorways.

Disability means a physical or mental impairment that substantially limits one or more major life activities, a record of one, being regarded as having one, or a developmental disability. The Act covers any dwelling except a single-family house rented by an owner who owns no more than three and rents without a real estate licensee and without a discriminatory advertisement, and rooms or units in a building of four or fewer units where you live in one of them.

You need not make a dwelling built for first occupancy before March 13, 1991 physically accessible yourself, except where another law requires it, and you need not rent to someone whose tenancy would be a direct threat to others' health or safety or would cause substantial physical damage to others' property.

Florida's statute, unlike the federal Fair Housing Act, says nothing about restoring the home when the tenant leaves: federal law lets a landlord, where it is reasonable, condition permission for a modification on the tenant agreeing to restore the interior to its prior condition, reasonable wear and tear excepted, but no Florida statute grants or forbids that condition, sets up a restoration escrow, or requires your lease to mention it. The library does not offer a lease clause on restoration for Florida for that reason. If you want restoration, agree it in writing with the tenant when the modification is requested, limit it to interior changes where restoration is reasonable, and take advice first.

Assistance animals have their own rules (see "Service and Emotional Support Animals" clause).

title: Asking Applicants About Protected Traits
bodyText: Florida has no separate statute, apart from its ban on discrimination, that forbids a landlord to ask applicants or tenants about, or keep records of, race, color, national origin, sex, disability, familial status or religion. Two Florida rules still limit what you ask. First, Florida's Fair Housing Act makes it unlawful to make, print or publish any notice, statement or advertisement about renting a dwelling that indicates a preference, limitation or discrimination based on any of those traits, or an intention to make one, so a question on an application or in a showing that signals a preference (for example, "Do you plan to have children?") can itself be unlawful. Second, when a tenant asks to keep an emotional support animal, you may ask for reliable information supporting the disability and the need for the animal only when they are not readily apparent, and you may not ask for information disclosing the diagnosis or severity of the disability or for medical records (the tenant may volunteer them). The Act applies to dwellings except a small single-family landlord renting without a licensee and without a discriminatory advertisement, and owner-occupied buildings of four or fewer units; the advertising and statement ban still binds the single-family landlord who wants that exemption. Cautious course: ask every applicant the same written questions, limited to what you need to decide (identity, income, rental history and the occupants' names), and don't ask about or note any protected trait.

title: No Staff Work-Card Rule for Senior Housing
bodyText: Florida has no rule requiring staff of 55-and-over or other age-restricted rental housing to carry a work card or identification card, and no screening rule tied to senior housing as such. Senior housing matters in Florida law for a different reason: housing that qualifies as housing for older persons may exclude families with children (see "Fair Housing"). Staff screening turns on the type of property, not the age of the residents. If your property is licensed as a nontransient or transient apartment, you must require each employee to undergo a background screening as a condition of employment (see "Background Screening of Apartment Employees"). Licensed care settings such as assisted living facilities and continuing care retirement communities have their own staff screening rules.

title: Crime of Refusing a Service Animal in Housing
bodyText: In Florida it is a crime for anyone providing housing for rent to discriminate against a person with a disability, and Florida's service-animal statute makes clear what that means for animals. A tenant or applicant with a disability who has or gets a service animal is entitled to full and equal access to all housing covered by the statute and may not be charged extra for the animal; no-pet rules, pet deposits and pet rent don't apply to it. The tenant is liable for any damage the animal does to the premises or to another person there, and you may ask for proof that its vaccinations are current. A service animal is one trained to do work or perform tasks directly related to the person's disability; for housing, the statute's limit to dogs and miniature horses does not apply. The statute covers any property used as a home or sleeping place, except a single-family residence whose occupants rent out no more than one room in it. A landlord, or a landlord's agent such as a property manager, who discriminates against a person with a disability commits a second-degree misdemeanor, punishable by up to 60 days in jail and a fine of up to $500. These service-animal rules do not apply to emotional support animals, which have their own statute (see "Service and Emotional Support Animals" clause). Florida's separate rule on public accommodations, which lets a business exclude an out-of-control or unhousebroken service animal, is written for hotels, transport and places open to the general public; it is not stated as a housing rule, so don't rely on it to remove a tenant's service animal, and get advice before acting on a problem animal. Treat your leasing office and any area you open to the public as a public accommodation for visitors with service animals. See also "Service Animal Penalties".

title: False Service or Support Animal Claims
bodyText:
Florida has two crimes for false animal claims, and both reach housing.
- First, anyone who knowingly and willfully misrepresents, by conduct or by spoken or written notice, that he or she uses and is qualified to use a service animal, or is a service-animal trainer, commits a second-degree misdemeanor and must do 30 hours of community service. The statute is written by the act, not by place, so it is not limited to stores and restaurants.
- Second, a person who falsifies information or documents, or knowingly gives fraudulent ones, for an emotional support animal request to a housing provider, or who otherwise knowingly and willfully misrepresents having a disability or a disability-related need for an emotional support animal, commits a second-degree misdemeanor and must do 30 hours of community service within 6 months after conviction. A second-degree misdemeanor carries up to 60 days in jail and a fine of up to $500.

An emotional support animal registration, certificate, ID card or patch obtained from the Internet is not, by itself, enough to establish a disability or the need for the animal, so you may ask for reliable supporting information when the disability or need is not readily apparent.

These are crimes for a prosecutor to charge; they give you no right to fine a tenant or end a tenancy on your own, and a suspicion of a false claim is not a reason to refuse an accommodation without following the request rules in "Service and Emotional Support Animals" clause. See also "Service Animal Penalties".

title: Marijuana in Rental Housing
bodyText:
Florida allows marijuana for medical use only, by registered qualified patients who buy it from a licensed medical marijuana treatment center. The constitutional amendment that created the program does not change the laws on non-medical use, possession, production or sale.

No Florida statute protects a medical marijuana patient or caregiver from being refused a lease or penalized as a tenant, and none requires you to allow medical marijuana in your rental. The medical marijuana statute says it does not impair any party's ability to restrict or limit smoking or vaping marijuana on his or her private property, so a lease may ban smoking and vaping marijuana anywhere on your property.

Growing marijuana at home is not part of lawful medical use: medical use covers only marijuana bought from a treatment center, and a patient who cultivates can lose registration. Lawful medical use also does not include smoking marijuana in an enclosed indoor workplace, which can include an apartment building's enclosed common areas where staff work, or using it in a public place except low-THC cannabis in a non-smokable form.

The library's optional marijuana clause ("Marijuana Restrictions" clause) lets you choose what to ban: smoking, vaping or other inhaling; growing; or possession and use in any form. Banning only smoking and vaping, and growing, is the narrower choice; a ban on all possession and use is not barred by any Florida statute, but a tenant with a disability may ask for an exception as an accommodation, so take advice before refusing one.

A certified recovery residence (sober home) must have a policy prohibiting marijuana on the premises, including marijuana certified for medical use.

title: Firearms in Rental Housing
bodyText:
No Florida statute says whether a private landlord may limit firearms inside a rental home, and none protects a tenant's possession of a firearm in the home against a lease term; no Florida statute exempts a concealed-weapon licensee from a lease restriction.

One statute does reach many landlords. A business that has employees (the statute counts workers, contractors and volunteers who are authorized to carry a concealed firearm under Florida law), including a landlord company or a property manager, may not prohibit a customer, employee or invitee from keeping a legally owned firearm locked inside or locked to a private motor vehicle in a parking lot, may not ask about or search a vehicle for one, and may not bar entry to the parking lot because a vehicle holds one out of sight. The statute does not use the word tenant, but its parking lot is any property used for parking and available to customers, employees or invitees, so the cautious course is to treat your tenants and their guests as covered and never restrict firearms locked in their vehicles in your parking areas. The Attorney General enforces it, a person harmed can also sue, and the court must award court costs and attorney's fees to the prevailing party.

Two crimes apply at any rental: knowingly discharging a firearm in a public place or over occupied premises, or recklessly or negligently discharging one outdoors on property used mainly as a dwelling site or zoned only residential, except in lawful defense of life or property, is a first-degree misdemeanor; and a person who stores or leaves a loaded firearm on premises he or she controls where a child under 16 is likely to get it without a parent's permission or required supervision must lock it up or use a trigger lock, and commits a second-degree misdemeanor if a child then gets it and has or shows it in public or in a threatening way.

Cities and counties may not regulate firearms, which the state preempts, and a government body that adopts or enforces a firearms rule faces penalties. If you are a public housing authority or other government landlord, get advice before adopting any firearms rule.

The library's optional clause ("Firearm Discharge and Storage" clause) makes unlawful discharge and unsafe storage a lease breach and keeps the vehicle rule.

title: Hurricanes and Declared Emergencies
bodyText: Florida has no statute that ends a residential tenancy because a disaster is declared, or that stops rent while a home is merely inaccessible after a storm. What applies instead: (1) If the premises (the home, the building it is part of, or the grounds and facilities held out for tenants) are damaged or destroyed, other than by the tenant's wrongful or negligent acts, so that the tenant's enjoyment of them is substantially impaired, the tenant may end the lease and move out at once, or move out of the unusable part and pay rent reduced by that part's fair rental value, and you must let the tenant collect belongings when it is safe or give notice of a date, within a reasonable time, when they can (see "Fire or Casualty: The Tenant's Options"). If the premises are undamaged but the tenant cannot reach the home, for example because a public road is closed, no statute stops the rent: the lease governs and rent stays due unless you agree otherwise in writing. (2) When the Governor declares a state of emergency, it is unlawful to rent or offer to rent a dwelling unit needed for habitation as a direct result of the emergency at an unconscionable price within the emergency area; a gross disparity from the average price during the 30 days before the declaration is evidence of that, unless the increase reflects added costs or market trends. The ban lasts up to 60 days under the first declaration and can be extended by executive order, and the state attorney or the Department of Legal Affairs enforces it. (3) The Governor's emergency orders have the force of law for up to 60 days at a time and may order evacuation and control the occupancy of premises in the emergency area, so check the orders in effect (they must be filed with the Division of Administrative Hearings, which publishes them). (4) Your ordinary duties continue: keep up the repairs and services the Act requires once it is safe, and you may enter the unit at any time to protect or preserve the premises, for example to board windows or stop water damage. (5) In a condominium or homeowners' association, the board's emergency powers can close parts of the property or require evacuation, but during a declared emergency it may not keep a tenant from getting to the unit when access is needed for a lease, or for the unit's habitability or the person's health and safety unless a government order or a federal public health directive bars that access; the association may still set reasonable restrictions on access.

title: No Rule on Housing Displaced Guests After a Disaster
bodyText: Florida has no statute letting a tenant house family or friends displaced by a hurricane or other disaster despite the lease's guest or occupancy limits, and none that suspends those limits during a declared emergency. Your lease's guest and occupant terms therefore still apply after a storm, and an unauthorized guest is the kind of breach the Act lets you address with a 7-day notice to cure. Two things can change that. The Governor's emergency orders have the force of law and may control the occupancy of premises in an emergency area and provide for temporary emergency housing, so read any order in effect before enforcing a guest limit in a disaster area. And a local occupancy restriction may also apply. The sensible course after a disaster is to agree in writing to a temporary guest, naming the person and an end date, rather than serve a notice; your consent for that period is not a waiver of the guest terms for later.

title: Nuisance Actions Against Rental Property
bodyText: Florida's nuisance laws can reach you as an owner when a tenant uses the property for crime. A person who owns or leases a place where any state law is violated, or a house of prostitution, illegal gambling, a criminal gang's activity or certain repeated crimes, is treated as maintaining a nuisance, and a dwelling used to keep, sell or deliver controlled substances, or visited to use them unlawfully, is a public nuisance; willfully keeping or maintaining a drug nuisance in a building is a third-degree felony. The Attorney General, a state attorney, a city or county attorney, the sheriff or any citizen of the county may sue to enjoin the nuisance, the people maintaining it and the owner or agent of the building, so neighbors can bring the case and you can be a named defendant. Before applying for a temporary injunction the plaintiff must give written notice to abate within 10 days, then a second notice with at least 15 more days (longer if another law or a signed repair contract makes that impossible). If a nuisance is proved, the court issues a permanent injunction and charges the costs to those who maintained it, with a lien on property at the place; if you are not among those who established or maintained the nuisance, a lien reaches your real estate only if you got the second notice and did not begin to abate within the time it gave; if you are found to be maintaining it, as an owner or lessor of a listed place can be, the costs and the lien on the real estate follow without that condition. If a tenant has been convicted of a drug or prostitution offense, the court may order the tenant to vacate within 72 hours when you and the tenant are both parties and the order will end the nuisance. Counties and cities may also create nuisance abatement boards that, after notice to you and a hearing, can order you to abate or close the premises or any part of it for up to a year and, where the local ordinance provides for them, impose fines of up to $250 a day (up to $500 after a year) and record orders that can become liens. A rental property that a local board declares a nuisance, or that the statute declares a nuisance because it was the site of more than two stolen-property, assault or battery, burglary, theft or sudden-snatching crimes within 6 months, may not be abated or forfeited for a nuisance someone else committed if you begin rehabilitating it within 30 days and finish within a reasonable time. No such safe harbor is written for a court action under the other nuisance statutes, such as a suit against a drug house or a place where any law is violated, so act at once on a notice to abate. Florida has no nuisance receivership, no rent escrow or subsidy suspension in a nuisance case, and no rule that a lease must summarize a criminal statute. Act on a criminal tenancy through the ordinary 7-day notices (see "Eviction Notices and Process") and keep records of every complaint and step you take.

title: No Drug-Free Lease Addendum Rule
bodyText: Florida has no statute that requires, prescribes or limits a drug-free or crime-free lease addendum for private rental housing. Florida's "drug-free" statutes are about workplaces, schools, treatment programs and recovery residences, which are defined as housing offering a peer-supported, alcohol-free and drug-free living environment. So a drug-free term is an ordinary lease term: it binds the tenant if it is in the lease, and you enforce it as a material lease provision through the 7-day notices the Act requires, never by a shortcut the lease invents (the notice requirements may not be waived in the rental agreement). The library's optional criminal-activity term (offered separately for Florida) covers drug manufacture, sale, delivery, keeping and use on the property; you don't need a separate addendum. Even without one, the tenant must not damage your property and must not unreasonably disturb the neighbors or breach the peace, and a dwelling used to keep, sell or deliver controlled substances is a public nuisance that can expose you, as owner, to an abatement suit (see "Eviction Notices and Process" for the notices). Federally assisted housing has its own lease rules.

title: No Statute on Tenants Calling Police or Emergency Help
bodyText: Florida has no statute giving a residential tenant an express right to call the police or emergency services, no rule voiding a lease term that penalizes a tenant for calls, and no presumption that an eviction filed soon after a call is retaliatory. The closest rule is the retaliation statute. You may not discriminatorily raise a tenant's rent, reduce services, or bring or threaten an eviction or other lawsuit primarily in retaliation against a tenant who acted in good faith. Its list of protected conduct (code complaints, tenant organizing, a 7-day notice to you, a servicemember's termination, paying rent to an association on its demand and exercising fair housing rights) does not mention calling the police, but the list is expressly not exhaustive, so a court could treat an eviction brought because a tenant called for help as retaliatory. Retaliation is a defense to eviction, which fails if you prove good cause, such as nonpayment or a lease violation, and the tenant must show different treatment. Cautious course: never count calls for police, fire or medical help against a tenant, don't put a term in your lease that does, and base any notice on the tenant's own conduct, documented separately (see "Retaliation").

title: Working With Law Enforcement
bodyText: No Florida statute requires a residential landlord, as a landlord, to cooperate generally with police investigations, report crimes at the property, hand over tenant records on request, or run a crime-free housing program, and none regulates crime-free lease addenda. But the reporting duties Florida puts on every person bind you and your staff: anyone who knows or has reasonable cause to suspect that a child is being abused, abandoned or neglected, or is a victim of sexual abuse, must report it immediately to the state's central abuse hotline, and knowingly and willfully failing to report is a third-degree felony; anyone who knows or suspects that a vulnerable adult is being abused, neglected or exploited must report it to the hotline, and a knowing and willful failure is a second-degree misdemeanor; a person who sees a sexual battery and can report it to police at once without danger must do so, unless a close relative of the victim or offender; and anyone who learns of a death from criminal violence, accident or another circumstance the medical examiner statute lists, as when a tenant is found dead in a unit, must report it at once to the medical examiner or police, and a knowing failure is a first-degree misdemeanor (Fla. Stat. § 406.12). Three other rules also reach you. First, a court order authorizing the interception of a tenant's communications, or a pen register or trap and trace device, can direct a landlord to furnish all information, facilities and technical assistance needed, unobtrusively; you must comply with such an order, you are entitled to reasonable compensation for your expenses, and no lawsuit lies against you for complying. Second, under the Florida Contraband Forfeiture Act real property used in a violation may be seized when someone who does not own it is arrested and the owner had actual knowledge of the criminal activity, and a written notice from a law enforcement agency that you acknowledged in writing can be used to prove that knowledge. So if police notify you in writing that your property was used for drug or other contraband crimes, act on it promptly. Third, a rental property that a local nuisance board declares a nuisance, or that the statute declares a nuisance for repeated stolen-property, assault or battery, burglary, theft or sudden-snatching crimes, can't be abated or forfeited for a tenant's crimes if you begin rehabilitating it within 30 days and finish within a reasonable time; that safe harbor does not cover a court action under the other nuisance statutes, such as a drug-house suit (see "Nuisance Actions Against Rental Property"). Outside a court order or subpoena, giving police a tenant's records or letting them into a unit is your decision; ask for a warrant or the tenant's consent before letting officers into an occupied unit, since your own right of entry is limited to the purposes the Act lists.

title: Entry for Scheduled Services
bodyText:
Florida's Act has no special rule for regularly scheduled services such as pest treatment or filter changes, and no rule letting you enter for them without notice if the lease says so conspicuously.

The general entry rules apply. The tenant may not unreasonably withhold consent to your entry to supply agreed services, among other purposes. For that purpose you may enter with the tenant's consent, in an emergency, when the tenant unreasonably withholds consent, or when the tenant has been absent for half the rental period (but if rent is current and the tenant told you about the absence, only with consent or to protect or preserve the premises).

Repairs are different: you may enter on at least 24 hours' notice between 7:30 a.m. and 8:00 p.m. You may always enter to protect or preserve the premises, and you must not abuse the right of access or use it to harass the tenant.

Because the statute speaks of agreed services, listing the scheduled services and their timing in the lease makes them agreed services and gives the tenant's consent in advance, and the library offers an optional clause that does this ("Entry for Agreed Scheduled Services" clause); it also says that if the tenant withdraws consent for a particular visit, you may enter only as the Act allows. Give notice of each visit anyway.

See "Landlord's Access to the Property" clause for the general entry clause.

title: No Right to Enter to Care for a Tenant's Animal
bodyText:
Florida law gives you no specific right to enter a rental to feed, care for or remove a tenant's animal when the tenant is hospitalized, detained or otherwise away.

The Act's entry rules list the purposes for which you may enter (inspection, repairs, agreed services and showings) and, for those purposes, the circumstances (consent, emergency, unreasonable refusal, or an absence of half the rental period). Caring for an animal is not on the list, although you may always enter to protect or preserve the premises, which can cover an animal that is causing damage.

If an animal appears to be neglected, a law enforcement officer, a certified animal control officer or an appointed agent of a humane society may take custody of it, or order the owner to provide care, and must then go to county court; calling them is the safe course when you can't reach the tenant.

The library offers an optional clause in which the tenant names a caregiver and consents to your letting that person in ("Animal Care if Tenant Is Absent" clause); without it, get the tenant's consent at the time, in writing if possible. If the last tenant has died, the Act's rules on a deceased tenant's property apply instead (see "When the Last Tenant Dies").

title: No Required Move-In or Move-Out Inspection
bodyText:
Florida does not require a move-in or move-out inspection, a written inventory or condition report, or a damage list that the tenant must sign or dispute.

What Florida does require at the end of the tenancy is the deposit claim notice: if you intend to keep any part of the deposit, you must send the tenant, within 30 days after the rental agreement ends, a written notice in the statutory form by certified mail to the last known mailing address (or by e-mail under the electronic-notice addendum), stating the amount and the reason; if you miss the 30 days you lose the right to claim against the deposit, though you may still sue for damages after returning it. The tenant then has 15 days to object in writing.

A record of the home's condition at move-in is your best evidence for that claim, so a signed, dated condition report with photographs is strongly recommended; the library offers one as an optional clause ("Move-In Condition Report" clause), and the lease's existing-condition acknowledgment ("Existing Condition of Property" clause) does not replace it.

One program does require a checklist: if you claim property-loss funding under the state's Homes for Veterans pilot, you must give the program administrator the move-out checklist with current photos and a copy of your deposit claim notice (see "Homes for Veterans Landlord Incentive Pilot").

The tenant may not unreasonably withhold consent to your entry to inspect during the tenancy (see "Landlord's Access to the Property" clause). Federally assisted housing and voucher programs have their own inspection rules.

title: No Inspection-Notice Penalty
bodyText: Florida does not require you to offer the tenant a move-in or move-out inspection or to tell the tenant about one, so there is no penalty for leaving such a notice out, and no statute sets a fixed penalty for entering without the notice the Act requires. What you face instead: (1) If you or the tenant fails to comply with the rental agreement or the Act, the other may recover the damages caused, so an entry without the required 24 hours' notice for repairs, or an entry that abuses the right of access or harasses the tenant, exposes you to the tenant's actual damages. (2) Locking the tenant out, removing doors, locks, walls or windows, cutting off utilities or removing the tenant's belongings is a separate prohibited practice that costs actual and consequential damages or 3 months' rent, whichever is greater, plus attorney's fees; an entry that turns into any of those carries that penalty. (3) The sharpest end-of-tenancy penalty is on the deposit, not the inspection: if you don't send the written claim notice within 30 days after the rental agreement ends, you forfeit the right to claim against the deposit (see "Florida Security Deposit Rules"). Give the notice the Act requires before entering, keep a record of each entry, and document the home's condition with a signed report and photos.

title: No Rule on Refused Subsidy Inspections
bodyText: No Florida statute says what happens when a tenant in a voucher or other subsidized unit refuses to let a program inspector in, or when you refuse a program inspection, and none makes a refusal a ground for ending the tenancy. Those consequences come from the federal program rules and your contract with the housing authority; read them, because that is where the sanction for a failed or refused inspection is. Florida law supplies the rest. The tenant may not unreasonably withhold consent to your entry to inspect, and you may enter for that purpose with consent, in an emergency, when the tenant unreasonably withholds consent, or after an absence of half the rental period; a tenant who keeps refusing a required inspection may be in material breach of the lease, which you handle with a 7-day notice to cure. Florida's fair housing law does not protect source of income, so declining to join a voucher program is not itself a state fair housing violation, as long as the real reason is not a protected trait. If you do rent under a program, Florida's security deposit statute does not apply where the program regulates the rent or deposit, and in an eviction a subsidized tenant need deposit into the court registry only the share of rent the tenant owes under the program.

title: Late Fees in Subsidized Tenancies
bodyText: Florida has no late-fee rule for subsidized or voucher tenancies, and no late-fee cap for any residential tenancy (see "No Late-Fee or Application-Fee Cap"). Three rules still shape what you may charge. First, for a Housing Choice Voucher tenancy, federal rules say the family is not responsible for the part of the rent covered by the housing assistance payment, and the housing authority's failure to pay it is not a lease violation; so charge a late fee, if at all, only on the tenant's own share and never because the authority's payment is late. Your contract with the housing authority may limit fees further. Second, Florida treats a subsidized tenant's share as the rent at stake in an eviction: a public housing or subsidized tenant who defends need deposit into the court registry only the portion of rent the tenant owes under the program. Third, a Florida court may refuse to enforce an unconscionable lease term, and a fee charged on money the tenant never owed invites that. Also note that Florida's rule that accepting rent with knowledge of a breach waives the right to terminate for it does not apply to the subsidy portion of rent received from a government program, although waiver still occurs if you don't file within 45 days after you learn of the breach.

title: The Tenant's Duties Under Florida Law
What a Florida Tenant May Not Do
bodyText: Florida's Act itself forbids three things to every tenant of a dwelling unit, whatever the lease says. The tenant may not destroy, deface, damage, impair or remove any part of the premises or your property in it, or let anyone else do so; may not behave, or let people on the premises with the tenant's consent behave, in a way that unreasonably disturbs the neighbors or breaches the peace; and may not unreasonably withhold consent to your entry to inspect, make necessary or agreed repairs, decorations, alterations or improvements, supply agreed services, or show the unit to prospective or actual buyers, mortgagees, tenants, workers or contractors. Florida's entry rules still bind you: entry for repairs needs at least 24 hours' notice and a time between 7:30 a.m. and 8:00 p.m., and other entries need consent or one of the listed circumstances (see "Landlord's Access to the Property" clause). Anything else you want to forbid, such as unauthorized pets, guests or vehicles, has to be in the lease or in reasonable rules. A breach the tenant should be allowed to fix gets a 7-day notice to cure; intentional destruction, damage or misuse of your or other tenants' property, and a repeated unreasonable disturbance, can get a 7-day notice of termination without a chance to cure (see "Eviction Notices and Process"). The library's no-disturbance clause ("No Disturbance or Nuisance" clause) and the tenant-maintenance clause ("Tenant Maintenance & Cleanliness" clause) carry these rules into the lease.

title: No Statutory Guest Rights
bodyText:
Florida has no statute giving a residential tenant the right to have guests, visitors, caregivers or service providers, none that limits how long a guest may stay, and none that bars a guest fee or a waiver of guest rights.

Guests are therefore a matter for your lease and reasonable rules: the library's guest clauses ("Guest Policy" clause, "Guest Policy (14-Day Limit)" clause) set the terms, and having or permitting unauthorized guests is one of the Act's own examples of a breach the tenant should be given 7 days to cure.

A guest who stays without your or the tenant's continuing permission and claims to live there may be removable as a transient occupant (see "Removing a Transient Occupant (Overstaying Guest)").

Fair housing law still applies: a guest limit may not be applied differently because of a protected trait, and a live-in aide or caregiver a tenant with a disability needs may be a reasonable accommodation (see "Fair Housing").

In a condominium, a tenant leasing a unit gets the owner's use rights in the association property and common elements, and the association may, after at least 14 days' written notice and a chance for a hearing, suspend a tenant's or guest's use of common elements for breaking the declaration, bylaws or rules, but not of the elements needed to reach the unit, parking spaces or elevators.

title: Home-Based Businesses
bodyText: Florida's home-based business statute stops cities and counties from banning or specially regulating a home-based business that meets its conditions: the business may operate in an area zoned residential and may not be regulated differently from other businesses, except as the statute allows. To qualify, the employees who work at the home must live there (up to two others may work there), business parking must be no greater than a similar home would normally need, the property must look residential from the street, the business must be secondary to the home's residential use, and it must follow the rules on signs, noise, fumes and hazardous materials. The statute does not apply to landlords or leases. No Florida statute gives a tenant a right to run a business from a rental or limits a lease term restricting one, and the statute itself says it does not override condominium, cooperative or homeowners' association declarations. So your lease decides: the library's residential-use clause ("Residential Use Only" clause) forbids any commercial use, and if you want to allow a quiet home office or similar business, say so in the lease and set the conditions you want, such as no customer visits, no employees and compliance with any association rules. A tenant's business may also need a local business tax receipt.

title: Family Child Care Homes in Rentals
bodyText:
Florida protects family child care homes against local zoning, not against landlords. A residence operated as a family child care home that is licensed or registered with the Department of Children and Families is a valid residential use for local zoning, and a city or county may not require a special exemption, use permit or waiver, or charge a special fee over $50, for it to operate in a residential zone. A family child care home is an occupied residence where child care is regularly provided for children from at least two unrelated families for a payment, fee or grant; a large family child care home also has at least two full-time child care staff, one of them the owner or occupant.

No Florida statute gives a tenant a right to run a child care home in a rental, and none sets the conditions a landlord may impose. So your lease decides: the library's residential-use clause ("Residential Use Only" clause) forbids commercial use, and if you want to allow child care, the library offers an optional clause setting conditions ("Family Child Care Home Conditions" clause).

Insurance matters here: under Florida law a residential property insurance policy does not cover liability for claims arising from a family child care home unless the policy, or a business rider or endorsement, specifically covers it, so check your own policy and require the tenant to carry coverage.

Fair housing law still bars refusing or ending a tenancy because the tenant has children of their own.

title: Flags, Signs and Displays
bodyText: Florida gives a residential tenant one display right against the landlord: you may not prohibit a tenant from displaying one portable, removable, cloth or plastic United States flag, no larger than 4 1/2 feet by 6 feet, in a respectful manner in or on the dwelling unit, whatever the lease says about flags or decorations. The tenant must display it without damaging the premises, it may not infringe on space rented by another tenant, and you are not liable for damage the flag causes. Stopping a tenant from flying it is a prohibited practice that costs actual and consequential damages or 3 months' rent, whichever is greater, plus costs and attorney's fees (see "Self-Help Eviction and Other Prohibited Practices"). Beyond that one flag, no Florida statute gives a tenant a right to post political or campaign signs, other flags, banners or other displays against the lease, and none requires the owner to get the tenant's consent before posting a sign. So your lease decides; the library's common-area clause ("Property and Common Area Use" clause) requires your consent for signs visible from outside and saves the displays the law protects. If the property is in a homeowners' association, the association may not stop parcel owners or their tenants from displaying items, including flags, that are not visible from the parcel's frontage, an adjacent parcel, a common area or a community golf course, and a homeowner may display up to two listed flags (the U.S. and Florida flags, military, POW-MIA and first responder flags) despite the association's rules; in a condominium, a unit owner may display a U.S. flag and, on listed holidays, military flags. Those association rights are written for owners.

title: Religious and Cultural Displays
bodyText: No Florida statute gives a residential tenant a right, against the landlord or the lease, to display a religious or cultural item such as a mezuzah, wreath or holiday decoration. The one religious-display rule is for condominium associations: an association may not refuse a unit owner's request for a reasonable accommodation to attach a religious object, no larger than 3 inches wide, 6 inches high and 1.5 inches deep, on the mantel or frame of the unit's door. That rule is written for unit owners; if you rent out a condominium unit, consider making the request yourself when your tenant asks. Fair housing law still applies to every landlord: a display rule written or enforced so that it treats one religion differently from others, for example allowing holiday decorations of one faith but not another, risks discrimination because of religion in the terms or privileges of the rental. Apply any decoration rule neutrally, and the library's common-area clause ("Property and Common Area Use" clause) saves displays the law protects.

title: No Candidate Access Rule for Rental Buildings
bodyText: Florida has no statute requiring a residential landlord to let political candidates, campaign volunteers, petition circulators or voter-registration workers into an apartment building or complex, and none barring you from limiting canvassing or soliciting on your property. Your access rules and lease terms decide, applied the same way to every candidate and cause. Three related rules exist outside ordinary rentals. In a condominium, the association may not unreasonably restrict a unit owner's right to peaceably assemble or to invite public officers or candidates for public office to appear and speak in the common elements, common areas and recreational facilities; homeowners' associations have the same rule for parcel owners. In a mobile home park governed by chapter 723, no rental agreement or park rule may infringe a mobile home owner's right to invite public officers or qualified candidates to speak in the park's common or recreational areas at reasonable times in an open public meeting, though the park owner may set rules on time, place and scheduling. Those rules are written for owners, not apartment tenants.

title: Tenant Organizing
bodyText: Florida protects tenant organizing through its retaliation statute. You may not discriminatorily raise a tenant's rent, reduce services, or bring or threaten an eviction or other lawsuit primarily because the tenant, acting in good faith, organized, encouraged or participated in a tenant organization. The tenant can raise retaliation as a defense to eviction, but the defense fails if you prove good cause, such as nonpayment of rent or a violation of the lease, reasonable rules or the Act, and the tenant must show you treated them differently. Beyond that, Florida gives apartment tenants no statutory right to hold meetings in common areas, distribute flyers door to door or canvass other tenants, and no rule requiring you to recognize or deal with a tenant association. Your reasonable rules on common areas apply, but apply them evenly and never enforce them against organizers in a way that looks like retaliation (see "Retaliation"). Mobile home parks are different: under chapter 723, no rental agreement or park rule may infringe the right of mobile home owners or tenants to communicate or assemble about park problems, or the right of mobile home owners to canvass for park association matters and to invite tenant organization representatives to speak in common areas, at reasonable times and in a reasonable manner.

title: Protecting Tenants' Personal Information
bodyText: No Florida landlord-tenant statute stops you from sharing a tenant's or applicant's information or requires the tenant's consent before you do. Florida's data-security statute does reach most landlords, though. It covers any sole proprietorship, partnership, corporation, trust, estate, cooperative, association or other commercial entity that acquires, maintains, stores or uses personal information, which includes a person's name with a Social Security number, a driver license or other government ID number, a financial account or card number with its access code, medical or health insurance information, biometric data or geolocation, or a user name or e-mail address with its password. If you hold that kind of information about applicants or tenants: (1) take reasonable measures to protect and secure it in electronic form; (2) if a breach occurs, notify each affected Florida resident by mail or e-mail as quickly as practicable and no later than 30 days after you determine or have reason to believe a breach occurred (unless a law enforcement agency asks in writing for a delay, or, after an appropriate investigation and consultation with law enforcement, you reasonably determine that no identity theft or other financial harm is likely, document that in writing, keep it for at least 5 years and give it to the Department of Legal Affairs within 30 days), notify the Department of Legal Affairs if 500 or more Floridians are affected, and notify the national credit bureaus if more than 1,000 are; and (3) when you no longer keep records containing personal information, dispose of them by shredding, erasing or otherwise making the information unreadable. A property manager or screening company that stores the data for you must tell you of a breach within 10 days. Violations are enforced by the Department of Legal Affairs as unfair or deceptive trade practices, with civil penalties of up to $500,000 for late breach notices; tenants have no private right to sue under this statute. Keep applications and screening reports in locked or encrypted storage, give access only to staff who need it, and share them only for the rental decision or as the law requires.

title: Tenant Records
bodyText: Florida has no general duty to keep a rent ledger, to give a tenant a ledger or payment history on request, or to keep tenant records for a set time. (If your rentals are taxable short rentals of 6 months or less, the sales tax law makes you keep complete rental records until the tax can no longer be assessed; see "Sales Tax on Short Rentals".) Three record rules do apply. First, if you send notices by e-mail under the electronic-notice addendum, you must keep a copy of each notice and evidence of its transmission. Second, when you sell the property or change rental agents, you must transfer all security deposits and advance rents to the new owner or agent with an accurate accounting showing the amount credited to each tenant's account; you are released from holding those funds only after the transfer and a written receipt. Third, if you are a business holding applicants' or tenants' personal information, such as Social Security, driver license or bank account numbers, you must take reasonable measures to protect it, and when you no longer keep those records you must dispose of them by shredding, erasing or otherwise making the information unreadable (see "Protecting Tenants' Personal Information" in this library for breach notices). Good records also decide disputes: in an eviction for unpaid rent the tenant's payment defense turns on proof of payment, and a deposit claim turns on your timely written notice, so keep a dated ledger of every charge and payment, copies of every notice and its proof of delivery, and the move-in condition record for at least as long as a claim could be brought.

title: Online Tenant Portals
bodyText:
Florida has no statute on tenant portals, so nothing bars you from offering one or from accepting rent through it.

Two rules limit what a portal can do.
- First, posting a notice on a portal is not delivery under the Act. The Act's 3-day notice for rent, its 7-day notices and the notices ending a periodic tenancy must be delivered by mail, by hand delivery of a true copy, by e-mail under a signed electronic-notice addendum in the statutory form, or, if the tenant is absent, by leaving a copy at the home, and the 3-day and 7-day delivery rules may not be waived in the lease. Other notices follow their own sections: the deposit claim notice, for example, must go by certified mail or by e-mail under the addendum. E-mail delivery requires the addendum, which each party may revoke at any time by written notice (see "Electronic Delivery of Notices Addendum" clause).
- Second, Florida's Uniform Electronic Transaction Act applies only between parties who agreed to deal electronically, and a party who agreed to conduct a transaction by electronic means may refuse to conduct other transactions by electronic means; that right cannot be waived by agreement.

So a lease can make the portal the usual way to pay and to send maintenance requests, but it should not make the portal the only way for every payment or signature for the whole tenancy. The cautious course is to name a non-electronic way to pay for a tenant who stops agreeing to pay electronically or when the portal is down.

The library offers an optional Florida portal clause that does this ("Online Portal" clause). Your payment-method clause ("Acceptable Forms of Payment" clause) sets the accepted methods.

title: Student Housing
