bodyText: Florida's Residential Landlord and Tenant Act does not apply to residence in a facility, public or private, when the residence is incidental to the provision of educational services, which describes a school's or college's own residence halls and dormitories. Apart from that exclusion, Florida has no student-housing rule for private landlords: no special lease terms, no different notices and no exemption for buildings rented mainly to students. So an apartment, house or purpose-built student complex that you own and rent to students is an ordinary dwelling unit, and every rule in the Act applies to it, including the deposit, entry, maintenance and eviction rules. The exclusion turns on whether the residence is incidental to educational services, not on who owns the building; if you lease a building to a college that houses its students there, or manage housing for a school, whether the Act applies to the students' occupancy depends on the arrangement, so get advice.

title: Housing Provided to an Employee
bodyText:
In Florida, a home or room you furnish to an employee as an incident of employment, with or without rent, is a dwelling unit under the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, so the Act's rules apply to the employee as a tenant, including its notices and the court process for possession; you may not simply change the locks when the job ends.

If the housing is furnished without rent and there is no agreement on how long the tenancy lasts, the tenancy runs by the wage period: week to week if wages are paid weekly or more often, month to month if they are paid monthly or not at all. Either party may end that tenancy by written notice of at least 7 days before the end of a weekly period, or 30 days before the end of a monthly period.

When the employee stops working for you, you are entitled to rent from the day after the employment ends until the day the employee moves out, at the rate charged for similar homes in the area. That default does not apply to an employee or resident manager of an apartment house or apartment complex who has a written agreement to the contrary, so for on-site staff put the terms in writing; the library offers an optional employee-housing clause.

Florida has no statute requiring a separate employee-housing disclosure, an offer of a rental agreement when the job ends, or a filing with the government for housing a sponsored worker. Housing for migrant farmworkers has its own permit and health rules.

title: No Pets-and-Eviction Fact Sheet
bodyText: Florida has no state fact sheet about pets and eviction, and no rule requiring you to give one to a tenant who has a dog, cat or other animal. The Act mentions pets twice: a pet deposit is deposit money that must be held and returned under the deposit rules, and having or permitting unauthorized pets is one of the Act's examples of a breach the tenant should be given 7 days to cure; if it recurs within 12 months, you may file for eviction without another notice. Your pet clause ("Pet Policy" clause) sets the rules. A tenant's service animal or emotional support animal is not a pet and is governed by its own rules (see "Service and Emotional Support Animals" clause). If a tenant leaves an animal behind after moving out or being evicted, get advice and contact local animal control rather than keeping or disposing of it yourself (see "No Right to Enter to Care for a Tenant's Animal" in this library).

title: Squatters, Cash Receipts and Registration
bodyText: Three rules found in other states' laws outside their landlord-tenant acts, and where Florida stands. (1) Squatters: Florida does have a specific remedy. A property owner or authorized agent may ask the county sheriff to remove people unlawfully occupying a residential dwelling, without a court case, by filing a sworn complaint in the statutory form, if the occupants entered unlawfully, the property was not open to the public, the owner told them to leave, they are not current or former tenants under a rental agreement the owner authorized, they are not the owner's immediate family, and no lawsuit about the property is pending between them; the sheriff serves a notice to vacate immediately and puts the owner in possession. A person wrongly removed may recover damages, including three times the fair market rent, and attorney's fees. A separate procedure covers transient occupants such as overstaying guests. Neither may be used against a tenant or former tenant, who must be evicted (see "Removing Squatters (Unauthorized Occupants)" and "Removing a Transient Occupant (Overstaying Guest)"). (2) Cash receipts: Florida has no duty to give a receipt for rent paid in cash, and no general right of a debtor to demand a receipt. The only rent receipt rule is that if you accept partial rent after serving a 3-day notice, you must, before filing for possession, give a receipt stating the date and amount received and the agreed date and balance due, put the partial rent in the court registry when you file, or serve a new 3-day notice. Give a written receipt for every cash payment anyway. (3) Registration before eviction: no landlord-tenant statute makes registration or a rental licence a condition of a judgment for possession, but Florida's trade-name and entity statutes can stop you from bringing the case. If you rent under a name other than your legal name, you must register that fictitious name with the Division of Corporations, and until you do you may not maintain any action, including an eviction, in a Florida court. An out-of-state limited liability company that owns income-producing property here is transacting business and may not maintain an action until it obtains a certificate of authority, and an out-of-state corporation transacting business here faces the same bar; whether merely renting out property is transacting business for a corporation is a case-law question (see "Out-of-State Landlords: Agents, Service and Foreign LLCs"). The missing registration does not void the lease, and the case may go forward once you register. Larger apartment properties need a state lodging license, which is a separate duty with its own penalties.

title: Other Rules Florida Does and Does Not Have
bodyText: Four rules found in other states, and where Florida stands. (1) Double letting: Florida has no statute on renting the same unit to two tenants for the same period and no special remedy for it; the tenant's general remedies for your failure to comply with the rental agreement apply, and the library's possession-delay clause covers a late start (see "Possession Delay" clause). (2) Smoke-alarm shield: Florida has no rule making your compliance or noncompliance with smoke or carbon monoxide alarm requirements inadmissible in an injury case, or limiting what an insurer may do because of it. The alarm duties themselves still apply (see "Smoke and Carbon Monoxide Alarms"). (3) False rental applications: Florida has no general right to end a lease because an application was false, but from October 1, 2026 it is a felony to enter into and take possession of a dwelling unit by knowingly and willfully making a materially false written statement about one's identity in a rental application, presenting forged or fictitious documents such as a driver license, bank statement or paystub, or impersonating another applicant, and that fraudulent entry lets you terminate on 7 days' written notice without a chance to cure (see "Fraudulent Entry: Termination Without Cure"). Any other material falsehood is a lease breach only if the lease makes it one (see "Accuracy of Rental Application" clause). (4) Payment-method fees: a lessor in a lease transaction who accepts credit cards may not impose a surcharge on a tenant for paying by credit card instead of cash, check or similar means, and a violation is a second-degree misdemeanor; a discount offered to everyone for paying by cash or check is allowed. Florida sets no cap on other payment-method fees, such as for electronic checks or money orders; charges for a returned or dishonored payment are limited separately (see "Returned Payments" clause). So don't add a card surcharge to rent; if card processing costs matter, build them into the rent or offer an across-the-board discount for non-card payment. A federal appeals court decision is reported to have found constitutional problems with the surcharge ban; the statute remains in the Florida Statutes, and the cautious course above stands.

title: Rights a Lease Cannot Waive
bodyText: Florida's main landlord-tenant law is the Florida Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, part II of chapter 83 of the Florida Statutes. It applies to the rental of a dwelling unit. It does not cover residence that is incidental to medical, geriatric, educational, counseling, religious or similar services; occupancy under a contract to buy the home once the buyer has paid at least 12 months' rent, or at least 1 month's rent and a deposit of at least 5 percent of the price; transient stays in hotels, motels, condominiums, rooming houses and similar public lodging or in a mobile home park; a cooperative's proprietary-lease holders; or a condominium owner living in their own unit. Where a mobile home is placed on a rented lot in a park of 10 or more lots, chapter 723 governs instead. A lease term is void and unenforceable to the extent it (1) tries to waive or shut off a right, remedy or requirement the Act sets out, or (2) tries to limit or shut off any liability you owe the tenant, or the tenant owes you, that arises under law. If you put a void term in a lease and the tenant suffers actual damages because of it, the tenant can recover them; the statute does not require that you knew the term was void. Several sections repeat the point for themselves: the notice rules for ending a tenancy for breach or nonpayment (the tenant's 7-day notice, your 7-day noncompliance notices and the 3-day rent notice, and how they must be delivered) may not be waived in the lease; and the winning party's right to recover reasonable attorney's fees in a suit on the lease or the Act may not be waived in a lease. A court may also refuse to enforce an unconscionable lease, enforce it without the unconscionable term, or limit that term, and every lease and every duty under the Act carries an obligation of good faith. The Act leaves some points to the parties. Rent is due at the start of each period without demand unless otherwise agreed. A written lease may change the tenant's 7-day move-out notice that preserves your deposit-claim notice. For a single-family home or duplex, your duty to comply with codes or keep the structure and plumbing in repair may be altered in writing. For other dwellings, extermination, locks and keys, common areas, garbage removal, heat, running water and hot water are your duties unless otherwise agreed in writing, and the lease may make the tenant pay for garbage removal, water, fuel or utilities. The waiver ban reaches rights set out in part II of chapter 83. Rules in other chapters carry their own terms, for example the ban on powers of attorney to confess judgment (see "No Confession of Judgment").

title: Waiving the Repair and Code Duties
bodyText: Florida lets a written agreement change your basic repair duty only for a single-family home or a duplex. Your basic duty is to comply with applicable building, housing and health codes or, where there are none, to keep the roof, windows, doors, floors, steps, porches, exterior walls, foundation and other structural parts in good repair and the plumbing in reasonable working condition, and to provide screens. For a single-family home or duplex, that duty may be altered or modified in writing. For every other dwelling it can't be changed by the lease: a term that tries to waive it is void, and the tenant can recover any actual damages the term causes (see "Rights a Lease Cannot Waive"). Altering your duty to the tenant does not change what building, housing and health codes themselves require of the property, which local code enforcement applies separately. Florida has no statute letting a tenant accept named defects in exchange for a stated rent reduction; any such deal for a home other than a single-family home or duplex would have to leave the basic duty intact. The nearest rule is different: if your failure of the basic duty is beyond your control and you keep making every reasonable effort to fix it, a tenant who stays pays rent reduced in proportion to the lost rental value for that period (Fla. Stat. § 83.56(1)(b); see "Tenant Remedies When the Landlord Breaches"). You are not responsible to the tenant for conditions caused by the negligent or wrongful act of the tenant, the tenant's family or a person on the premises with the tenant's consent. The extra duties for other dwellings (pest control, locks, common areas, garbage, heat and water) are covered in "Repair Duties a Written Lease May Change". The library's optional maintenance-shift clause for houses and duplexes is "Tenant-Maintained Items (Single-Family Home or Duplex)" clause.

title: Repair Duties a Written Lease May Change
bodyText: For a dwelling other than a single-family home or duplex (for example an apartment or a unit in a building of three or more), Florida adds duties on top of the basic code and structural duty, and each of them applies "unless otherwise agreed in writing": reasonable provisions for extermination of rats, mice, roaches, ants, wood-destroying organisms and bedbugs; locks and keys; the clean and safe condition of common areas; garbage removal and outside receptacles; and functioning facilities for heat during winter, running water and hot water. So a written lease may assign one of these items differently, for example by making the tenant responsible for pest control inside the unit. It cannot reduce the basic duty to comply with building, housing and health codes for those dwellings, so where a code requires heat, water or hot water, a lease term dropping it gives you no protection. For a single-family home or duplex, the duty to install working smoke detection devices at the start of the tenancy also applies unless otherwise agreed in writing, and the basic code and structural duty itself may be altered in writing (see "Waiving the Repair and Code Duties"). Whatever the dwelling, the lease may make the tenant pay for garbage removal, water, fuel or utilities. A tenant cannot use your failure to meet these added duties as a defense to an eviction, but can claim damages for it, and can end the lease over it only where the duty is also a material provision of the lease. These duties do not cover a mobile home the tenant owns.

title: Termination Notices a Lease Cannot Waive
bodyText: A Florida lease can't waive or shorten the notices you must give before ending a tenancy. The 3-day notice for unpaid rent, the 7-day notices for other lease violations (with or without a chance to cure), and the tenant's 7-day notice for your failure to make repairs must be in writing and delivered by mail, by hand, by e-mail under a signed electronic-notice addendum, or, if the tenant is absent, by leaving a copy at the home, and the statute says these notice requirements may not be waived in the rental agreement. The notice to end a periodic tenancy (7 days for week-to-week, 30 days for month-to-month or quarter-to-quarter, 60 days for year-to-year, each before the end of a period) is also part of the Act, so a lease term cutting it down is void under the Act's general waiver rule (see "Rights a Lease Cannot Waive"). For a lease with a fixed term, the lease may require advance notice of non-renewal from both sides, but not less than 30 days or more than 60 days (see "Notice Before Vacating at End of Term" clause).

title: Notice Before Showings
bodyText:
Florida sets no advance-notice period for entering to show the home to prospective tenants, buyers, lenders or contractors, so there is no notice period for a lease to waive.

Instead, the tenant may not unreasonably withhold consent to entry from time to time to inspect, make necessary or agreed repairs or improvements, supply agreed services, or show the home. For those purposes you may enter with the tenant's consent, in an emergency, when the tenant unreasonably withholds consent, or when the tenant has been absent for half a rent period (but not if the rent is current and the tenant told you of the absence, unless the tenant consents or you need to protect the premises).

The only fixed notice rule is for repairs: at least 24 hours' notice and entry between 7:30 a.m. and 8:00 p.m. You may enter at any time to protect or preserve the premises, and you may not abuse the right of access or use it to harass the tenant.

These are rights under the Act, so a lease cannot take them away (see "Rights a Lease Cannot Waive").

The library's entry clause ("Landlord's Access to the Property" clause) asks for consent each time.

title: Deposit Rights a Lease Cannot Waive
bodyText: Florida's deposit statute has no non-waiver sentence of its own, but the deposit rules are part of the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, so a lease term that tries to waive them is void and the tenant can recover any actual damages it causes (see "Rights a Lease Cannot Waive"). That covers how you hold the money, the 15-day return or 30-day claim-notice deadlines, the tenant's 15 days to object, the transfer of deposits on a sale, and interest where owed. Two points are open to the lease. First, a written lease may change the rule that a tenant who moves out must give at least 7 days' written notice, with a forwarding address, to keep you from being excused from the claim-notice deadline. Second, a fee in lieu of a security deposit is allowed only under its own statute, and that agreement may not contain any clause that contradicts the unconscionability or void-term rules. A tenant who misses the 15-day objection period does not give up the right to sue for the deposit later.

title: Smoke Drift and Shared Indoor Areas
bodyText: Florida has no statute about smoke drifting between rental units and none that lets a tenant waive a claim about it, so there is no Florida smoke-drift waiver to put in a lease. Two rules do reach rental buildings. First, Florida's Clean Indoor Air Act and the state constitution ban tobacco smoking and vaping in any enclosed indoor workplace, defined as any enclosed place where one or more people engage in work, whether or not anyone is working at the moment. Private residences are excepted, except while used commercially to provide child care, adult care or health care. An enclosed common hallway, lobby, laundry room or office in an apartment building where staff or contractors work appears to fall within that definition, so the cautious course is to treat enclosed indoor common areas as no-smoking and no-vaping and post them that way. Second, you may ban or limit smoking more broadly: the constitution says nothing in the workplace rule stops the owner, lessee or other person in control of an enclosed indoor workplace from prohibiting or limiting smoking or vaping further, and Florida's medical-marijuana law does not impair any party's ability to restrict smoking or vaping marijuana on their private property. The library's smoking clause is "Smoking Policy" clause. Local governments may not regulate smoking (the state preempts it, with exceptions for public beaches and parks and for vaping).

title: Jury Trials in Eviction Cases
bodyText:
In Florida a jury hears an eviction only if a party asks for one in time. The state constitution secures the right of trial by jury, and in the summary eviction procedure any party may demand a jury, if a jury trial is authorized by law, in a pleading or a separate paper served no later than 5 days after the case comes to issue; a party who fails to make a timely demand waives a jury. The Florida Bar's court-approved answer form for residential evictions warns tenants that they may have waived this right in the lease.

No Florida statute permits or forbids a jury waiver in a residential lease. The right comes from the constitution and the court rules, not from the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, so the Act's ban on lease waivers does not by its own words reach it.

Whether a court will enforce a lease jury waiver depends on case law. So if you use one, use the narrow optional clause "Jury Trial Waiver for Possession", which applies only to possession and the rent claimed with it, is mutual, and is set apart for both parties to initial.

If the case is tried by the court rather than a jury, the court decides any rent reduction for a repair defense.

title: No Confession of Judgment
bodyText: Don't put a confession-of-judgment or warrant-of-attorney term in a Florida lease. Florida law makes every power of attorney for confessing or suffering a judgment, by default or otherwise, given before the lawsuit is brought, absolutely null and void, and the same goes for a general release of errors given in advance. The rule applies to every contract, not only leases. A lease term like that is also void under the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act's ban on waiving the tenant's rights and remedies (see "Rights a Lease Cannot Waive"), and the tenant can recover any actual damages caused by including it. The way to a judgment for possession and unpaid rent is the court eviction procedure (see "Eviction Notices and Process").

title: Liability Waivers and Indemnity Terms
bodyText: A Florida lease term is void to the extent it tries to limit or shut off any liability you owe the tenant, or the tenant owes you, that arises under law, and if you include one and the tenant suffers actual damages because of it, the tenant can recover them, whether or not you knew the term was void. That is why the library uses parking, storage and renter's-insurance clauses that do not disclaim your liability ("Parking" clause, "Storage Space" clause, "Tenant's Property & Renter's Insurance" clause), and why its service and utility clause limits itself to causes beyond your reasonable control. A term making the tenant responsible for damage the tenant, the tenant's guests or the tenant's pets cause is different: it allocates the tenant's own liability rather than excusing yours (see "Damage Caused by Tenant" clause). Florida has no statute that specifically addresses a lease clause requiring the tenant to indemnify you for your own negligence; such a clause is void to the extent it limits your liability to the tenant, and whether it is enforceable for claims by others is a case-law question, so don't use one.

title: Unconscionable Lease Terms
bodyText: If a court finds as a matter of law that a Florida lease, or any term of it, was unconscionable when it was made, the court may refuse to enforce the lease, enforce the rest of the lease without that term, or limit how the term applies so as to avoid an unconscionable result. When a party claims a term may be unconscionable, or it appears so to the court, both sides must get a reasonable chance to present evidence about its meaning, the parties' relationship, and its purpose and effect. Florida has no statutory list of unconscionable residential lease terms; unconscionability is judged case by case under case law. Every lease and every duty under the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act also carries an obligation of good faith, meaning honesty in fact. A late fee, a fee in lieu of deposit and any other charge Florida does not cap remain subject to this power. Separately, Florida's price-gouging law treats renting, within a declared emergency area, a dwelling unit needed for habitation as a direct result of the emergency at an unconscionable price as a violation of the state's consumer-protection law (see "Raising the Rent").

title: Attorney Fees in Lease Disputes
bodyText: In any lawsuit to enforce a Florida lease or the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, the party who wins a judgment may recover reasonable attorney's fees and court costs from the losing party, and a lease cannot waive that right. The rule runs both ways, whatever the lease says, and it does not allow fees on a personal-injury claim based on your repair duty. Other Florida rules point the same way: the winner of a lawsuit over a security deposit recovers court costs and a reasonable attorney's fee; in an eviction for nonpayment the court may award the prevailing party attorney's fees and costs along with the money judgment; a tenant who wins a claim for a lockout, utility shut-off or other prohibited practice recovers costs including attorney's fees; and, for any contract signed since October 1, 1988, a clause letting one party recover fees for enforcing the contract lets the court award fees to the other party if that party wins. So write any fee clause as a prevailing-party clause, as the library's default clause does ("Tenant Default" clause). A lease cannot make the tenant pay your attorney's fees when you lose; the cautious course is to seek fees only as a court awards them.

title: Collection Fees
bodyText:
No Florida statute authorizes or forbids a lease charge for collecting past-due rent or other amounts, and none caps one.

Three rules limit it.
- First, Florida's consumer collection law bars any person collecting a consumer debt from trying to enforce a debt the person knows is not legitimate, or claiming a legal right the person knows does not exist; a violator owes actual damages, up to $1,000 more in statutory damages, court costs and attorney's fees, and a court may add punitive damages, and the suit must be brought within 2 years. Whether unpaid residential rent is a consumer debt under that law is a question of case law, so treat it as one.
- Second, a charge the lease doesn't state has no basis, and a charge that isn't designated as rent can't be demanded in a 3-day notice for unpaid rent (see "Fees and Rent").
- Third, a court may refuse to enforce an unconscionable term.

Attorney's fees are separate: only the winner of a lawsuit recovers them, and a lease can't change that (see "Attorney Fees in Lease Disputes"). If you want to pass on a collection agency's charge, use the optional clause "Collection Agency Charges", which is limited to what the agency actually charges, up to a cap you set.

title: Charging for Notices
bodyText:
No Florida statute authorizes, forbids or caps a lease charge for preparing or serving a notice.

What Florida does provide: either party may recover the damages caused by the other's failure to comply with the lease or the Act; the winner of a lawsuit on the lease recovers court costs and reasonable attorney's fees (see "Attorney Fees in Lease Disputes"); and a lease term is void to the extent it limits a legal liability or waives the tenant's rights.

A flat notice fee set in advance, beyond what the notice actually cost, may be treated as a penalty under case law. A charge that isn't designated as rent can't go into a 3-day notice for unpaid rent, and the notice rules themselves can't be waived (see "Termination Notices a Lease Cannot Waive").

The library's optional clause "Cost of Delivering Required Notices" recovers only the actual out-of-pocket cost of delivering a required notice, such as a process server's or certified-mail charge.

title: Fixed Eviction Charges
bodyText: Florida has no statute that bans, or authorizes, a lease clause charging the tenant a set fee if you file an eviction. What the law provides instead: the prevailing party gets judgment for court costs; in an eviction for nonpayment the court enters a money judgment for the rent found due and may award the prevailing party attorney's fees and costs; and in any suit on the lease the winner recovers reasonable attorney's fees, a right the lease cannot waive. A flat eviction fee charged whether or not you win, or beyond your actual cost, would duplicate what the court decides and may be treated as an unenforceable penalty under case law. So don't put a fixed eviction fee in the lease. Recover costs and fees through the court, and use "Cost of Delivering Required Notices" clause only for the actual cost of delivering a required notice.

title: Liquidated Damages and Early Termination Fees
bodyText:
Florida allows a lease to set liquidated damages or an early termination fee for a tenant who leaves early, but only on the statute's terms. The amount may not exceed 2 months' rent; for an early termination fee, the tenant may be required to give no more than 60 days' notice; and the remedy is available only if, when the lease was made, the tenant accepted it by signing a separate addendum in substantially the statutory form, which also states that you waive the right to seek more rent beyond the month in which you retake possession.

On top of the agreed amount you may collect rent and other charges through the end of the month in which you retake possession, and charges for damage to the unit.

This remedy does not apply where the breach is the tenant's failure to give the end-of-term notice the lease requires; for that, a fixed-term lease may provide liquidated damages, owed only if you first send the tenant a written notice, delivered as the termination-notice rules require, within 15 days before the notice period starts, stating the tenant's notice obligation and the date the lease ends and listing all fees, penalties and other charges.

Florida has no general statute on liquidated damages in other contracts (the commercial code's rule covers sales and leases of goods, not homes).

The library's clauses are "Early Termination" clause, "Early Termination Fee Addendum" clause and "Notice Before Vacating at End of Term" clause.

title: Accepting Rent After a Breach
bodyText: In Florida, if you accept rent knowing that the tenant has broken the lease, or accept performance that differs from what the lease requires, you give up the right to end the lease or sue over that breach, though not over a later or continuing one. The same rule binds a tenant who pays rent knowing you are in breach. Partial rent is different: accepting part of the rent for a period does not waive your right to end the lease or sue for that nonpayment, but if you accept partial rent after posting a 3-day notice, you must do one of three things: give the tenant a receipt stating the date and amount received and the agreed date and balance due before you file for possession; put the partial rent in the court registry when you file; or post a new 3-day notice for the new amount due. The waiver rule doesn't apply to the government-subsidy portion of the rent, but waiver occurs if you have not filed within 45 days after you learn of the breach. Because this is a right under the Act, a lease clause saying acceptance of rent never waives anything can't override it (see "Rights a Lease Cannot Waive"). Cautious course: after delivering a notice, don't accept full rent for the breach period unless you mean to drop that breach, and follow one of the three steps whenever you take partial rent.

title: Penalty for Using a Void Lease Term
bodyText: Florida does not require that you knew a lease term was unlawful. If a lease you enter into, extend or renew contains a term the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act makes void (a waiver of the tenant's rights or remedies under the Act, or a limit on your legal liability), and either party suffers actual damages because the term was included, that party may recover them. There is no fixed or multiple-damages penalty for a void term as such. Knowledge matters under other laws: the consumer collection law penalizes trying to enforce a debt you know is not legitimate, or claiming a legal right you know does not exist, with actual damages and up to $1,000 more in statutory damages (see "Collection Fees"). Separately, the prohibited-practices section (lockouts, utility shut-offs, removing doors or belongings) carries actual and consequential damages or 3 months' rent, whichever is greater, plus costs and attorney's fees. See "Rights a Lease Cannot Waive" for what is void.

title: Can the Lease Change Casualty or Reletting Rules?
bodyText: Florida has statutory rules on both points, and they work differently. Casualty: if the premises are damaged or destroyed, other than by the tenant's wrongful or negligent acts, so that enjoyment is substantially impaired, the tenant may end the lease and move out at once, or move out of the unusable part and pay reduced rent, and must be given a chance to collect belongings (see "Fire or Casualty: The Tenant's Options"). That is a tenant right under the Act, so a lease term taking it away is void (see "Rights a Lease Cannot Waive"). Reletting: when a tenant breaches and you have a writ of possession or the tenant has surrendered or abandoned the unit, Florida lets you choose among four remedies: end the lease and the tenant's further liability; retake possession for the tenant's account, holding the tenant liable for the shortfall, in which case you must make a good-faith effort to relet; stand by and hold the tenant liable for rent as it comes due; or, if the tenant agreed in a separate addendum when the lease was made, charge liquidated damages or an early termination fee of up to 2 months' rent (see "Landlord's Remedies When a Tenant Leaves Early" and "Liquidated Damages and Early Termination Fees"). So Florida imposes a reletting duty only if you choose to relet for the tenant's account. A lease term removing a tenant's statutory protection is void; whether a lease may add a remedy the statute does not list is a case-law question, so the cautious course is to rely on the four listed remedies.

title: Lock Changes for Victims of Violence
bodyText: Florida has no statute giving a victim of domestic violence, dating violence, sexual violence or stalking a right to have the locks changed, and none requiring you to change them on request. Two rules matter. A court hearing a domestic-violence injunction may award the victim exclusive use and possession of the home the parties share, or exclude the abuser from the victim's residence, and may order an officer to help put the victim in possession. And Florida forbids you to prevent a tenant from gaining reasonable access to the home by changing the locks or otherwise; a lockout makes you liable for actual and consequential damages or 3 months' rent, whichever is greater, plus costs and attorney's fees. So: change or rekey the locks at a victim's request if you are willing, at no cost to the victim if you can; but don't lock out someone who is also a tenant on the lease unless a court order excludes that person, and keep a copy of the order. For other dwellings than a single-family home or duplex, reasonable provisions for locks and keys are already your duty unless the lease says otherwise. In federally assisted housing, federal law adds protections for victims (see "Evicting a Tenant Who Is a Victim of Violence").

title: Evicting a Tenant Who Is a Victim of Violence
bodyText: No Florida statute bars evicting a tenant because the tenant is a victim of domestic violence, dating violence, sexual violence or stalking, or limits using incidents of abuse (police calls, damage, disturbance) against the victim. Florida's retaliation rule protects tenants who complain to code agencies, join tenant organizations or use fair-housing rights, among others, but it does not list victims of violence (see "Retaliation"). Federal law does protect victims in federally covered housing, including public housing, Section 8 housing and low-income housing tax credit properties: you may not deny, end assistance to, or evict a tenant because the tenant is or has been a victim, an incident of abuse is not a serious or repeated lease violation by the victim or good cause to end the victim's tenancy, and you may split the lease to evict only the abuser. If your property is in one of those programs, follow the program's rules. Fair-housing law may also apply, and a court injunction can give a victim exclusive use of a shared home.

title: Keeping Victim Information Confidential
bodyText: No Florida statute requires a private landlord to keep confidential what a tenant tells you about domestic violence, dating violence, sexual violence or stalking. Florida's confidentiality rules on this subject bind others: a person petitioning for a domestic-violence injunction may give the court their address in a separate confidential filing, and the Attorney General's Address Confidentiality Program lets a certified victim of domestic or dating violence use a substitute address that state and local agencies must accept, but that program binds government agencies, not landlords. In federally covered housing (public housing, Section 8, low-income housing tax credit properties and other covered programs), federal law requires you to keep in confidence any information a tenant gives you to claim the federal protections, including the fact that the tenant is a victim, and not to enter it in a shared database or disclose it except with the tenant's written consent, for use in an eviction proceeding, or as other law requires. Cautious course for every rental: keep such information private, share it only with staff who need it, and don't disclose a victim's new address.

title: Deposit Timing After a Victim Moves Out
bodyText: Florida has no statute letting a victim of domestic violence end a lease early (see "No Domestic Violence Lease Termination Right"), so it has no special deposit rule for that situation. The ordinary deposit rules apply: if you won't claim against the deposit, return it with any interest within 15 days after the lease ends and the tenant vacates; if you will, send the written claim notice within 30 days (see "Florida Security Deposit Rules"). Where one co-tenant leaves and others stay, the lease has not ended for the others, and Florida law doesn't say how to divide a shared deposit; the cautious course is to hold the deposit until the tenancy ends for everyone, unless all tenants agree in writing to a different split.

title: Documents a Victim Must Show
bodyText: Florida has no tenancy protections for victims of domestic violence, dating violence, sexual violence or stalking (no early termination, lock-change, eviction-defense or confidentiality right), so it has no list of documents a tenant must give you to claim one. The documents Florida law knows are court injunctions: for domestic violence, and for repeat, sexual or dating violence and stalking. A domestic-violence injunction may give the victim exclusive use of a shared home. In federally covered housing, federal law lets you ask in writing for a certification form, a statement signed by a victim-service provider, attorney or medical or mental-health professional, or a police, court or agency record, and gives the tenant 14 business days to provide it; follow your program's rules there.

title: Where Florida Protection Orders Are Found
bodyText: Florida's protection-order statutes have not moved. The injunction for protection against domestic violence is in section 741.30 of the Florida Statutes, with domestic violence defined in section 741.28. Injunctions against repeat violence, sexual violence and dating violence are in section 784.046, and stalking injunctions are in section 784.0485. All three were amended in 2024-2026, most recently effective July 1, 2026 (sections 741.28 and 741.30) and July 1, 2025 (sections 784.046 and 784.0485), but kept their numbers. Of these, only the domestic-violence injunction may award the victim exclusive use and possession of a shared home. None of these statutes gives a tenant a lease right against a landlord (see "No Domestic Violence Lease Termination Right").

title: How a Florida Deposit Must Be Held
bodyText:
Florida gives you three ways to hold a security deposit or advance rent (other than rent for the next rental period), and you must use one.
- (1) A separate non-interest-bearing account in a Florida financial institution, for the tenant's benefit.
- (2) A separate interest-bearing account in a Florida financial institution, in which case the tenant receives interest of at least 75 percent of the account's annualized average rate, or 5 percent a year simple interest, as you choose.
- (3) A surety bond filed with the clerk of the circuit court in the county where the unit is, in the total amount of the deposits and advance rent you hold or $50,000, whichever is less, and you then pay the tenant 5 percent a year simple interest; a landlord renting in five or more counties may instead file one bond with the Secretary of State for the total held or $250,000, whichever is less.

With either account you may not commingle the money with your own or pledge or use it until it is actually due to you. Where interest is owed, pay it to the tenant or credit it against the current month's rent at least once a year; a tenant who wrongfully ends the tenancy early gets none.

If you rent five or more units, you must tell the tenant in writing, in the lease or within 30 days, where the money is held and whether interest is paid, using the statutory notice (see "Security Deposit and Advance Rent Notice" clause). A real estate broker holding a rental deposit complies by following this section.

The library's clause for choosing the method is "Security Deposit: Holding Method and Vacating Notice" clause.

title: Deposits When the Property Is Sold
bodyText: When a Florida rental property is sold or title passes to a new owner, or when you change the designated rental agent, every security deposit and advance rent being held for the tenants must be transferred to the new owner or agent, together with any earned interest and an accurate accounting showing the amount credited to each tenant. Once the funds and records are transferred and a written receipt for them is given, the former owner or agent is released from the duty to hold the money. A new owner or agent is presumed to have received each tenant's deposit from the previous owner or agent, but that presumption is limited to 1 month's rent, and the transfer does not excuse any earlier violation by whoever held the deposit. If you are buying, get the accounting and the funds at closing; if you are selling, get the buyer's written receipt.

title: What Happens If You Break the Deposit Rules
bodyText: Florida's deposit statute has no double or triple damages. Its consequences are these. If you don't send the written claim notice within 30 days after the lease ends, by certified mail to the tenant's last known address or by e-mail under a signed electronic-notice addendum, you forfeit the right to impose a claim on the deposit and may not set off against it; you must return it, though you may still sue the tenant for damages afterward. In any lawsuit over the deposit, the winner recovers court costs plus a reasonable attorney's fee, and the court must advance the case on its calendar. A bonded landlord's surety bond runs to the Governor for the benefit of any tenant injured by a violation. A landlord holding a public lodging license (for example an apartment building licensed as a nontransient apartment) who fails to comply with the Act may be fined, or have the license suspended or revoked, by the Division of Hotels and Restaurants. Beyond these, a tenant may recover the actual damages any breach of the Act causes. Missing the 5-unit notice of where the deposit is held is not a defense to paying rent.

title: Tenant's Move-Out Notice and the Deposit Clock
bodyText:
Florida's deposit deadlines run from the end of the lease once the tenant vacates: 15 days to return the deposit if you won't claim against it, or 30 days to send the written claim notice.

A tenant who vacates or abandons before the end of the term, or who leaves a periodic tenancy, must give you at least 7 days' written notice by certified mail or personal delivery before leaving, including an address where the tenant can be reached, unless a written lease provides otherwise. If the tenant doesn't give that notice, you are relieved of the claim-notice requirement, but the tenant keeps any right to the deposit.

Florida doesn't define when a unit is "returned" for this purpose beyond vacating, so the cautious course is to start counting the day the tenant moves out and gives up possession, ask for a forwarding address in writing, and send any claim notice to the tenant's last known mailing address by certified mail. The library's clause carrying the 7-day notice duty is "Security Deposit: Holding Method and Vacating Notice" clause.

title: Quick Resolution of Deposit Disputes
bodyText: No Florida statute sets a separate fast-track procedure for deposit disputes, but the deposit statute speeds them up in two ways. First, the deposit timetable is short: return within 15 days if you won't claim, or send the claim notice within 30 days; the tenant then has 15 days to object in writing, and without an objection you deduct your claim and send the balance within 30 days after your notice. Second, if either side sues to decide who is entitled to the deposit, the court must advance the case on its calendar, and the winner recovers court costs and a reasonable attorney's fee. The deposit notice the statute requires also tells both sides to try to resolve a dispute informally before suing. Small claims procedure is set by court rules. If a tenant abandons the unit, the same timetable applies from the end of the tenancy; see "Tenant's Move-Out Notice and the Deposit Clock".

title: Last Month's Rent Collected in Advance
bodyText:
In Florida, last month's rent you collect at signing is "advance rent": money paid to be applied to a future rent period, as opposed to rent paid ahead for the current period. Advance rent for any period other than the next immediate one is treated like a security deposit for holding purposes: it must be kept in one of the three ways the statute allows (separate account or surety bond; see "How a Florida Deposit Must Be Held"), and if you rent five or more units it must be disclosed in the deposit notice.

You may move advance rent from the deposit account to yourself when the rental period it covers begins, without notice to the tenant. Because it is earmarked for that month, apply it to that month; don't use it to cover damage.

Florida does not stop you from collecting both a security deposit and last month's rent, and sets no cap on either. The library's clause listing amounts due at signing is "Amounts Due Upfront" clause.

title: Paying a Deposit in Installments
bodyText: Florida provides for paying a security deposit in installments only inside the fee-in-lieu-of-deposit program. If you offer that program, you may let a participating tenant pay the deposit in monthly installments in an amount you agree on, and your written notice of the program must tell the tenant that the tenant may choose to do so while participating (see "Fee in Lieu of Security Deposit" clause). Outside that program, no Florida statute requires or limits installment payment of a deposit; you may agree to it in writing. Money received in installments is still deposit money and must be held as the statute requires from the time you receive it (see "How a Florida Deposit Must Be Held").

title: Preset Cleaning and Carpet Charges
bodyText: Florida's statutes say nothing about preset cleaning or carpet charges against a deposit: none lets a lease fix them in advance with a special notice, and none bars them. What controls a deduction is the deposit procedure: within 30 days after the lease ends you must send written notice of the claim and the reason, in the statutory form; the tenant has 15 days to object; and in a dispute the court decides what you may keep. A deposit secures the tenant's performance of the lease, including damage caused by the tenant's breach, so the cautious course is to charge cleaning or carpet costs only to the extent the unit is left dirtier or more damaged than at move-in, beyond ordinary wear, and to claim the actual cost, as the library's deposit clause provides ("Use of Security Deposit" clause). A flat charge set in advance may be attacked as unconscionable or as a penalty under case law.

title: Posting Deposit Standards
bodyText: No Florida statute requires a landlord, however many units it has, to post or hand out the standards it uses to set security deposits, and none limits the amount (see "No Security Deposit Cap"). What limits you is fair-housing law: you may not set different deposit terms because of race, color, national origin, sex, disability, familial status or religion (see "Fair Housing"), and you may not require a deposit or extra charge for a service animal or for an emotional support animal you have approved as a reasonable accommodation (see "Pet Deposits, Pet Fees and Pet Rent"). Cautious course: apply one written deposit policy to all applicants for comparable units and keep it on file.

title: Nonrefundable Deposits and Fees
bodyText: Florida has no statute regulating nonrefundable fees in a residential lease or requiring a notice for them, with one exception: in the fee-in-lieu-of-deposit program, your written notice must say whether the fee is nonrefundable (see "Fee in Lieu of Security Deposit" clause). Calling money "nonrefundable" doesn't take it outside the deposit rules if it is really held as security. Florida defines deposit money broadly, to include damage deposits, security deposits, advance rent, pet deposits and any contractual deposit agreed between you and the tenant, in writing or orally, and a security deposit is any money held as security for the tenant's performance of the lease. So money you hold to cover damage or unpaid rent must be held, accounted for and returned under the deposit statute, whatever the lease calls it. A true fee (for example an application or move-in fee) is a charge, not a deposit; state its amount and purpose in the lease and say it is not refundable. Don't label any part of a security deposit nonrefundable.

title: Separate Notice of Nonrefundable Charges
bodyText: Florida does not require a nonrefundable fee to be disclosed in a separate notice or document, or to be separately signed or initialed. The only nonrefundable disclosure in Florida's landlord-tenant law is the fee-in-lieu-of-deposit notice, which must state in writing whether the program fee is nonrefundable; the fee-in-lieu agreement itself must be in writing and signed by both of you (see "Fee in Lieu of Security Deposit" clause). For any other nonrefundable fee, list it by name, amount and purpose in the lease and say it is not refundable (see "Nonrefundable Deposits and Fees"). Remember that money held as security is always deposit money, whatever the paperwork calls it.

title: State Licence for Apartment Buildings
bodyText: Florida has no general landlord registry, but an apartment property large enough to be a "public lodging establishment" must be licensed by the Division of Hotels and Restaurants of the Department of Business and Professional Regulation. A building or complex rented to tenants for periods of at least 30 days is a nontransient public lodging establishment, and one in which 75 percent or more of the units are available for nontransient tenants is classified as a nontransient apartment. Excluded are places renting four or fewer units (unless held out to the public for transient stays) and condominium, cooperative or timeshare units and one- to four-family houses rented for at least 30 days or a calendar month and not advertised or held out as regularly rented for less than a month, as long as no more than four rental units in a single complex are available. If your property needs a licence, you must get it before you start renting, renew it every year, display it in the office or lobby, keep an online account with the Division, and pay a fee set by rule based on the number of units (up to $1,000 a year, not counting an initial or change-of-ownership fee or a late-renewal fee, each up to $50). Operating without one is a second-degree misdemeanor, and a licensee who fails to comply with the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act may be fined or have the licence suspended or revoked. Owners of houses and small buildings need no state licence to rent long-term, though anyone renting under a business name other than their own legal name must register it as a fictitious name before doing business under it, and cannot bring any suit until it is registered (see "Squatters, Cash Receipts and Registration"). Florida has no statute requiring an out-of-state individual owner to hire a local broker or agent, but an out-of-state limited liability company that owns income-producing property here must obtain a certificate of authority naming a Florida registered agent (see "Out-of-State Landlords: Agents, Service and Foreign LLCs"). Anyone who rents or manages property for others for pay generally needs a Florida real estate licence (see the same row). Whether a city or county rental-registration program survives the state's preemption depends on what it regulates (see "State Preemption of Local Landlord-Tenant Rules").

title: State Inspections of Apartment Buildings
bodyText: Florida's Division of Hotels and Restaurants must inspect each licensed nontransient or transient apartment property at least once a year, and at other times when it decides an inspection is needed for public health, safety and welfare (see "State Licence for Apartment Buildings" for which properties need a licence). For inspections and enforcement, the Division has the right of entry and access to licensed public lodging establishments at any reasonable time. The Division may refuse to issue or renew a licence for an establishment not built and maintained according to law and its rules. Local code inspections are separate and appear to fall outside the state's landlord-tenant preemption to the extent they enforce building, housing and health codes, which Florida requires landlords to comply with and defines to include local ordinances. Florida law does not say whether a lease can make a tenant admit an inspector without separate consent. Your own entry rights are those in the Act: the tenant may not unreasonably withhold consent to entry to inspect, and you may enter with consent, in an emergency, or when consent is unreasonably withheld (see "Notice Before Showings"). Cautious course: tell the tenant in advance when an inspector will come, ask for consent, and accompany the inspector.

title: Housing Vouchers and Source of Income
bodyText: Florida law does not require you to accept housing vouchers, such as Section 8, or bar refusing a tenant because of the source of the tenant's income. Florida's Fair Housing Act protects race, color, national origin, sex, disability, familial status and religion, not source of income. Some counties and cities have adopted ordinances that add source of income as a protected class; a landlord where such an ordinance exists should treat it as enforceable until a court rules otherwise (see "State Preemption of Local Landlord-Tenant Rules"). If you do rent to a voucher holder, the program's lease addendum and rules govern, and Florida's deposit statute does not apply where the amount of rent or deposit is regulated by law or by a public body's rules, including federally regulated housing programs; the cautious course is to keep following the deposit statute unless the program's rules conflict. A refusal policy can't be used as a cover for discrimination against a protected class.

title: State Statement of Tenant Rights
bodyText: Florida has no state-agency statement or summary of tenant rights that you must give tenants, attach to the lease, or have them sign. The closest thing is the deposit disclosure that a landlord renting five or more units must give, in the lease or within 30 days, which ends by telling the tenant that the disclosure is basic and to refer to part II of chapter 83 for their rights and obligations (see "Security Deposit and Advance Rent Notice" clause). The fee-in-lieu-of-deposit agreement carries a similar capitalized disclosure (see "Fee in Lieu of Security Deposit" clause). Cities and counties may not require their own disclosures about the landlord's and tenant's rights and responsibilities, which state law preempts.

title: State Rights and Responsibilities Guide
bodyText: No Florida statute requires you to give a tenant a state-published guide to landlord and tenant rights and responsibilities, before signing or at renewal, or to get a signed acknowledgment of one. The only statutory texts Florida makes you hand over on this subject are the deposit disclosure for landlords of five or more units and the fee-in-lieu disclosure, both of which tell the tenant to refer to the statutes (see "State Statement of Tenant Rights"). Local governments may not add such a requirement.

title: Raising the Rent
bodyText: Florida has no statute setting a notice period for a rent increase in an ordinary residential rental, and it bars local rent control. During a fixed-term lease, the rent is what the lease says; you can't raise it mid-term unless the lease itself provides for the increase. On a month-to-month or other periodic tenancy, Florida's way to change the rent is to end the tenancy by the statutory notice (30 days before the end of a monthly or quarterly period, 7 days for week-to-week, 60 days for year-to-year) and offer a new tenancy at the new rent; the cautious course is to give the rent change in writing at least that far ahead, delivered as the termination notice must be. The 90-day notice of a lot rent increase you may see cited belongs to mobile home parks under chapter 723, not ordinary rentals. During a declared state of emergency, renting a dwelling unit needed as a direct result of the emergency at an unconscionable price is a violation of Florida's consumer-protection law; a gross disparity from the average rent charged in the 30 days before the declaration is prima facie evidence, unless the increase reflects added costs or market trends, and the rule lasts for the initial emergency period (up to 60 days) unless extended by executive order. No city or county may adopt or keep any measure that would impose controls on rents.

title: Changing Lease Terms
bodyText: Florida has no statute setting a notice period for changing the terms of a residential tenancy, whether rent, a fee or another term. During a fixed term, change a term only as the lease provides or by written agreement with the tenant. On a month-to-month or other periodic tenancy, the cautious course is to treat a change as ending the tenancy by the statutory termination notice and offering a new tenancy on the new terms, with the change stated in writing at least that far ahead (see "Raising the Rent"). The Act does require notice for some specific changes: if you change how or where you hold a security deposit or advance rent after giving the deposit notice, you must notify the tenant within 30 days after the change, and either party may change the e-mail address used for electronic notices by written notice. Mobile home parks have their own 90-day notice for rule changes and reductions in services.

title: Screening Applicants
bodyText: Florida has no tenant-screening statute: no rule on when you may run a criminal background check, what look-back periods apply, minimum-income tests or the use of eviction records, and cities and counties may not regulate the screening process landlords use, which state law preempts. The rules that do apply are these. Fair-housing law bars discrimination in renting because of race, color, national origin, sex, disability, familial status or religion (see "Fair Housing"), and requests for emotional support animals have their own documentation rules (see "Service and Emotional Support Animals" clause). If you require a rental application, a servicemember's application must be decided in writing within 7 days (see "Rental Application Fees"). You may not use an applicant's choice to pay a fee in lieu of a deposit as a screening criterion. You may not discriminate against a servicemember in offering a unit for rent or in any lease term. An applicant's credit freeze does not block tenant-screening databases. Florida's background-screening statute for apartment employees covers your staff, not tenants (see "Background Screening of Apartment Employees"). Federal credit-reporting rules on adverse-action notices also apply when a screening report leads you to deny or condition a tenancy.

title: Rental Application Fees
bodyText: Florida sets no cap on rental application or screening fees, requires no refund when an applicant isn't chosen, and requires no advance disclosure of screening criteria, and cities and counties may not regulate application fees or the screening process, which state law preempts. A few state rules still apply to applications. If a servicemember applies and you require an application, you must finish processing it within 7 days and tell the servicemember in writing whether it is approved or denied and, if denied, why; if you don't deny it in time, you must lease to the servicemember if all other terms are met, and these rules can't be waived. If you offer a fee in lieu of a security deposit, you may not use an applicant's choice to pay it, or offer to pay it, as a reason to approve or deny the application. Fair-housing law applies to screening (see "Fair Housing"). An applicant's credit freeze does not block a tenant-screening agency's own database, but where a freeze blocks a credit report you may treat the application as incomplete until the applicant lifts it. Cautious course: charge one stated fee to every applicant, say in writing what it covers, and keep it to what screening actually costs.

title: Holding Deposits Before the Lease
bodyText: Florida has no statute on holding deposits, reservation fees or earnest money taken from an applicant before a lease is signed. Florida's deposit statute speaks of money deposited by a tenant on a rental agreement, and defines deposit money to include any contractual deposit agreed between landlord and tenant in writing or orally, so whether money taken before any lease exists is covered is unsettled. Cautious course: put the terms of any holding deposit in a short signed writing that states the amount, how long you will hold the unit, whether the money becomes part of the security deposit or the first month's rent if the lease is signed, and when it will be refunded or kept if the applicant backs out or is turned down; once a lease is signed, treat any amount carried into the security deposit or advance rent as deposit money held under the statute (see "How a Florida Deposit Must Be Held"). A real estate licensee who receives such a deposit has escrow duties under the licensing rules, which the deposit statute treats as satisfied by compliance with it once a rental agreement exists.

title: Listing Fees in the Lease
bodyText:
Florida does not require a lease to list every fee, to state a total monthly payment, or to give notice before adding a fee, and, apart from the 2-month-rent limit on an agreed early termination fee or liquidated damages (see "Liquidated Damages and Early Termination Fees"), it caps no landlord fee; cities and counties may not regulate fees charged by the landlord.

Two Florida rules still make a complete fee list in the lease worth having.
- First, your right to any fee rests on the lease, and a fee is rent only if the written lease designates it as rent, so a fee the lease doesn't state is hard to collect and can't go into a 3-day notice for unpaid rent (see "Fees and Rent").
- Second, a court may refuse to enforce an unconscionable charge.

The library's clause listing all fees and charges is "Fees and Charges" clause. During a fixed term, you can't add a fee the lease doesn't provide for unless the tenant agrees, and the cautious course is to get that agreement in writing; on a month-to-month tenancy, a new fee is a change of terms (see "Changing Lease Terms").

title: All-In Pricing and Fee Disclosure
bodyText: Florida has no rental fee-transparency or all-in-pricing law: no statute requires the lease or an advertisement to show rent and mandatory fees as one total, to put fees on the first page, or to disclose fees before an application. Local rules on landlord fees are preempted. What does apply is Florida's Deceptive and Unfair Trade Practices Act, which covers the rental of property and makes unfair or deceptive acts in trade or commerce unlawful; it is read in line with federal trade-practice law, and it continues to reach residential tenancies (see "Florida Consumer Protection Law and Leases"). Cautious course: list every mandatory fee in the lease with its amount (the library's "Fees and Charges" clause does this), state any advertised rent together with the mandatory fees, and never charge a fee you didn't disclose.

title: Fees for Services Not Provided
bodyText: No Florida statute specifically bars you from charging a fee for a service you don't provide, such as an amenity, valet trash or a utility the tenant doesn't receive. But a charge with nothing behind it has three problems in Florida: your right to a fee rests on the lease, so a fee for a service the lease promises but you don't deliver is open to challenge as a breach (and the tenant may end the lease after 7 days' written notice if the failure is material); the Deceptive and Unfair Trade Practices Act reaches rental of property (see "Florida Consumer Protection Law and Leases"); and a court may refuse to enforce an unconscionable charge. Cautious course: charge a service or amenity fee only for a service the tenant actually receives or can use, describe it in the lease, and stop charging it if the service ends.

title: Pet Deposits, Pet Fees and Pet Rent
bodyText:
Florida treats a pet deposit as deposit money: it must be held, accounted for and returned under the same rules as a security deposit (see "How a Florida Deposit Must Be Held" and "Florida Security Deposit Rules").

Florida sets no cap on a pet deposit, pet fee or pet rent. Pet rent is rent only if the written lease designates it as rent, which the library's pet clause does ("Pet Policy" clause), so unpaid pet rent can support a 3-day notice for rent, while an unpaid pet fee that isn't designated as rent cannot.

A tenant with a disability who has a service animal is entitled to full and equal access to housing and may not be required to pay extra compensation for the animal, though the tenant is liable for any damage it causes and you may ask for proof of vaccination; that rule does not cover an emotional support animal, whose requests are governed by Florida's emotional-support-animal statute and federal law (see "Service and Emotional Support Animals" clause). That statute also provides that a person allowed to keep an emotional support animal as a reasonable accommodation may not be required to pay extra compensation for it.

Don't charge any pet deposit, fee or rent for a service animal or an approved emotional support animal.

title: Late Fee Limits
bodyText: Florida sets no maximum late fee and no required grace period for residential rentals, and local caps are preempted. The library's late-fee clause lets you set the grace period and amount. A late fee is still subject to the court's power to refuse to enforce an unconscionable term, and it is not rent unless the lease designates it as rent, so don't include it in a 3-day notice for unpaid rent (see "Fees and Rent"). Late-fee caps you may see in Florida law belong to other relationships: condominium, cooperative and homeowners' associations charging owners, and self-storage facilities. A mobile home park may recover late charges on lot rent under its own chapter.

title: Rent Receipts
bodyText: Florida has no general duty to give a tenant a receipt for rent, cash or otherwise, and no general statute giving a debtor the right to demand a receipt from a creditor. There is one receipt rule in the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act: if you accept partial rent after posting a 3-day notice for nonpayment, then before filing for possession you must either give the tenant a receipt stating the date and amount received and the agreed date and balance of rent due, place the partial rent in the court registry when you file, or post a new 3-day notice for the new amount due. Florida also has no rule presuming earlier rent paid when a later receipt is produced. Cautious course: give a written or electronic receipt for every cash payment, and keep a ledger of all payments; in an eviction, the tenant's defense of payment turns on records.

title: Who Keeps the Repair Duty When Rents Are Assigned
bodyText: Some states say that whoever collects the rent keeps the landlord's repair duties, whatever a lease, assignment, deed or mortgage says. Florida has no statute like that. Florida's duties fall on the "landlord", defined as the owner or lessor of the dwelling unit, and the Act's ban on lease waivers keeps a lease from shifting them away (see "Rights a Lease Cannot Waive"). An assignment of rents to a lender is governed by Florida's mortgage statute on assignments of rents, which concerns the lender's right to the rent, not the repair duty. When a condominium or homeowners' association demands that a unit owner's tenant pay rent to it, the association may evict as if it were the landlord, but that statute does not make it the landlord for repairs. Cautious course: if you assign rents or hire a manager, keep the repair duties clearly with the owner or put them on the manager in writing, and give tenants the name and address for notices (see "Landlord's Name and Address" clause).

title: No Lockouts for Unpaid Rent
bodyText: No. Florida forbids you to prevent a tenant from gaining reasonable access to the home by any means, including changing the locks or using a bootlock or similar device, and forbids you to cut off utilities the tenant uses, whether or not you control or pay for them. That holds even if the rent is late and even if the lease has an opt-in lockout clause, which would be void. A violation makes you liable for the tenant's actual and consequential damages or 3 months' rent, whichever is greater, plus costs and attorney's fees, with a separate award for each later violation that is not contemporaneous with the first, and it counts as irreparable harm for an injunction. You may recover possession only through the court eviction procedure, or when the tenant has surrendered or abandoned the unit or, in limited cases, the last remaining tenant has died. After a judgment, the sheriff executes the writ after 24 hours' notice, and you may then change the locks with the sheriff standing by (see "Eviction Notices and Process").

title: Checks Marked 'Paid in Full'
bodyText: Florida follows the Uniform Commercial Code rule on checks marked 'paid in full' (Fla. Stat. § 673.3111). If a tenant, or anyone else you have a claim against, gives you a check or other payment instrument for less than you claim, with a conspicuous statement, on the check or in a writing with it, that it is offered in full satisfaction of the claim, then cashing it settles your whole claim, the unpaid balance included. This applies only when the payment was offered in good faith and the amount was not yet fixed or was subject to a genuine (bona fide) dispute, so writing 'paid in full' on a short check for rent nobody disputes does not by itself settle the rent owed. Writing 'under protest' or 'without prejudice' when you endorse the check does not save the balance: the rule on reserving your rights does not apply to an accord and satisfaction (Fla. Stat. § 671.207(2)). There are two ways out. If you are an organization (for example an LLC) and, within a reasonable time before the check, sent the tenant a conspicuous statement that communications about disputed debts, including checks offered in full satisfaction, must go to a named person, office or place, the claim is not settled if the check or the writing with it was not received there. And whether or not you are an organization, the claim is not settled if you offer to repay the amount of the check within 90 days after it is paid; an organization that sent the statement just described cannot use this second way out. Neither way out works if you, or your agent responsible for the disputed debt, knew within a reasonable time before the check was collected that it was offered in full satisfaction. The cautious course: don't cash a check for less than you claim that is marked as payment in full of a disputed amount; return it, and if one is cashed by mistake, offer the money back within 90 days.

title: Duty of Good Faith
bodyText: Florida's landlord-tenant act imposes a duty of good faith: every rental agreement, and every duty under the residential tenancy part of the statutes, carries an obligation of good faith in its performance or enforcement (Fla. Stat. § 83.44). That binds you and the tenant alike. In practice: give notices, enter, handle the deposit, enforce lease terms and end a tenancy honestly and for the purpose the law or the lease gives you the right, not as a pretext.

title: Offering a Fee in Lieu of a Deposit
bodyText: Whether to offer tenants a fee in lieu of a security deposit is up to you; you don't have to offer one. If you offer it to a tenant, you may not use a prospective tenant's choice to pay, or offer to pay, the fee as a reason to approve or deny an application, and you must offer the option to all new tenants renting a unit on the same premises, unless you end the fee option for all new rental agreements going forward. The agreement must be in writing and signed by you or your agent and by the tenant. The library's clause is "Fee in Lieu of Security Deposit" clause.

title: Passing Government Rental Fees to the Tenant
bodyText: Florida law neither requires nor bars passing a government fee on to a residential tenant, so the tenant pays one only if the lease says so. If you want the tenant to reimburse fees that apply specifically to renting the property, such as a rental registration, rental license or rental inspection fee, use the optional clause "Government Fees on the Rental".

title: Government Fines the Tenant Caused
bodyText: Florida has no statute deciding whether a landlord may pass a government fine on to the tenant who caused it, so the tenant pays one only if the lease says so. The optional clause "Government Fines Caused by Tenant" covers fines and repair or abatement charges for a condition the tenant, a household member or a guest caused.
